The touch-screen MacBook Pro will retain a full trackpad and keyboard — mirroring the approach of PC makers like Dell Technologies Inc., Acer Inc., Lenovo Group Ltd. and Microsoft Corp.
That means users won’t have to rely on the touch display if they don’t want to.
For the revamped MacBook Pro, Apple is retiring the “notch” — the cutout at the top of the screen that houses the camera.
In its place, the company will adopt a so-called hole-punch design that leaves a display area around the sensor.
The company has also developed a reinforced hinge and screen hardware to prevent the display from bouncing back or moving when touched, a common drawback of existing touch PCs.
Because of the pricier components, the new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros are likely to cost a few hundred dollars more than current versions.
Today’s non-touch models with high-end chips start at $1,999 for the 14-inch version and $2,499 for the larger one.
The current MacBook Pro design dates back to 2021, though Apple refreshed the 14-inch base version with an M5 chip on Wednesday.
The company is planning M5 Pro and M5 Max iterations for early 2026 that retain the current look, Bloomberg News has reported.
As of now, Apple isn’t actively developing additional touch-screen Macs.
Instead, it’s waiting to see the market’s reaction to the touch version of the MacBook Pro, the people said.
This follows a typical strategy for Apple, which offers new features on its top-end devices before bringing them down-market.
For years, Apple resisted the idea of touch-screen Macs, arguing that PCs with the feature were difficult to use and not ergonomic.
It instead pushed users who want touch interfaces to buy iPads.
The late Jobs, then Apple’s chief executive officer, said in 2010 that “touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical,” suggesting that they wouldn’t make sense for a computer screen.
Apple tried a compromise in 2016 with the Touch Bar, a touch-screen strip that sat above the keyboard.
There have been concerns within Apple that touch-screen computers would cannibalize sales of iPads.
But tablet growth has already slowed in recent years, and touch screens have increasingly become must-have features for PCs.
And Apple has bridged the gap between iPads and Macs in other ways: The devices now have unified interfaces, processors and app ecosystems.
Apple’s iPad Magic Keyboard, introduced in 2020, also showed that customers were interested in combining a touch display with a traditional keyboard and trackpad.
The accessory has become central to the iPad Pro’s sales pitch, letting users easily shift between touch and traditional controls.
Adding a touch screen to the MacBook Pro could push users upmarket, creating new revenue opportunities for Apple.
While the $999 MacBook Air remains the company’s bestselling laptop, a high-end touch-enabled MacBook Pro might entice customers to trade up — or switch from a Windows PC.
Other new Macs in development include updated MacBook Airs with the M5 chip.
The company is also working on a refreshed Mac Studio, Mac mini, and a pair of external Mac monitors dubbed J427 and J527.
Apple is exploring another major Mac change as well: a shift from the Touch ID fingerprint scanner to Face ID.

extraction.body: (Bloomberg) -- After two decades of spurning the idea, Apple Inc. unveiled an overhauled MacBook Pro that includes a touch screen, giving its flagship laptop a feature that has become a must-have in the personal computer industry. The thinner and lighter machine, which comes in 14- and 16-inch sizes, is also the first Mac with OLED — short for organic light-emitting diode — a display technology used on recent iPhones, iPads and other Apple devices. It’s also the first Mac with a Dynamic Island, the screen element familiar to iPhone users.The computer has a redesigned software interface optimized for touch and is offered with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. The 14-inch version is priced from $2,899, while the 16-inch model starts at $3,399. A maxed-out version with 16 terabytes of storage and 128 gigabytes of memory costs $14,549.Johny Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer, called the new machine a “monumental step forward for the Mac.” It was introduced on stage by new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus, who took the reins from Tim Cook last month. Customers have been prodding the company for years to embrace touch displays, which the iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch helped popularize. But Apple had to overcome some deep-seated opposition that has existed for nearly two decades. Co-founder Steve Jobs famously lambasted touch Macs in the later stages of his career, once calling them “ergonomically terrible.” Cook, his successor, said combining a laptop and tablet would be like merging a fridge and toaster. Other company executives laughed at the idea in interviews.But about four years ago Cook and Ternus became proponents of ditching past orthodoxy and moving to a touch display on the MacBook Pro, Bloomberg News has reported. The hope is to give the Mac new momentum and raise revenue with higher prices driven by more premium features.Still, Apple is releasing the new machines at a turbulent time for the laptop market. Higher memory chip prices have increased computer prices and hurt demand, sending the industry into a downward spiral. Global PC shipments tumbled 20% in the third quarter, according to researcher IDC. Apple suffered its own decline in the period, though it wasn’t as severe as the industry average.The new 14-inch MacBook Pro weighs 3 pounds, down from 3.5 on the non-touch model, while the 16-inch version now comes in at 4 pounds. That’s down from 4.7 pounds on the prior generation. It also has an Apple logo that lights up on the back, marking the return of an old feature. Bloomberg News first reported in January 2023 on Apple’s plans to bring touch screens to the MacBook Pro and subsequently detailed the new displays, software interface, processors, pricing and design changes.Earlier this week, Apple launched a new low-end MacBook Pro with an M6 chip and 14-inch screen, an updated iMac and an overhauled iPad mini with an OLED screen and higher price. The launches cap a strong new product year for Apple, which put the iPhone Duo on sale last Friday. (Updated with more product details starting in third paragraph.)More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

sources.title: Apple adds touchscreen to MacBook Pro, reversing Jobs-era stance - Chosunbiz
passages: Apple unveiled the first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen in Mac history.
After 20 years of refusing to add a touchscreen since the MacBook's 2006 launch, Apple changed course under new CEO John Turnus.
Apple founder Steve Jobs once said, "Touchscreen notebooks are ergonomically terrible."
Apple had long been negative about adding touchscreens to laptops.

2010, founder Jobs said, "Touch surfaces don't want to be vertical," adding, "After a short period, you start to fatigue, and after an extended period, your arm wants to fall off." He called them "ergonomically terrible" and kept touchscreens off the Mac.
The 14-inch model of the touchscreen MacBook Pro weighs 1.38 kg, down 220 g from its predecessor, and the 16-inch model weighs 1.82 kg, 320 g lighter, improving portability.
Unified memory goes up to 128GB, and storage up to 16TB.
Apple will begin preorders today in 30 countries, including the United States, and on the 30th in Korea.
Apple said it reduced latency by integrating the touch sensor into the panel itself rather than placing it on top of the display.

extraction.body: Apple unveiled the first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen in Mac history. After 20 years of refusing to add a touchscreen since the MacBook's 2006 launch, Apple changed course under new CEO John Turnus. Apple founder Steve Jobs once said, "Touchscreen notebooks are ergonomically terrible." On the 28th (local time), Apple held a product launch event in Los Angeles, California, and unveiled 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros equipped with a touchscreen and M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. CEO Turnus said, "That's right. We are bringing touch to the Mac for the first time." Johny Srouji, Apple's chief hardware officer (CHO), said, "By introducing touch to MacBook Pro, we created a completely new way for pro users to interact with content." Apple had long been negative about adding touchscreens to laptops. At the "Back to the Mac" event in Oct. 2010, founder Jobs said, "Touch surfaces don't want to be vertical," adding, "After a short period, you start to fatigue, and after an extended period, your arm wants to fall off." He called them "ergonomically terrible" and kept touchscreens off the Mac. Bloomberg reported, "Former CEO Tim Cook and CEO Turnus thought customers had begun to expect a touchscreen on the Mac," adding, "But Apple's industrial design team still opposed the idea." It said the touchscreen MacBook ultimately emerged as a compromise: keeping the keyboard and trackpad as the primary input while using touch as a secondary method when needed. Apple said it reduced latency by integrating the touch sensor into the panel itself rather than placing it on top of the display. The 14-inch model of the touchscreen MacBook Pro weighs 1.38 kg, down 220 g from its predecessor, and the 16-inch model weighs 1.82 kg, 320 g lighter, improving portability. Battery life is up to 24 hours. Unified memory goes up to 128GB, and storage up to 16TB. Prices start at $2,899 for the 14-inch M5 Pro model and $3,399 for the 16-inch. The M5 Max model starts at $4,499 for the 14-inch and $4,799 for the 16-inch. Apple will begin preorders today in 30 countries, including the United States, and on the 30th in Korea. It goes on sale on Nov. 6.

extraction.body: Apple Inc. is preparing to finally launch a touch-screen version of its Mac computer, reversing course on a stance that dates back to co-founder Steve Jobs. The company is readying a revamped MacBook Pro with a touch display for late 2026 or early 2027, according to people with knowledge of the matter. In making the move, Apple is following the rest of the computing industry, which embraced touch-screen laptops more than a decade ago. The company has taken years to formulate its approach to the market, aiming to improve on current designs. Bloomberg News first reported in January 2023 that Apple was working on a touch-screen MacBook Pro. The new laptops will feature displays with OLED technology — short for organic light-emitting diode — the same standard used in iPhones and iPad Pros, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the products haven’t been announced. A spokesperson for Cupertino, Calif.a-based Apple declined to comment. Apple shares pared their losses Thursday after Bloomberg reported on the plans. The touch-screen MacBook Pro will retain a full trackpad and keyboard — mirroring the approach of PC makers like Dell Technologies Inc., Acer Inc., Lenovo Group Ltd. and Microsoft Corp. That means users won’t have to rely on the touch display if they don’t want to. For the revamped MacBook Pro, Apple is retiring the “notch” — the cutout at the top of the screen that houses the camera. In its place, the company will adopt a so-called hole-punch design that leaves a display area around the sensor. The company has also developed a reinforced hinge and screen hardware to prevent the display from bouncing back or moving when touched, a common drawback of existing touch PCs. Because of the pricier components, the new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros are likely to cost a few hundred dollars more than current versions. Today’s non-touch models with high-end chips start at $1,999 for the 14-inch version and $2,499 for the larger one. The current MacBook Pro design dates back to 2021, though Apple refreshed the 14-inch base version with an M5 chip on Wednesday. The company is planning M5 Pro and M5 Max iterations for early 2026 that retain the current look, Bloomberg News has reported. As of now, Apple isn’t actively developing additional touch-screen Macs. Instead, it’s waiting to see the market’s reaction to the touch version of the MacBook Pro, the people said. This follows a typical strategy for Apple, which offers new features on its top-end devices before bringing them down-market. For years, Apple resisted the idea of touch-screen Macs, arguing that PCs with the feature were difficult to use and not ergonomic. It instead pushed users who want touch interfaces to buy iPads. The late Jobs, then Apple’s chief executive officer, said in 2010 that “touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical,” suggesting that they wouldn’t make sense for a computer screen. Apple tried a compromise in 2016 with the Touch Bar, a touch-screen strip that sat above the keyboard. There have been concerns within Apple that touch-screen computers would cannibalize sales of iPads. But tablet growth has already slowed in recent years, and touch screens have increasingly become must-have features for PCs. And Apple has bridged the gap between iPads and Macs in other ways: The devices now have unified interfaces, processors and app ecosystems. Apple’s iPad Magic Keyboard, introduced in 2020, also showed that customers were interested in combining a touch display with a traditional keyboard and trackpad. The accessory has become central to the iPad Pro’s sales pitch, letting users easily shift between touch and traditional controls. Adding a touch screen to the MacBook Pro could push users upmarket, creating new revenue opportunities for Apple. While the $999 MacBook Air remains the company’s bestselling laptop, a high-end touch-enabled MacBook Pro might entice customers to trade up — or switch from a Windows PC. Other new Macs in development include updated MacBook Airs with the M5 chip. The company is also working on a refreshed Mac Studio, Mac mini, and a pair of external Mac monitors dubbed J427 and J527. Apple is exploring another major Mac change as well: a shift from the Touch ID fingerprint scanner to Face ID.

It’s also the first Mac with a Dynamic Island, the screen element familiar to iPhone users.The computer has a redesigned software interface optimized for touch and is offered with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. The 14-inch version is priced from $2,899, while the 16-inch model starts at $3,399. A maxed-out version with 16 terabytes of storage and 128 gigabytes of memory costs $14,549.Johny Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer, called the new machine a “monumental step forward for the Mac.” It was introduced on stage by new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus, who took the reins from Tim Cook last month. Other company executives laughed at the idea in interviews.But about four years ago Cook and Ternus became proponents of ditching past orthodoxy and moving to a touch display on the MacBook Pro, Bloomberg News has reported. The hope is to give the Mac new momentum and raise revenue with higher prices driven by more premium features.Still, Apple is releasing the new machines at a turbulent time for the laptop market. Higher memory chip prices have increased computer prices and hurt demand, sending the industry into a downward spiral. Global PC shipments tumbled 20% in the third quarter, according to researcher IDC. Apple suffered its own decline in the period, though it wasn’t as severe as the industry average.The new 14-inch MacBook Pro weighs 3 pounds, down from 3.5 on the non-touch model, while the 16-inch version now comes in at 4 pounds. That’s down from 4.7 pounds on the prior generation. It also has an Apple logo that lights up on the back, marking the return of an old feature. The thinner and lighter machine, which comes in 14- and 16-inch sizes, is also the first Mac with OLED — short for organic light-emitting diode — a display technology used on recent iPhones, iPads and other Apple devices.

It’s also the first Mac with a Dynamic Island, the screen element familiar to iPhone users.The computer has a redesigned software interface optimized for touch and is offered with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.
The 14-inch version is priced from $2,899, while the 16-inch model starts at $3,399.

A maxed-out version with 16 terabytes of storage and 128 gigabytes of memory costs $14,549.Johny Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer, called the new machine a “monumental step forward for the Mac.” It was introduced on stage by new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus, who took the reins from Tim Cook last month.
Customers have been prodding the company for years to embrace touch displays, which the iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch helped popularize.
But Apple had to overcome some deep-seated opposition that has existed for nearly two decades.

Co-founder Steve Jobs famously lambasted touch Macs in the later stages of his career, once calling them “ergonomically terrible.” Cook, his successor, said combining a laptop and tablet would be like merging a fridge and toaster.

Other company executives laughed at the idea in interviews.But about four years ago Cook and Ternus became proponents of ditching past orthodoxy and moving to a touch display on the MacBook Pro, Bloomberg News has reported.
The hope is to give the Mac new momentum and raise revenue with higher prices driven by more premium features.Still, Apple is releasing the new machines at a turbulent time for the laptop market.
Higher memory chip prices have increased computer prices and hurt demand, sending the industry into a downward spiral.
Global PC shipments tumbled 20% in the third quarter, according to researcher IDC.

Apple suffered its own decline in the period, though it wasn’t as severe as the industry average.The new 14-inch MacBook Pro weighs 3 pounds, down from 3.5 on the non-touch model, while the 16-inch version now comes in at 4 pounds.
That’s down from 4.7 pounds on the prior generation.
It also has an Apple logo that lights up on the back, marking the return of an old feature.

Bloomberg News first reported in January 2023 on Apple’s plans to bring touch screens to the MacBook Pro and subsequently detailed the new displays, software interface, processors, pricing and design changes.Earlier this week, Apple launched a new low-end MacBook Pro with an M6 chip and 14-inch screen, an updated iMac and an overhauled iPad mini with an OLED screen and higher price.

The launches cap a strong new product year for Apple, which put the iPhone Duo on sale last Friday. (Updated with more product details starting in third paragraph.)More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

extraction.body: Apple unveiled the first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen in Mac history. After 20 years of refusing to add a touchscreen since the MacBook's 2006 launch, Apple changed course under new CEO John Turnus. Apple founder Steve Jobs once said, "Touchscreen notebooks are ergonomically terrible." On the 28th (local time), Apple held a product launch event in Los Angeles, California, and unveiled 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros equipped with a touchscreen and M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. CEO Turnus said, "That's right. We are bringing touch to the Mac for the first time." Johny Srouji, Apple's chief hardware officer (CHO), said, "By introducing touch to MacBook Pro, we created a completely new way for pro users to interact with content." Apple had long been negative about adding touchscreens to laptops. At the "Back to the Mac" event in Oct. 2010, founder Jobs said, "Touch surfaces don't want to be vertical," adding, "After a short period, you start to fatigue, and after an extended period, your arm wants to fall off." He called them "ergonomically terrible" and kept touchscreens off the Mac. Bloomberg reported, "Former CEO Tim Cook and CEO Turnus thought customers had begun to expect a touchscreen on the Mac," adding, "But Apple's industrial design team still opposed the idea." It said the touchscreen MacBook ultimately emerged as a compromise: keeping the keyboard and trackpad as the primary input while using touch as a secondary method when needed. Apple said it reduced latency by integrating the touch sensor into the panel itself rather than placing it on top of the display. The 14-inch model of the touchscreen MacBook Pro weighs 1.38 kg, down 220 g from its predecessor, and the 16-inch model weighs 1.82 kg, 320 g lighter, improving portability. Battery life is up to 24 hours. Unified memory goes up to 128GB, and storage up to 16TB. Prices start at $2,899 for the 14-inch M5 Pro model and $3,399 for the 16-inch. The M5 Max model starts at $4,499 for the 14-inch and $4,799 for the 16-inch. Apple will begin preorders today in 30 countries, including the United States, and on the 30th in Korea. It goes on sale on Nov. 6.

sources.title: Hands-on with Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro
passages: The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display weighs just 3 pounds, which is noticeably lighter than the current generation of non-touch MacBook Pros, which start at 3.4 pounds for the newly introduced M6 models.
Touch works almost exactly like you’d expect it to with Apple’s first-party apps.
Steve Jobs famously called touchscreen laptops “ergonomically terrible,” and for over a decade, Apple stridently refused to make one.
Today that all changes with the MacBook Pro — the company’s first laptop to embrace a touch interface.
That’s why it’s just a MacBook Pro variant and not an entirely new product line.
And while MacBook Pro hinges are pretty solid, yes, you can make it wobble pretty easily with some firm taps toward the top of the screen.
While it’s unlikely that Apple can fix all the “terrible” ergonomics of having to lift your arm up and touch a laptop screen, the company has put some effort into making macOS more touch-friendly.

Apple is trying to address this, at least slightly, by magnifying some controls when you poke at them — like the red, yellow, and green traffic light buttons in the top left corner of windows to close, minimize, and maximize an app.
On first impression, at least, the touchscreen doesn’t seem likely to revolutionize the MacBook.

extraction.body: Steve Jobs famously called touchscreen laptops “ergonomically terrible,” and for over a decade, Apple stridently refused to make one. Today that all changes with the MacBook Pro — the company’s first laptop to embrace a touch interface. While it’s unlikely that Apple can fix all the “terrible” ergonomics of having to lift your arm up and touch a laptop screen, the company has put some effort into making macOS more touch-friendly. The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display weighs just 3 pounds, which is noticeably lighter than the current generation of non-touch MacBook Pros, which start at 3.4 pounds for the newly introduced M6 models. The difference is even bigger when you jump to the 16-inch model, which clocks in at 4 pounds, while the M5 Pro version without a touchscreen is 4.7. It still has heft, but it feels better balanced when picking it up from a corner with one hand. Putting it side by side with a current 16-inch MacBook Pro, you see that it’s slightly thinner and has a footprint a smidge smaller. It’s a seemingly minor feature, but one that definitely got the audience excited during the introduction, and marks the return of a bit of flair to the MacBook lineup, which, let’s be fair, has grown a bit utilitarian-looking over the years. Touch works almost exactly like you’d expect it to with Apple’s first-party apps. That said, anyone who has tried to “click” a tiny button in an app with their finger knows it’s a pretty fiddly experience at best and infuriating at worst. Apple is trying to address this, at least slightly, by magnifying some controls when you poke at them — like the red, yellow, and green traffic light buttons in the top left corner of windows to close, minimize, and maximize an app. And while MacBook Pro hinges are pretty solid, yes, you can make it wobble pretty easily with some firm taps toward the top of the screen. The OLED is punchy, bright, contrasty, and saturated. Without more time to do side-by-side comparisons, it’s hard to tell just how much of an improvement the OLED XDR display is. On first impression, at least, the touchscreen doesn’t seem likely to revolutionize the MacBook. That’s why it’s just a MacBook Pro variant and not an entirely new product line. Unsurprisingly, there is a price premium for the new MacBook Pro PROLED XDR. The touchscreen OLED model starts at $2,899, $400 more than the otherwise similarly-specced M5 Pro MacBook Pro.

passages: I’m looking forward to spending more time with the new MacBook Pro, but for right now, it seems to follow in the lineup’s existing tradition: impressively high-end components like an outstanding OLED panel, but a very steep price to match.
Though after well over a decade of speculation and back-and-forth, you’d be forgiven for being surprised that the touchscreen thing actually finally happened.
But while it’s not about the touchscreen capability for me, I was impressed by the OLED screen itself—and I’m quite the display snob, if I’m being honest.
The peak brightness, absolute blacks, well-balanced color, and dynamic range were genuinely remarkable.

extraction.body: It’s not as different from the previous model as you might have expected. LOS ANGELES—For about five minutes on an extremely crowded showroom floor, I got to take pictures of the new MacBook Pro and test out some of its new features. First impressions: It’s not as much of a departure from the previous design as I expected, but the outstanding OLED display steals the show regardless. The first thing I noticed was that it’s lighter. My daily driver is a 14-inch MacBook Pro (M1 Max), and it’s a bit weighty for a 14-incher. Picking up the new model, I could immediately tell it was lighter. It’s not like it’s in a different general weight class, but it’s a noticeable difference. The next thing I noticed was the Dynamic Island. Given the larger screen real estate of a laptop, it’s much less dominant on the screen than it is on an iPhone. I do worry about what will happen with fullscreen games, which I wasn’t able to test today. The notch MacBook Pro has an option to maximize apps or games to just below the notch, so it doesn’t cut into the image. I’m curious to test in the full review whether that remains the case with this little cutout. And lastly, the Apple logo on the back glows again! Some find this tacky, some find it essential. I just think it’s a little bit nostalgic. Of course, you might make the case that the most notable thing about this laptop is not its weight or the Dynamic Island. For years, people have debated whether Apple should introduce a touchscreen laptop. Steve Jobs was famously against it. A few years ago—there were reports that under Tim Cook and now John Ternus—Apple decided to move ahead with the idea. I played with it a bit, and it works just about exactly as you expect for a laptop touchscreen. A few of the things I did with the touchscreen during my brief time with the laptop: All of that is nice to have, I guess, but there’s not much you can do with it that you couldn’t already do with trackpad gestures, at least at the OS level; some creative apps, like finger painting on the screen, seemed to offer a bit more. When the credible reports emerged that the MacBook Pro would get a touchscreen, I imagined a convertible with Apple Pencil support—something you could use as a large iPad or drawing tablet, essentially. That’s not what this is; it only takes the usual laptop shape, and I was told it does not support the Apple Pencil. It’s just a MacBook Pro, in its normal form factor, but you can use your fingers on the screen to do things like drag files around, swipe between desktop spaces, or pinch-to-zoom on maps or images. But while it’s not about the touchscreen capability for me, I was impressed by the OLED screen itself—and I’m quite the display snob, if I’m being honest. The peak brightness, absolute blacks, well-balanced color, and dynamic range were genuinely remarkable. It’s an enormous upgrade over the MiniLED screen in the previous MacBook Pro. It took far too long for OLED to come to the MacBook Pro, but unsurprisingly, Apple spared no expense and cut no immediately obvious corners on quality. I was also happy to see that the cutout near the top of the screen that has replaced the camera notch is what Apple calls a Dynamic Island; it can resize to show live activities and other information on the fly. That’s one of my favorite features on the iPhone, as I’ve been impressed with Apple’s ability to turn something that should be an albatross into an appealing feature. Based on my time with the device and today’s announcement, the screen seems to be the main draw (though it’s nice that it noticeably weighs less, too), but the price is the real barrier. A 16-inch model with an M5 Max, 64 GB of RAM, and 2 TB of storage is currently priced at $5,799. Sure, that’s a high-end spec, but that’s some serious cash. Much of that is due to the storage and memory; upgrading from 64GB to 128GB adds a whopping $1,600 to that. Sure, most people don’t need anywhere near that much RAM—but some might for future-proofing for local AI workflows. I’m looking forward to spending more time with the new MacBook Pro, but for right now, it seems to follow in the lineup’s existing tradition: impressively high-end components like an outstanding OLED panel, but a very steep price to match. No surprises here! Though after well over a decade of speculation and back-and-forth, you’d be forgiven for being surprised that the touchscreen thing actually finally happened. But while it’s not about the touchscreen capability for me, I was impressed by the OLED screen itself—and I’m quite the display snob, if I’m being honest.
The peak brightness, absolute blacks, well-balanced color, and dynamic range were genuinely remarkable.

When the credible reports emerged that the MacBook Pro would get a touchscreen, I imagined a convertible with Apple Pencil support—something you could use as a large iPad or drawing tablet, essentially.

extraction.body: A great-sounding display, but Apple seems out of touch for the touchscreen. Senior Editor / Computers and Gaming Hardware Surpassed only by the iPhone Duo , this year’s most anticipated Apple announcement is its launch of both a 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen display — the company’s last-to-the-party use of both technologies in one of its laptops. And despite the awful name, it’s more than just a fancy new display. It’s really a complete design overhaul that, at least on paper, brings its feature set up to the front of the class for professional content creation, albeit with the same processor options and ports as the other MacBook Pros. Aside from a screen that brings its capabilities more in line with the Studio Display XDR , the new model adds: It doesn’t come cheap, though; as predicted, you pay a $400 premium over the standard models. The 14-inch M5 Pro model starts at $2,899 compared with $2,499 for the same non-OLED version, and the M5 Max model begins at $4,499 compared with $4,099. If you want to upgrade to 16TB, you have to bump to the M5 Max — that’s a minimum buy-in of $11,499 with only 36GB of memory. Preorders started on Wednesday, and systems are slated to start shipping Nov. 6. One of the most popular changes won’t be the whizzy features, but the drop in weight to 3 pounds for the 14-inch model (down from 3.4 pounds) and to 4 pounds (down from 4.7 pounds) for the 16-inch. Also, while Apple updated its sound system to deliver better bass and incorporated Dolby Atmos support to its spatial audio, one of the more notable enhancements is the claimed improvements to the sound when the MacBook is closed. A lot of the traditional advantages of OLED over alternatives like IPS with array backlights — such as a wider color gamut and true blacks — are less pronounced than they used to be. That’s even more true for the current MacBook Pro’s mini-LED-backlit Liquid Retina XDR screens: They already deliver excellent deep blacks and 100% P3 gamut coverage, along with great color accuracy sufficient for prosumer creative work. But the PROLED XDR screen sounds top-notch. While I take Apple’s claim of a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio with 10,000,000 grains of salt — the arithmetic ratio of peak brightness to minimum black isn’t really meaningful, especially beyond about a million — the display has an expanded gamut that covers the Adobe RGB color space and more of Rec. 2020, a space for mastering video. The latter is still only 80%, but at the moment, that’s the best you can get in a laptop display. Peak brightness is also similar to the desktop display at 2,000 nits. As with the current screens, though, you can set the SDR brightness only up to 1,000 nits; above that, it’s automated to compensate only for bright sunlight. That can get frustrating for people like me who find auto- brightness distracting. The display can do 1,000 nits full screen in both SDR and HDR, though. Microsoft’s recently shipped Surface Laptop Ultra also hits 2,000 nits, the first Windows laptop that does, but uses mini-LED. Oddly, Apple still quotes a 1-nit minimum brightness spec, similar to its mini-LED screens, though OLED’s native minimum is a lot lower: Theoretically, it’s zero, but professional colorimeters have measured it a lot lower. That may be because Apple has adopted it as a standard, and possibly clamped it, to tonally match its mini-LED models. Apple also refers to its panel technology generically as “tandem OLED,” which is a little annoying, since there is a raft of tandem OLED types. But it is “state of the art!” There are a couple of potential disappointments, though. For one, the battery life is unchanged. While the MacBook Pro’s battery life has always been good, it’s clear that the OLED display didn’t provide any power savings, or at least savings that weren’t spent elsewhere in the system. Touch looks like the biggest mixed bag, though. The hardware is only a small aspect of the implementation; operating system interfaces like those of iOS and iPadOS are built around considerations like your finger is bigger and fatter than a cursor. Simply porting the mobile interfaces to a laptop isn’t necessarily a solution, either. We use laptops in part because a hardware keyboard is sometimes the best input choice, and even navigating the mobile devices via touch can get annoying, so those interfaces don’t necessarily translate optimally. The point is, a lot is riding on how Apple has adapted MacOS for touch. For instance, the Touch Bar floundered in part because it felt grafted on rather than integral to the OS’ interface, as well as arguably superfluous. And since Apple didn’t launch the capability with MacOS 27 at its developer conference, WWDC , this year, it sounds like the applications will be behind. That’s not something you beta test on a pro-level production system. Pros rely heavily on muscle memory. It should really have launched with a MacBook Air. Plus, to adapt to touchscreen use, Apple had to stiffen the hinge — poking the screen makes that necessary — and add image stabilization to the webcam in case you poke the screen during video calls. Apple seemed like it was really stretching to find meaningful uses for touch. Playing piano on a screen that forces your hand to an awkward angle? No thanks. The one application that sounded like it might be OK was for developers to simulate mobile app interfaces. I was also kind of hoping for increased refresh rates beyond 120Hz or the ability to manually set it above 60Hz. Apple seems to position ProMotion as a power-saving technology rather than for gaming. Apple also seems to think 60fps is a great frame rate, so it’s not surprising. © 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

The hardware is only a small aspect of the implementation; operating system interfaces like those of iOS and iPadOS are built around considerations like your finger is bigger and fatter than a cursor. Simply porting the mobile interfaces to a laptop isn’t necessarily a solution, either.

We use laptops in part because a hardware keyboard is sometimes the best input choice, and even navigating the mobile devices via touch can get annoying, so those interfaces don’t necessarily translate optimally.

The point is, a lot is riding on how Apple has adapted MacOS for touch. For instance, the Touch Bar floundered in part because it felt grafted on rather than integral to the OS’ interface, as well as arguably superfluous.

extraction.body: Steve Jobs famously called touchscreen laptops “ergonomically terrible,” and for over a decade, Apple stridently refused to make one. Today that all changes with the MacBook Pro — the company’s first laptop to embrace a touch interface. While it’s unlikely that Apple can fix all the “terrible” ergonomics of having to lift your arm up and touch a laptop screen, the company has put some effort into making macOS more touch-friendly. The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display weighs just 3 pounds, which is noticeably lighter than the current generation of non-touch MacBook Pros, which start at 3.4 pounds for the newly introduced M6 models. The difference is even bigger when you jump to the 16-inch model, which clocks in at 4 pounds, while the M5 Pro version without a touchscreen is 4.7. It still has heft, but it feels better balanced when picking it up from a corner with one hand. Putting it side by side with a current 16-inch MacBook Pro, you see that it’s slightly thinner and has a footprint a smidge smaller. It’s a seemingly minor feature, but one that definitely got the audience excited during the introduction, and marks the return of a bit of flair to the MacBook lineup, which, let’s be fair, has grown a bit utilitarian-looking over the years. Touch works almost exactly like you’d expect it to with Apple’s first-party apps. That said, anyone who has tried to “click” a tiny button in an app with their finger knows it’s a pretty fiddly experience at best and infuriating at worst. Apple is trying to address this, at least slightly, by magnifying some controls when you poke at them — like the red, yellow, and green traffic light buttons in the top left corner of windows to close, minimize, and maximize an app. And while MacBook Pro hinges are pretty solid, yes, you can make it wobble pretty easily with some firm taps toward the top of the screen. The OLED is punchy, bright, contrasty, and saturated. Without more time to do side-by-side comparisons, it’s hard to tell just how much of an improvement the OLED XDR display is. On first impression, at least, the touchscreen doesn’t seem likely to revolutionize the MacBook. That’s why it’s just a MacBook Pro variant and not an entirely new product line. Unsurprisingly, there is a price premium for the new MacBook Pro PROLED XDR. The touchscreen OLED model starts at $2,899, $400 more than the otherwise similarly-specced M5 Pro MacBook Pro.

extraction.body: It’s not as different from the previous model as you might have expected. LOS ANGELES—For about five minutes on an extremely crowded showroom floor, I got to take pictures of the new MacBook Pro and test out some of its new features. First impressions: It’s not as much of a departure from the previous design as I expected, but the outstanding OLED display steals the show regardless. The first thing I noticed was that it’s lighter. My daily driver is a 14-inch MacBook Pro (M1 Max), and it’s a bit weighty for a 14-incher. Picking up the new model, I could immediately tell it was lighter. It’s not like it’s in a different general weight class, but it’s a noticeable difference. The next thing I noticed was the Dynamic Island. Given the larger screen real estate of a laptop, it’s much less dominant on the screen than it is on an iPhone. I do worry about what will happen with fullscreen games, which I wasn’t able to test today. The notch MacBook Pro has an option to maximize apps or games to just below the notch, so it doesn’t cut into the image. I’m curious to test in the full review whether that remains the case with this little cutout. And lastly, the Apple logo on the back glows again! Some find this tacky, some find it essential. I just think it’s a little bit nostalgic. Of course, you might make the case that the most notable thing about this laptop is not its weight or the Dynamic Island. For years, people have debated whether Apple should introduce a touchscreen laptop. Steve Jobs was famously against it. A few years ago—there were reports that under Tim Cook and now John Ternus—Apple decided to move ahead with the idea. I played with it a bit, and it works just about exactly as you expect for a laptop touchscreen. A few of the things I did with the touchscreen during my brief time with the laptop: All of that is nice to have, I guess, but there’s not much you can do with it that you couldn’t already do with trackpad gestures, at least at the OS level; some creative apps, like finger painting on the screen, seemed to offer a bit more. When the credible reports emerged that the MacBook Pro would get a touchscreen, I imagined a convertible with Apple Pencil support—something you could use as a large iPad or drawing tablet, essentially. That’s not what this is; it only takes the usual laptop shape, and I was told it does not support the Apple Pencil. It’s just a MacBook Pro, in its normal form factor, but you can use your fingers on the screen to do things like drag files around, swipe between desktop spaces, or pinch-to-zoom on maps or images. But while it’s not about the touchscreen capability for me, I was impressed by the OLED screen itself—and I’m quite the display snob, if I’m being honest. The peak brightness, absolute blacks, well-balanced color, and dynamic range were genuinely remarkable. It’s an enormous upgrade over the MiniLED screen in the previous MacBook Pro. It took far too long for OLED to come to the MacBook Pro, but unsurprisingly, Apple spared no expense and cut no immediately obvious corners on quality. I was also happy to see that the cutout near the top of the screen that has replaced the camera notch is what Apple calls a Dynamic Island; it can resize to show live activities and other information on the fly. That’s one of my favorite features on the iPhone, as I’ve been impressed with Apple’s ability to turn something that should be an albatross into an appealing feature. Based on my time with the device and today’s announcement, the screen seems to be the main draw (though it’s nice that it noticeably weighs less, too), but the price is the real barrier. A 16-inch model with an M5 Max, 64 GB of RAM, and 2 TB of storage is currently priced at $5,799. Sure, that’s a high-end spec, but that’s some serious cash. Much of that is due to the storage and memory; upgrading from 64GB to 128GB adds a whopping $1,600 to that. Sure, most people don’t need anywhere near that much RAM—but some might for future-proofing for local AI workflows. I’m looking forward to spending more time with the new MacBook Pro, but for right now, it seems to follow in the lineup’s existing tradition: impressively high-end components like an outstanding OLED panel, but a very steep price to match. No surprises here! Though after well over a decade of speculation and back-and-forth, you’d be forgiven for being surprised that the touchscreen thing actually finally happened. extraction.body: A great-sounding display, but Apple seems out of touch for the touchscreen. Senior Editor / Computers and Gaming Hardware Surpassed only by the iPhone Duo , this year’s most anticipated Apple announcement is its launch of both a 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen display — the company’s last-to-the-party use of both technologies in one of its laptops. And despite the awful name, it’s more than just a fancy new display. It’s really a complete design overhaul that, at least on paper, brings its feature set up to the front of the class for professional content creation, albeit with the same processor options and ports as the other MacBook Pros. Aside from a screen that brings its capabilities more in line with the Studio Display XDR , the new model adds: It doesn’t come cheap, though; as predicted, you pay a $400 premium over the standard models. The 14-inch M5 Pro model starts at $2,899 compared with $2,499 for the same non-OLED version, and the M5 Max model begins at $4,499 compared with $4,099. If you want to upgrade to 16TB, you have to bump to the M5 Max — that’s a minimum buy-in of $11,499 with only 36GB of memory. Preorders started on Wednesday, and systems are slated to start shipping Nov. 6. One of the most popular changes won’t be the whizzy features, but the drop in weight to 3 pounds for the 14-inch model (down from 3.4 pounds) and to 4 pounds (down from 4.7 pounds) for the 16-inch. Also, while Apple updated its sound system to deliver better bass and incorporated Dolby Atmos support to its spatial audio, one of the more notable enhancements is the claimed improvements to the sound when the MacBook is closed. A lot of the traditional advantages of OLED over alternatives like IPS with array backlights — such as a wider color gamut and true blacks — are less pronounced than they used to be. That’s even more true for the current MacBook Pro’s mini-LED-backlit Liquid Retina XDR screens: They already deliver excellent deep blacks and 100% P3 gamut coverage, along with great color accuracy sufficient for prosumer creative work. But the PROLED XDR screen sounds top-notch. While I take Apple’s claim of a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio with 10,000,000 grains of salt — the arithmetic ratio of peak brightness to minimum black isn’t really meaningful, especially beyond about a million — the display has an expanded gamut that covers the Adobe RGB color space and more of Rec. 2020, a space for mastering video. The latter is still only 80%, but at the moment, that’s the best you can get in a laptop display. Peak brightness is also similar to the desktop display at 2,000 nits. As with the current screens, though, you can set the SDR brightness only up to 1,000 nits; above that, it’s automated to compensate only for bright sunlight. That can get frustrating for people like me who find auto- brightness distracting. The display can do 1,000 nits full screen in both SDR and HDR, though. Microsoft’s recently shipped Surface Laptop Ultra also hits 2,000 nits, the first Windows laptop that does, but uses mini-LED. Oddly, Apple still quotes a 1-nit minimum brightness spec, similar to its mini-LED screens, though OLED’s native minimum is a lot lower: Theoretically, it’s zero, but professional colorimeters have measured it a lot lower. That may be because Apple has adopted it as a standard, and possibly clamped it, to tonally match its mini-LED models. Apple also refers to its panel technology generically as “tandem OLED,” which is a little annoying, since there is a raft of tandem OLED types. But it is “state of the art!” There are a couple of potential disappointments, though. For one, the battery life is unchanged. While the MacBook Pro’s battery life has always been good, it’s clear that the OLED display didn’t provide any power savings, or at least savings that weren’t spent elsewhere in the system. Touch looks like the biggest mixed bag, though. The hardware is only a small aspect of the implementation; operating system interfaces like those of iOS and iPadOS are built around considerations like your finger is bigger and fatter than a cursor. Simply porting the mobile interfaces to a laptop isn’t necessarily a solution, either. We use laptops in part because a hardware keyboard is sometimes the best input choice, and even navigating the mobile devices via touch can get annoying, so those interfaces don’t necessarily translate optimally. The point is, a lot is riding on how Apple has adapted MacOS for touch. For instance, the Touch Bar floundered in part because it felt grafted on rather than integral to the OS’ interface, as well as arguably superfluous. And since Apple didn’t launch the capability with MacOS 27 at its developer conference, WWDC , this year, it sounds like the applications will be behind. That’s not something you beta test on a pro-level production system. Pros rely heavily on muscle memory. It should really have launched with a MacBook Air. Plus, to adapt to touchscreen use, Apple had to stiffen the hinge — poking the screen makes that necessary — and add image stabilization to the webcam in case you poke the screen during video calls. Apple seemed like it was really stretching to find meaningful uses for touch. Playing piano on a screen that forces your hand to an awkward angle? No thanks. The one application that sounded like it might be OK was for developers to simulate mobile app interfaces. I was also kind of hoping for increased refresh rates beyond 120Hz or the ability to manually set it above 60Hz. Apple seems to position ProMotion as a power-saving technology rather than for gaming. Apple also seems to think 60fps is a great frame rate, so it’s not surprising. © 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

extraction.body: Apple on Tuesday unveiled its new 14-inch MacBook Pro, powered by its latest M6 chip. The new MacBook Pro has 24 hours of battery life and now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity. The laptop starts at $1,999 and is available in space black and silver. Apple also announced its latest iMac , which is also powered by the M6 chip. The tech giant revealed the new devices just a day before its “Pro and Tell” event scheduled for Wednesday. On Monday, Apple announced its new iPad mini . The tech giant says the M6 chip features a 12-core CPU with the world’s fastest CPU core and a 12-core GPU that delivers more responsive performance, up to 30% faster graphics, and up to 25% faster AI workloads compared with the M5 chip. The M6 delivers up to 13 times the LLM prompt-processing speed of the M1 MacBook Pro and up to 1.3 times faster performance than the M5 model, Apple says. The M6 MacBook Pro starts with 16GB of unified memory, configurable up to 32GB, and has memory bandwidth of up to 170GB/s, up from the 153GB/s on the M5 chip. It includes HDMI, MagSafe 3, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, an SDXC card slot, and a headphone jack. Like previous models, the laptop features a 12-megapixel camera. The M6 MacBook Pro supports fast charging, reaching up to 50% charge in 30 minutes with a compatible high-wattage USB-C power adapter. As for the new M6-powered iMac, it features a faster CPU and GPU, with Neural Accelerators built into every core. Apple says the M6 delivers smooth multitasking and powerful performance for everyday apps, photo editing, and video production. The new iMac starts at $1,499 and comes in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange, and silver. The company also notes that the new iMac delivers up to five times faster on-device AI performance than the M4 model. It features a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display, an advanced camera and audio system, up to four Thunderbolt 4 ports, color-matched accessories, and macOS 27. Both the new MacBook Pro and iMac can be preordered starting October 28 and will be available starting November 6. Aisha is a consumer news reporter at TechCrunch. “The 14-inch MacBook Pro is the pro laptop of choice for a wide range of users — from college students, to business professionals across every industry, to multidisciplinary creators doing it all on one device,” said Shelly Goldberg, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. “With the powerful M6 chip, we’re taking performance to the next level, with a boost in CPU speed and graphics and even more powerful capabilities for on-device AI. With its amazing battery life, remarkable Liquid Retina XDR display, and even faster connectivity, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 delivers a fantastic combination of performance, capability, and value.”
M6: Blazing-Fast Performance and On-Device AI Capabilities

M6 brings even more performance and next-level AI capabilities to the 14-inch MacBook Pro. Featuring a powerful 12-core CPU, a 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each core, Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and faster unified memory, MacBook Pro with M6 is faster and more responsive.

The 12-core CPU, with two more cores than before, brings blazing-fast single- and multithreaded performance, so users can fly through everything from multitasking across apps to compiling code to handling complex creative workflows. The 12-core GPU, also with two additional cores, delivers up to 30 percent faster graphics performance when compared to M5. 2 Everything from 3D modeling to photo editing and gaming feels incredibly fast, enhanced by a third-generation ray-tracing engine and Dynamic Caching to optimize on-chip memory. It also brings up to 25 percent faster performance for on-device AI workloads, like LLM prompt processing, compared to M5. 3 The Dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers up to 1.9x faster performance than M5 and works with the advanced GPU to dramatically accelerate AI workloads like image generation, Super Resolution, and AI upscaling. 2 The Neural Engine also powers Apple Intelligence, enabling advanced and energy-efficient on-device AI processing. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 does all this with industry-leading performance per watt and up to 24 hours of battery life, the longest ever in a Mac. With 16GB of unified memory standard, configurable up to 32GB, and higher memory bandwidth up to 170GB/s, MacBook Pro makes multitasking and working with demanding apps and large projects even faster.

There’s never been a better time for customers to upgrade from a previous-generation MacBook Pro with Apple silicon or an Intel-based Mac. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 delivers remarkable value thanks to major performance improvements and powerful AI capabilities. The new 14-inch MacBook Pro also features all of the compelling capabilities that have made it so popular, including:

The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 comes to life with macOS 27, which includes Siri AI, a profoundly more capable, conversational, and personal assistant; helpful Apple Intelligence features across everyday apps; and improvements that make the Mac even more responsive and reliable. Siri AI can draw on personal context to help users find what they need in the moment across messages, emails, photos, and more; answer questions about virtually any topic; and get things done across apps — all with groundbreaking privacy protections. Siri AI is integrated into Spotlight and systemwide context menus, and users can ask Siri about what’s on their display with Visual Intelligence using a dedicated keyboard shortcut. Users can also write and edit with Siri almost anywhere they type.

Additionally, Apple Intelligence makes apps smarter and more useful. In Safari, it powers new tools that automatically organize a user’s tabs into topics; notify them of website changes, like product restocks or price drops; and enable the creation of custom extensions based on a description. Users can also easily create an automation in Shortcuts by simply describing it, or tap into intelligent photo editing tools in the Photos app. The new 14-inch MacBook Pro gets even more responsive, reliable, and delightful with refinements to design, performance, search, and more. Updates to Liquid Glass deliver an even more focused and approachable experience. A new slider in Settings gives users the option to personalize Liquid Glass, adjusting it anywhere from ultraclear to fully tinted to match their preference, and app icons are sharper and more defined.
14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 and the Environment

The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 was built with the environment in mind and drives progress toward Apple’s ambitious plan to be carbon neutral across its entire footprint by 2030. It is made with 45 percent recycled content overall, 6 including 100 percent recycled aluminum in the enclosure, 100 percent recycled cobalt in the battery, and, in a first for Apple, 100 percent recycled tantalum in multiple capacitors. It is manufactured with 60 percent renewable electricity, such as wind and solar, across the supply chain. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 is designed to be durable and repairable, and meets Apple’s high standards for energy efficiency and safe chemistry. As with all Apple products, its paper packaging is 100 percent fiber-based 7 and designed to be recycled.

Apple revolutionized personal technology with the introduction of the Macintosh in 1984. Today, Apple leads the world in innovation with iPhone, iPad, Mac, AirPods, Apple Watch, and Apple Vision Pro. Apple’s six software platforms — iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, visionOS, and tvOS — provide seamless experiences across all Apple devices and empower people with breakthrough services including the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Pay, iCloud, and Apple TV. Apple’s more than 150,000 employees are dedicated to making the best products on earth and to leaving the world better than we found it.
The latest news and updates, direct from Apple.

passages: Apple has announced refreshes for the iMac and the entry-level, 14-inch MacBook Pro .
Both machines are getting the M6 chip, which was introduced in the Mac mini several weeks ago.
In this case, that means up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to double the Neural Engine performance.
Apple skipped the M5 and went straight to the M6 here.
It caps out at 32GB of RAM but can go to 4TB of storage.

extraction.body: Additionally, the N1 chip brings Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Apple has announced refreshes for the iMac and the entry-level, 14-inch MacBook Pro . Both machines are getting the M6 chip, which was introduced in the Mac mini several weeks ago. The M6 is split into two variants for the iMac. Picking the “M6 chip with two Thunderbolt ports” option gets you a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, whereas picking “M6 chip with four Thunderbolt ports” gets you 12 cores for each, instead. The two-port variant maxes out at 24 GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, whereas the four-port one maxes out at 32GB of RAM and 2TB of storage. There’s only one M6 chip option for the MacBook Pro—the one with the 12-core GPU and CPU. It caps out at 32GB of RAM but can go to 4TB of storage. It’s a more substantial refresh for the iMac, as its previous update introduced the M4. Apple skipped the M5 and went straight to the M6 here. In terms of performance gains moving from the M4 to the M6, Apple said with the Mac mini that users can expect up to 40 percent faster CPU performance, up to double graphics performance, and nearly five times faster on-device AI. All that largely matches what we saw when we tested the M6 Mac mini last month, and users of the new iMac should expect similar numbers. The M6 iMac should see up to double SSD read/write performance compared to the M4 model, too. The previous entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro had the M5, so that one is just stepping up a single generation. In this case, that means up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to double the Neural Engine performance. In addition to the M6 chip, both computers now have the N1 chip for wireless connectivity (that means Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6). The iMac is now configurable with up to 2.5Gb Ethernet, while the MacBook Pro still lacks an Ethernet port. There are no outward design changes to either device; they both look exactly the same as their immediate predecessors. The iMac starts at $1,499 for the two-port version, or $1,699 for the four-port version. The M6 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999. Preorders start October 28, and they ship November 6. sources.title: Apple's M6 chip brings serious on-device AI power to the entry-level MacBook Pro and the colorful iMac - XDA
passages: Ahead of its upcoming "Pro and Tell" event, Apple has revealed its refreshed 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac , powered by its M6 chip.
This means the new MacBook Pro features three Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports, a MagSafe 3 charging port, a full HDMI port, and an SD card slot.
While this isn't exactly surprising, given Apple's MacBook Pro design has been around for several years now, it would have been nice to see it evolve in some way.
Apple also refreshed its all-in-one iMac with the M6 chip .
This update comes two years after the colorful computer got the M4 chip (the iMac skipped the M5 series entirely).
The base M6 configuration in the iMac features a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, a step up from the 8-core M4 CPU in the last-generation iMac.

Apple says that the M6 features a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, emphasizing that it's a powerful platform for local LLMs and that the chip is designed to take full advantage of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence.
The MacBook M6 also features Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, alongside returning features like the 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and Liquid Retina XDR display with optional nano-texture.
The entry-level iMac starts at $1,500 and will be available to pre-order on October 28th, with shipping starting on November 6th.
Apple also recently revealed its A20-powered iPad mini .
At its upcoming event, the tech giant is expected to show off its long-rumored touchscreen MacBook for the first time.

extraction.body: Ahead of its upcoming "Pro and Tell" event, Apple has revealed its refreshed 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac , powered by its M6 chip. The tech giant says the M6 features a 12-core CPU, paired with a 12-core GPU that delivers 30 percent faster graphics and 25 percent faster AI workload performance compared to last year's M5 chip. Interestingly, the company also compares the M6 to the M1 in its press release, highlighting that the newer, more powerful chip offers 11x faster graphics and up to 13x faster AI performance. Apple says that the M6 features a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, emphasizing that it's a powerful platform for local LLMs and that the chip is designed to take full advantage of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence. The MacBook M6 also features Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, alongside returning features like the 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and Liquid Retina XDR display with optional nano-texture. Beyond the bump up to the M6 chip, the entry-level 14-inch MacBook features the same overall design and port layout as last year's M5 upgrade and, in fact, the year prior's M4 refresh. This means the new MacBook Pro features three Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports, a MagSafe 3 charging port, a full HDMI port, and an SD card slot. While this isn't exactly surprising, given Apple's MacBook Pro design has been around for several years now, it would have been nice to see it evolve in some way. Pricing for the 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro starts at $2,000 for the 16GB version, which matches last year's pricing. Pre-orders start on October 28th, with shipping beginning on November 6th. Apple also refreshed its all-in-one iMac with the M6 chip . This update comes two years after the colorful computer got the M4 chip (the iMac skipped the M5 series entirely). The base M6 configuration in the iMac features a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, a step up from the 8-core M4 CPU in the last-generation iMac. There's also a more expensive 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU configuration Beyond the chip upgrade, there isn't much else new. The refreshed iMac features Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 like the new 14-inch MacBook Pro. It also has the same Thunderbolt ports as the M4 iMac — two on the 10-core and four on the 12-core. The colors are all the same too: Blue, Purple, Pink, Orange, Yellow, Green, and Silver. At the very least, it would have been great to see an iMac color refresh and a port selection that made a bit more sense. The entry-level iMac starts at $1,500 and will be available to pre-order on October 28th, with shipping starting on November 6th. The M6 MacBook Pro and iMac follow the M6 Mac Mini that Apple revealed earlier this year, which the company somewhat confusingly showed off alongside the M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studio. The M6 is Apple's first 2nm chip and bumps up to a 12-core CPU from the M5's 10 cores. Apple also recently revealed its A20-powered iPad mini . At its upcoming event, the tech giant is expected to show off its long-rumored touchscreen MacBook for the first time. The redesigned tablet also features a thinner and lighter design. I love my MacBook Pro M5 and hope it lasts me as long as my M1 did. What confuses me is why so much emphasis is put on the device's bigger, better performance, but most people are running most things online now, so the performance is surely about the weakest link... Usually the speed of the internet and connection at the time you are using it. Nobody really focuses on that. I'm sure my Antigravity work sessions would be improved greatly by a much better and consistent internet connection than a slightly faster processor in my Mac. Just food for thought.

Apple has rolled out a new 24-inch iMac and an entry-level MacBook Pro with a 14-inch screen, marking key updates in an end-to-end overhaul of the company’s computer line. The new iMac and MacBook Pro, unveiled on Oct 27 , are visually similar to their predecessors – with the main changes happening internally. Both machines now include the M6 chip, which debuted in the Mac mini in September. The iMac is moving from an M4 processor, while the MacBook Pro received the M5 in 2025 . The updates represent a second day of Apple announcements this week, with the company rolling out a revamped iPad mini on Oct 26 with a new screen and water resistance. Apple will cap the launches on Oct 28 with its first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen, Bloomberg News has reported. The updated iMac and low-end MacBook Pro become available for pre-orders on Oct 28 and will arrive beginning Nov 6, Apple said, matching the new iPad mini. The new iMac starts at US$1,499 (S$1,920), while the MacBook Pro begins at US$1,999. Apple said the M6 chip makes the iMac five times faster than the prior model from 2024 for artificial intelligence, while the new MacBook Pro is 30% speedier than its predecessor for graphics. The company continues to sell higher-end M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros, which have more advanced main processing and graphics cores compared with the entry M6 machines. The updated 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac also include Bluetooth 6 and Wi-Fi 7, while the laptop gets faster charging. Both machines go on sale Nov. 6 after pre-orders open on Oct 28 . The new Macs come as part of a slew of changes to the company’s computer line. Beyond the push into touchscreen displays, Apple is preparing a refreshed MacBook Neo and MacBook Air for the first half of 2027 . The company is also working on a redesigned low-end MacBook Pro and the release of its first M7, M7 Pro and M7 Max chips in 2027. It is planning an M7 Ultra and a new Mac Studio in 2028. Apple’s overhauled MacBook Pro with a touchscreen – coming on Oct 28 – will include a lighter and slightly thinner design, slimmer bezels around the display and OLED technology, Bloomberg reported.

extraction.body: Additionally, the N1 chip brings Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Apple has announced refreshes for the iMac and the entry-level, 14-inch MacBook Pro . Both machines are getting the M6 chip, which was introduced in the Mac mini several weeks ago. The M6 is split into two variants for the iMac. Picking the “M6 chip with two Thunderbolt ports” option gets you a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, whereas picking “M6 chip with four Thunderbolt ports” gets you 12 cores for each, instead. The two-port variant maxes out at 24 GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, whereas the four-port one maxes out at 32GB of RAM and 2TB of storage. There’s only one M6 chip option for the MacBook Pro—the one with the 12-core GPU and CPU. It caps out at 32GB of RAM but can go to 4TB of storage. It’s a more substantial refresh for the iMac, as its previous update introduced the M4. Apple skipped the M5 and went straight to the M6 here. In terms of performance gains moving from the M4 to the M6, Apple said with the Mac mini that users can expect up to 40 percent faster CPU performance, up to double graphics performance, and nearly five times faster on-device AI. All that largely matches what we saw when we tested the M6 Mac mini last month, and users of the new iMac should expect similar numbers. The M6 iMac should see up to double SSD read/write performance compared to the M4 model, too. The previous entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro had the M5, so that one is just stepping up a single generation. In this case, that means up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to double the Neural Engine performance. In addition to the M6 chip, both computers now have the N1 chip for wireless connectivity (that means Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6). The iMac is now configurable with up to 2.5Gb Ethernet, while the MacBook Pro still lacks an Ethernet port. There are no outward design changes to either device; they both look exactly the same as their immediate predecessors. The iMac starts at $1,499 for the two-port version, or $1,699 for the four-port version. The M6 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999. Preorders start October 28, and they ship November 6. Beyond the push into touchscreen displays, Apple is preparing a refreshed MacBook Neo and MacBook Air for the first half of 2027 . It is planning an M7 Ultra and a new Mac Studio in 2028. The company continues to sell higher-end M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros, which have more advanced main processing and graphics cores compared with the entry M6 machines.

Apple has rolled out a new 24-inch iMac and an entry-level MacBook Pro with a 14-inch screen, marking key updates in an end-to-end overhaul of the company’s computer line. The new iMac and MacBook Pro, unveiled on Oct 27 , are visually similar to their predecessors – with the main changes happening internally. Both machines now include the M6 chip, which debuted in the Mac mini in September. The iMac is moving from an M4 processor, while the MacBook Pro received the M5 in 2025 . The updates represent a second day of Apple announcements this week, with the company rolling out a revamped iPad mini on Oct 26 with a new screen and water resistance. Apple will cap the launches on Oct 28 with its first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen, Bloomberg News has reported. The updated iMac and low-end MacBook Pro become available for pre-orders on Oct 28 and will arrive beginning Nov 6, Apple said, matching the new iPad mini. The new iMac starts at US$1,499 (S$1,920), while the MacBook Pro begins at US$1,999. Apple said the M6 chip makes the iMac five times faster than the prior model from 2024 for artificial intelligence, while the new MacBook Pro is 30% speedier than its predecessor for graphics. The company continues to sell higher-end M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros, which have more advanced main processing and graphics cores compared with the entry M6 machines. The updated 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac also include Bluetooth 6 and Wi-Fi 7, while the laptop gets faster charging. Both machines go on sale Nov. 6 after pre-orders open on Oct 28 . The new Macs come as part of a slew of changes to the company’s computer line. Beyond the push into touchscreen displays, Apple is preparing a refreshed MacBook Neo and MacBook Air for the first half of 2027 . The company is also working on a redesigned low-end MacBook Pro and the release of its first M7, M7 Pro and M7 Max chips in 2027. It is planning an M7 Ultra and a new Mac Studio in 2028. Apple’s overhauled MacBook Pro with a touchscreen – coming on Oct 28 – will include a lighter and slightly thinner design, slimmer bezels around the display and OLED technology, Bloomberg reported.

passages: Apple has officially announced the all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display , its first touchscreen laptop.
While Apple has innovated with multi-touch on the iPhone and iPad, the Mac has been resistant to touch input for years.
Back in March, Apple upgraded the standard 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro laptops to the current M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.
MacBook Pro features Touch for the first time, bringing pros a whole new way to interact with their content.
Crafted specifically for the Mac, every touch interaction feels incredibly responsive and refined.

Everyday tasks are simple and intuitive, allowing users to scroll through a webpage with a natural swipe; pinch to zoom in on a photo; drag and drop slides from one presentation to another; and double-tap a window to fill the screen, or flick to tile it into place.
And the touch sensor is built directly into the display panel — not layered on top of it — reducing latency so users feel like they’re touching the content itself.
Apple also touts the use of a new hinge technology in the MacBook Pro, in part to support touch input without compromising on stability:
The existing MacBook Pro configurations from March stick around at the same prices.
You just lose OLED, the glowing Apple logo, and the thinner and lighter design.
The new machines still use Touch ID with no Face ID support.
We’ll have to keep waiting for Face ID and built-in cellular connectivity.
Pre-orders are available starting today with deliveries starting November 6.
The new machine was first hinted at by Apple on October 19 with the company’s “Pro and tell” experience teaser .
Earlier today, new Apple CEO John Ternus shared a “spotlight” teaser for the laptop as well.
Remember when Apple introduced the Touch Bar?
It was supposed to be a big deal, but eventually Apple removed it.
Now they’re adding a touchscreen to the MacBook.
Apple’s Mac lineup consists of MacBook, MacBoo…
The new MacBook Pros look awesome with glowing Apple logos.
Touch also introduces entirely new ways of working for pro users.

In addition, a newly designed hinge provides greater stability while using Touch, and advanced video stabilization automatically smooths the camera feed in real time while using Touch on a video call.

I can’t help wondering whether Steve Jobs would have approved of this direction.
