extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro. DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.” Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security . He can be reached via encrypted message at zackwhittaker.1337 on Signal. You can also contact him by email, or to verify outreach, at [email protected] .

The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff .
Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE.
A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.
We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected.
We will update the public when more information is available.”
The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access.
Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years.
One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media.

One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status .

The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest.
“They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen.
The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out.
Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch.
More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S.
Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry.

The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon.

extraction.body: The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics, seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. The DHS and DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer. “If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify, a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members. Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.” More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy. Most records also name a supervisor, which could allow anyone analyzing the dataset to reconstruct reporting relationships across the department. More than 100 HSI agents, including undercover operatives, took part in an operation that included widespread surveillance and infiltration of group chats. Adam Steinbaugh, a senior attorney at the nonprofit civil liberties group FIRE, says that the Trump administration has taken an expansive view of 18 USC 119, a law that prohibits people from sharing “restricted personal information” about federal officers or their families with the intent to threaten them. “This is information that would be on a business card,” says Steinbaugh of the names and basic work details included in the archive. “That’s not something the government can criminalize." Despite the potential sensitivity of other records in the leaked data, the creators of Icepick do not consider it doxing. “If they weren't hiding their involvement in the repressive arm of the US government, there would be no need for us to expose them in the first place.”

sources.title: ‘Icepick’ Leak Exposes Thousands of Homeland Security Personnel, Groups and More - Unicorn Riot
passages: Washington, DC — There’s been yet another major security breach among federal agencies.

The Department of Homeland Security’s ‘single sign-on’ (SSO) login system was reportedly subverted by a hacker going by “Department of Peace” (DoP), which has revealed thousands upon thousands of federal employee records.
Offices and locations are identified in great detail, from Canadian airports to agents in U.S. embassies around the world.
Groups assigned within the SSO system, going back at least to 2011, are also exposed, showing the names of globe-spanning activities, and management personnel handling undercover operations.

To name one example, the JKR HSI CUC , which would likely be a certified undercover operation group involving Homeland Security Investigations, shows personnel at “ JKR – ICE COLOCATION SAN ANTONIO ” which is likely an HSI office on Jackson Keller Road in the Texas city.

A good example is deployment and development around the widely used Raven suite. “Raven” references a few products Homeland Security has developed internally, with major privacy implications for Americans . “RavenGo UEM Prod” has more than 3400 members including organizational units like “AI” within it.

DoP said back in March amid a leak of “details of 6,681 organizations that applied for contracts” that state violence in Minnesota — the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti — had motivated hacking into Homeland Security.
Martin Lagunas is in the Icepick data as a “supervisory detention deportation officer” based out of the ICE field office in Chicago.
He’s listed on more than 30 groups, including “Broadview Mailbox Users” .
Broadview is the notorious ICE detention facility near Chicago, and has seven other ICE agents listed , abbreviated as “BRV”.
Indeed, Unraveled reporting confirmed Lagunas was highly active at Broadview .
Many other groups from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) are also included in the leak.
Thousands of personnel records include supervisors and subordinates, which enabled generating gigantic organizational charts automatically across these agencies.

Combine this with the groups (some officials tagged in dozens) and one can easily browse around the highest levels of activities, including thousands of groups dealing with surveillance, special operations, finance, social media, and much, much more.

The icepi.cx site includes more than 20 “CUC” groups (Active Directory / Okta workgroups) . (CUC is ICE jargon for “certified undercover” operations.) Each group can be checked for its individual members, which include leadership like assistant director and assistant special agents in charge, who are top personnel at individual field offices.
Top personnel are included in dozens of these software groups simultaneously.
For example groups called SG-AMO-EGIS-ITAK-TAK and SG-BEMS-EGIS-OFO-TAK would be used by 140 and 269 CBP personnel respectively for “Team Awareness Kit” access. (More on TAK below.)

The “Twitter.com” group includes not just “web communications,” multimedia and graphics design personnel, but many watch officers, “intelligence operations specialist” and National Operations Center (NOC) personnel. “Organizational Units” in that group include “Proxy Exceptions” which likely indicates their web traffic is handled in a special fashion — inside government agencies, data to external servers is often sent to specialized proxy computers that are controlled firewall gateways to the outside internet.
There are two entries in the database for “Christian Castro,” including an ICE agent stationed in Harlingen, Texas , where he was arrested.
The leaked groups are a kind of breadcrumb trail for software access controls and activities related to major websites like Twitter and Instagram.
The website highlights more than 50 ICE and HSI figures , including agents, officers, supervisors, managers and legal counsel based in Chicago.

extraction.body: Now posted on Internet: Officials in sensitive locations worldwide, thousands of groups, phone numbers, and countless other details cracked from Homeland Security login system Washington, DC — There’s been yet another major security breach among federal agencies. The Department of Homeland Security’s ‘single sign-on’ (SSO) login system was reportedly subverted by a hacker going by “Department of Peace” (DoP), which has revealed thousands upon thousands of federal employee records. Around one-fifth of Homeland Security’s personnel have been exposed. Offices and locations are identified in great detail, from Canadian airports to agents in U.S. embassies around the world. Groups assigned within the SSO system, going back at least to 2011, are also exposed, showing the names of globe-spanning activities, and management personnel handling undercover operations. Thousands of personnel records include supervisors and subordinates, which enabled generating gigantic organizational charts automatically across these agencies. Combine this with the groups (some officials tagged in dozens) and one can easily browse around the highest levels of activities, including thousands of groups dealing with surveillance, special operations, finance, social media, and much, much more. Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), a U.S.-based transparency nonprofit that “archives and publishes hacked and leaked documents in the public interest,” reported the records were provided by DoP and released on Wednesday, October 28, with help from a Swiss hacktivist and journalist, maia crimew . A searchable website called icepi.cx helps dig around this data which has “been enriched” with updates according to the FAQ ; the whole data set is now online . DoP said back in March amid a leak of “details of 6,681 organizations that applied for contracts” that state violence in Minnesota — the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti — had motivated hacking into Homeland Security. Both of Pretti’s killers appear to be in the leaked data. “Why hack the DHS? I can think of a couple Pretti Good reasons! I’m releasing this because the DHS is killing us and people deserve to know which companies support them and what they’re working on.” Many of the locations were not previously known as ICE or DHS offices. For example a suite on Parthenia Street in Northridge, California, has not been listed as an HSI office but is identified in the data . Keep in mind it could be inaccurate or out of date, but it is thought that journalists and local people will have a lot of places to check on. Jesus Ochoa was named as one of the agents who killed Alex Pretti, and a CBP “Supply chain security specialist” by that name based in Laredo, Texas is listed in the database, and is in various Laredo-related groups like SG-LAR029A-SEALS with more than 60 other Texas CBP personnel. Location 0000A2 , located at the Hidalgo/Pharr/Anzalduas Enrollment Center on South Stewart Road in Mission, Texas, is listed as the work site of Pretti’s other killer, Raymundo Gutierrez, who shared that space with four other “SRT OPERATOR” (an acronym for Special Response Team) and Special Operation Supervisors. A mosaic of Gutierrez’ access to DHS systems is revealed from his group memberships. For example groups called SG-AMO-EGIS-ITAK-TAK and SG-BEMS-EGIS-OFO-TAK would be used by 140 and 269 CBP personnel respectively for “Team Awareness Kit” access. (More on TAK below.) The site notes, “This is not a comprehensive list of all DHS employees. All data is provided as-is; inaccuracies are from source data and may be reproduced.” The icepi.cx site includes more than 20 “CUC” groups (Active Directory / Okta workgroups) . (CUC is ICE jargon for “certified undercover” operations.) Each group can be checked for its individual members, which include leadership like assistant director and assistant special agents in charge, who are top personnel at individual field offices. To name one example, the JKR HSI CUC , which would likely be a certified undercover operation group involving Homeland Security Investigations, shows personnel at “ JKR – ICE COLOCATION SAN ANTONIO ” which is likely an HSI office on Jackson Keller Road in the Texas city. 46 people are indexed at that location. This CUC activity also links to an office in Crystal City, Arlington, VA, called the “NGI – ARLINGTON OFFICE” with 50 people , many of whom are associated with technical programs with titles including R&D computer science, DevOps, senior data engineer, as the assigned workgroups show in exhaustive detail. (More on the Arlington office below.) There are 26 locations linked in Minnesota (filters by state are available). For example, the Grand Marais office at 518 E. HWY 61 is listed with five Customs and Border Protection personnel. 78 personnel associated to the Whipple Federal Building are listed at Fort Snelling, MN but one person’s records are erroneously under Saint Paul. This data could be significant in ongoing federal lawsuits since plaintiffs have named anonymous government officials as “John Doe,” including a lawsuit filed over Renée Good ‘s killing. Emma Best at DDoSecrets mentioned groups that stood out like “ERO-AD REMOVAL AWARD NOMINATION SR APPROVERS” which “hits hard” because their purpose is to congratulate ICE agents for deportations. There are more than 30 groups like this . The leaked groups are a kind of breadcrumb trail for software access controls and activities related to major websites like Twitter and Instagram. The “Twitter.com” group includes not just “web communications,” multimedia and graphics design personnel, but many watch officers, “intelligence operations specialist” and National Operations Center (NOC) personnel. “Organizational Units” in that group include “Proxy Exceptions” which likely indicates their web traffic is handled in a special fashion — inside government agencies, data to external servers is often sent to specialized proxy computers that are controlled firewall gateways to the outside internet. The 30 members in “NOC Twitter Access” appear similar in purpose, such as NOC desk officers and senior watch officers. Top personnel are included in dozens of these software groups simultaneously. A typical one is Citrix . Several groups include “WS1” (not to be confused with AWS, which likely means Amazon Web Services), such as “WS1-DHS-HQ-PROD-Sync-Users” . WS1 is a common federal abbreviation for Omnissa Workspace One . Major software packages are typically managed by service vendors. Just days ago Carahsoft obtained a nearly $2.7 billion blanket purchase agreement under a sole-source justification for dozens of vendors including Omnissa . Cellebrite is a cellphone data extraction vendor which is included in the Carahsoft sole-source agreement and mentioned in two groups. The SG-EDN006A-INTEL-CELLEBRITE group has 52 members , mostly CBP intelligence officers in Texas. The personnel index can be sorted by international locations as well, which are often five zeroes followed by a two-letter country code. In London, two CBP and three HSI personnel operate from the prominent, cube-shaped U.S. Embassy at 33 Nine Elms Lane . Some agents carry the title FSNI or “Foreign Service National Investigator” as ICE or its HSI subdivision; “Mission Support Specialist” is another common title. Three personnel, two of them investigators, are listed as in country “HN” , which is likely to mean Honduras, at the “TGK – U.S. EMBASSY” which likely means Tegucigalpa, the capital. Seven HSI investigators and other staff are listed at the BUE – Consular Section in Bangkok, Thailand. New Delhi, India has four HSI investigators listed. Three HSI investigators are listed in the ICE attache office in Phnom Penh, Thailand . Seven HSI personnel operate from the U.S. Embassy in Manila, the Philippines . In Canada, 13 CBP personnel are listed at the Calgary airport . 22 CBP personnel are listed at the Vancouver International Airport and 27 CBP personnel are listed at the international airport in Toronto. Two more HSI agents are listed at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto . Three HSI personnel are listed at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa . Ten CBP personnel are listed at an address near the airport in Nassau, the Bahamas . Six CBP personnel are listed at the Dublin airport in Ireland. A CBP officer specializing in “Container Security” is listed at a seaport address in Tokyo. Six agents (five HSI and one ICE-ERO Attache) are listed at the U.S. Embassy in Mexico City . The website highlights more than 50 ICE and HSI figures , including agents, officers, supervisors, managers and legal counsel based in Chicago. We reviewed a series of records about DHS agents in Chicago courtesy of Unraveled Press , who have been probing agents that turn up repeatedly. Martin Lagunas is in the Icepick data as a “supervisory detention deportation officer” based out of the ICE field office in Chicago. He’s listed on more than 30 groups, including “Broadview Mailbox Users” . Broadview is the notorious ICE detention facility near Chicago, and has seven other ICE agents listed , abbreviated as “BRV”. Indeed, Unraveled reporting confirmed Lagunas was highly active at Broadview . Lagunas is also assigned BRV_Home_Drive and BRV_Share groups, which would likely be linked with Broadview data. A few other entries matching Unraveled Press records: Alfredo Alvillar is listed in the records as a “1st Level Supervisor” in CBP based in Texas. He claimed to be assaulted in Chicago in an October 2025 incident . Michael Sveum, another CBP first level supervisor from El Paso, Texas, is listed ; he was at the site of Renée Good’s killing in Minneapolis alongside Greg Bovino. Edgar Vazquez, another Texas CBP agent at the site of the Good killing, seems to have two entries listed in different Texas cities, with different spellings for the email address. Sveum and Vazquez were both active in fighting protesters in Chicago as well. Note that the name search requires entering “%lagunas” to search for names ending that way – the % symbol is a wildcard. The leaks map out personnel, programs and systems at the highest levels of DHS & ICE technological research and implementation, which serves agents on American streets. A good example is deployment and development around the widely used Raven suite. “Raven” references a few products Homeland Security has developed internally, with major privacy implications for Americans . “RavenGo UEM Prod” has more than 3400 members including organizational units like “AI” within it. The “IC_raven_cloudbees_developers” group, while small, has several research & development computer science figures in it, and is colocated between the “NGI – ARLINGTON OFFICE” and Sandia National Laboratories in New Mexico. Cloudbees is an agentic coding vendor . Raven is short for Repository for Analytics in a Virtualized Environment, which is an AI-enhanced platform . (Additionally, per an attachment on contract award HSHQDC-12-D-00014 Raven is built on Blackberry United Endpoint Management (UEM).) Raven Compliance Automation Tool is another program in the suite. The Brennan Center investigated several vendors profiting from Raven development . passages: Now posted on Internet: Officials in sensitive locations worldwide, thousands of groups, phone numbers, and countless other details cracked from Homeland Security login system

Washington, DC — There’s been yet another major security breach among federal agencies. The Department of Homeland Security’s ‘single sign-on’ (SSO) login system was reportedly subverted by a hacker going by “Department of Peace” (DoP), which has revealed thousands upon thousands of federal employee records. Around one-fifth of Homeland Security’s personnel have been exposed. Offices and locations are identified in great detail, from Canadian airports to agents in U.S. embassies around the world. Groups assigned within the SSO system, going back at least to 2011, are also exposed, showing the names of globe-spanning activities, and management personnel handling undercover operations.

Thousands of personnel records include supervisors and subordinates, which enabled generating gigantic organizational charts automatically across these agencies. Combine this with the groups (some officials tagged in dozens) and one can easily browse around the highest levels of activities, including thousands of groups dealing with surveillance, special operations, finance, social media, and much, much more.

Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), a U.S.-based transparency nonprofit that “archives and publishes hacked and leaked documents in the public interest,” reported the records were provided by DoP and released on Wednesday, October 28, with help from a Swiss hacktivist and journalist, maia crimew . A searchable website called icepi.cx helps dig around this data which has “been enriched” with updates according to the FAQ ; the whole data set is now online .

DoP said back in March amid a leak of “details of 6,681 organizations that applied for contracts” that state violence in Minnesota — the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti — had motivated hacking into Homeland Security. Both of Pretti’s killers appear to be in the leaked data.
“Why hack the DHS? I can think of a couple Pretti Good reasons! I’m releasing this because the DHS is killing us and people deserve to know which companies support them and what they’re working on.”

Many of the locations were not previously known as ICE or DHS offices. For example a suite on Parthenia Street in Northridge, California, has not been listed as an HSI office but is identified in the data . Keep in mind it could be inaccurate or out of date, but it is thought that journalists and local people will have a lot of places to check on.

Jesus Ochoa was named as one of the agents who killed Alex Pretti, and a CBP “Supply chain security specialist” by that name based in Laredo, Texas is listed in the database, and is in various Laredo-related groups like SG-LAR029A-SEALS with more than 60 other Texas CBP personnel.

Location 0000A2 , located at the Hidalgo/Pharr/Anzalduas Enrollment Center on South Stewart Road in Mission, Texas, is listed as the work site of Pretti’s other killer, Raymundo Gutierrez, who shared that space with four other “SRT OPERATOR” (an acronym for Special Response Team) and Special Operation Supervisors. A mosaic of Gutierrez’ access to DHS systems is revealed from his group memberships. For example groups called SG-AMO-EGIS-ITAK-TAK and SG-BEMS-EGIS-OFO-TAK would be used by 140 and 269 CBP personnel respectively for “Team Awareness Kit” access. (More on TAK below.)
The site notes, “This is not a comprehensive list of all DHS employees. All data is provided as-is; inaccuracies are from source data and may be reproduced.”

The icepi.cx site includes more than 20 “CUC” groups (Active Directory / Okta workgroups) . (CUC is ICE jargon for “certified undercover” operations.) Each group can be checked for its individual members, which include leadership like assistant director and assistant special agents in charge, who are top personnel at individual field offices.

To name one example, the JKR HSI CUC , which would likely be a certified undercover operation group involving Homeland Security Investigations, shows personnel at “ JKR – ICE COLOCATION SAN ANTONIO ” which is likely an HSI office on Jackson Keller Road in the Texas city. 46 people are indexed at that location. This CUC activity also links to an office in Crystal City, Arlington, VA, called the “NGI – ARLINGTON OFFICE” with 50 people , many of whom are associated with technical programs with titles including R&D computer science, DevOps, senior data engineer, as the assigned workgroups show in exhaustive detail. (More on the Arlington office below.)
There are 26 locations linked in Minnesota (filters by state are available). For example, the Grand Marais office at 518 E. HWY 61 is listed with five Customs and Border Protection personnel.

78 personnel associated to the Whipple Federal Building are listed at Fort Snelling, MN but one person’s records are erroneously under Saint Paul. This data could be significant in ongoing federal lawsuits since plaintiffs have named anonymous government officials as “John Doe,” including a lawsuit filed over Renée Good ‘s killing.

Emma Best at DDoSecrets mentioned groups that stood out like “ERO-AD REMOVAL AWARD NOMINATION SR APPROVERS” which “hits hard” because their purpose is to congratulate ICE agents for deportations. There are more than 30 groups like this .
The leaked groups are a kind of breadcrumb trail for software access controls and activities related to major websites like Twitter and Instagram.

The “Twitter.com” group includes not just “web communications,” multimedia and graphics design personnel, but many watch officers, “intelligence operations specialist” and National Operations Center (NOC) personnel. “Organizational Units” in that group include “Proxy Exceptions” which likely indicates their web traffic is handled in a special fashion — inside government agencies, data to external servers is often sent to specialized proxy computers that are controlled firewall gateways to the outside internet. The 30 members in “NOC Twitter Access” appear similar in purpose, such as NOC desk officers and senior watch officers.

Top personnel are included in dozens of these software groups simultaneously. A typical one is Citrix . Several groups include “WS1” (not to be confused with AWS, which likely means Amazon Web Services), such as “WS1-DHS-HQ-PROD-Sync-Users” . WS1 is a common federal abbreviation for Omnissa Workspace One . Major software packages are typically managed by service vendors. Just days ago Carahsoft obtained a nearly $2.7 billion blanket purchase agreement under a sole-source justification for dozens of vendors including Omnissa .

Cellebrite is a cellphone data extraction vendor which is included in the Carahsoft sole-source agreement and mentioned in two groups. The SG-EDN006A-INTEL-CELLEBRITE group has 52 members , mostly CBP intelligence officers in Texas.
The personnel index can be sorted by international locations as well, which are often five zeroes followed by a two-letter country code.

In London, two CBP and three HSI personnel operate from the prominent, cube-shaped U.S. Embassy at 33 Nine Elms Lane . Some agents carry the title FSNI or “Foreign Service National Investigator” as ICE or its HSI subdivision; “Mission Support Specialist” is another common title.
Three personnel, two of them investigators, are listed as in country “HN” , which is likely to mean Honduras, at the “TGK – U.S. EMBASSY” which likely means Tegucigalpa, the capital.

Seven HSI investigators and other staff are listed at the BUE – Consular Section in Bangkok, Thailand. New Delhi, India has four HSI investigators listed. Three HSI investigators are listed in the ICE attache office in Phnom Penh, Thailand . Seven HSI personnel operate from the U.S. Embassy in Manila, the Philippines .

In Canada, 13 CBP personnel are listed at the Calgary airport . 22 CBP personnel are listed at the Vancouver International Airport and 27 CBP personnel are listed at the international airport in Toronto. Two more HSI agents are listed at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto . Three HSI personnel are listed at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa .

Ten CBP personnel are listed at an address near the airport in Nassau, the Bahamas . Six CBP personnel are listed at the Dublin airport in Ireland. A CBP officer specializing in “Container Security” is listed at a seaport address in Tokyo. Six agents (five HSI and one ICE-ERO Attache) are listed at the U.S. Embassy in Mexico City .
The website highlights more than 50 ICE and HSI figures , including agents, officers, supervisors, managers and legal counsel based in Chicago.
We reviewed a series of records about DHS agents in Chicago courtesy of Unraveled Press , who have been probing agents that turn up repeatedly.

Martin Lagunas is in the Icepick data as a “supervisory detention deportation officer” based out of the ICE field office in Chicago. He’s listed on more than 30 groups, including “Broadview Mailbox Users” . Broadview is the notorious ICE detention facility near Chicago, and has seven other ICE agents listed , abbreviated as “BRV”. Lagunas is also assigned BRV_Home_Drive and BRV_Share groups, which would likely be linked with Broadview data.

He claimed to be assaulted in Chicago in an October 2025 incident . Michael Sveum, another CBP first level supervisor from El Paso, Texas, is listed ; he was at the site of Renée Good’s killing in Minneapolis alongside Greg Bovino. Edgar Vazquez, another Texas CBP agent at the site of the Good killing, seems to have two entries listed in different Texas cities, with different spellings for the email address. Many other groups from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) are also included in the leak.

coreStoryFacts.text: This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit .
TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database.
The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff .
Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE.
A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.
We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected.
We will update the public when more information is available.”
The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access.
Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years.
One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media.

One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status .

The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest.
“They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen.
The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out.
Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch.
More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S.
Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry.

The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon.
More than 100 HSI agents, including undercover operatives, took part in an operation that included widespread surveillance and infiltration of group chats.
ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing.

Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot.

Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry.

More than 100 HSI agents, including undercover operatives, took part in an operation that included widespread surveillance and infiltration of group chats.
ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing.

Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot.
Washington, DC — There’s been yet another major security breach among federal agencies.

The Department of Homeland Security’s ‘single sign-on’ (SSO) login system was reportedly subverted by a hacker going by “Department of Peace” (DoP), which has revealed thousands upon thousands of federal employee records.
Offices and locations are identified in great detail, from Canadian airports to agents in U.S. embassies around the world.
Groups assigned within the SSO system, going back at least to 2011, are also exposed, showing the names of globe-spanning activities, and management personnel handling undercover operations.

To name one example, the JKR HSI CUC , which would likely be a certified undercover operation group involving Homeland Security Investigations, shows personnel at “ JKR – ICE COLOCATION SAN ANTONIO ” which is likely an HSI office on Jackson Keller Road in the Texas city.

A good example is deployment and development around the widely used Raven suite. “Raven” references a few products Homeland Security has developed internally, with major privacy implications for Americans . “RavenGo UEM Prod” has more than 3400 members including organizational units like “AI” within it.

DoP said back in March amid a leak of “details of 6,681 organizations that applied for contracts” that state violence in Minnesota — the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti — had motivated hacking into Homeland Security.
Martin Lagunas is in the Icepick data as a “supervisory detention deportation officer” based out of the ICE field office in Chicago.
He’s listed on more than 30 groups, including “Broadview Mailbox Users” .
Broadview is the notorious ICE detention facility near Chicago, and has seven other ICE agents listed , abbreviated as “BRV”.
Indeed, Unraveled reporting confirmed Lagunas was highly active at Broadview .
Many other groups from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) are also included in the leak.
Thousands of personnel records include supervisors and subordinates, which enabled generating gigantic organizational charts automatically across these agencies.

Combine this with the groups (some officials tagged in dozens) and one can easily browse around the highest levels of activities, including thousands of groups dealing with surveillance, special operations, finance, social media, and much, much more.
Top personnel are included in dozens of these software groups simultaneously.
For example groups called SG-AMO-EGIS-ITAK-TAK and SG-BEMS-EGIS-OFO-TAK would be used by 140 and 269 CBP personnel respectively for “Team Awareness Kit” access. (More on TAK below.)

The “Twitter.com” group includes not just “web communications,” multimedia and graphics design personnel, but many watch officers, “intelligence operations specialist” and National Operations Center (NOC) personnel. “Organizational Units” in that group include “Proxy Exceptions” which likely indicates their web traffic is handled in a special fashion — inside government agencies, data to external servers is often sent to specialized proxy computers that are controlled firewall gateways to the outside internet.
There are two entries in the database for “Christian Castro,” including an ICE agent stationed in Harlingen, Texas , where he was arrested.
The leaked groups are a kind of breadcrumb trail for software access controls and activities related to major websites like Twitter and Instagram.
The website highlights more than 50 ICE and HSI figures , including agents, officers, supervisors, managers and legal counsel based in Chicago.

extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro. DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.” Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security . He can be reached via encrypted message at zackwhittaker.1337 on Signal. You can also contact him by email, or to verify outreach, at [email protected] .

In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics, seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. The DHS and DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer. “If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify, a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members. Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.” More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy. Most records also name a supervisor, which could allow anyone analyzing the dataset to reconstruct reporting relationships across the department. More than 100 HSI agents, including undercover operatives, took part in an operation that included widespread surveillance and infiltration of group chats. Adam Steinbaugh, a senior attorney at the nonprofit civil liberties group FIRE, says that the Trump administration has taken an expansive view of 18 USC 119, a law that prohibits people from sharing “restricted personal information” about federal officers or their families with the intent to threaten them. “This is information that would be on a business card,” says Steinbaugh of the names and basic work details included in the archive. “That’s not something the government can criminalize." Despite the potential sensitivity of other records in the leaked data, the creators of Icepick do not consider it doxing. “If they weren't hiding their involvement in the repressive arm of the US government, there would be no need for us to expose them in the first place.”

sources.title: ‘Icepick’ Leak Exposes Thousands of Homeland Security Personnel, Groups and More - Unicorn Riot
passages: Washington, DC — There’s been yet another major security breach among federal agencies.

The Department of Homeland Security’s ‘single sign-on’ (SSO) login system was reportedly subverted by a hacker going by “Department of Peace” (DoP), which has revealed thousands upon thousands of federal employee records.
Offices and locations are identified in great detail, from Canadian airports to agents in U.S. embassies around the world.
Groups assigned within the SSO system, going back at least to 2011, are also exposed, showing the names of globe-spanning activities, and management personnel handling undercover operations.

To name one example, the JKR HSI CUC , which would likely be a certified undercover operation group involving Homeland Security Investigations, shows personnel at “ JKR – ICE COLOCATION SAN ANTONIO ” which is likely an HSI office on Jackson Keller Road in the Texas city.

A good example is deployment and development around the widely used Raven suite. “Raven” references a few products Homeland Security has developed internally, with major privacy implications for Americans . “RavenGo UEM Prod” has more than 3400 members including organizational units like “AI” within it.

DoP said back in March amid a leak of “details of 6,681 organizations that applied for contracts” that state violence in Minnesota — the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti — had motivated hacking into Homeland Security.
Martin Lagunas is in the Icepick data as a “supervisory detention deportation officer” based out of the ICE field office in Chicago.
He’s listed on more than 30 groups, including “Broadview Mailbox Users” .
Broadview is the notorious ICE detention facility near Chicago, and has seven other ICE agents listed , abbreviated as “BRV”.
Indeed, Unraveled reporting confirmed Lagunas was highly active at Broadview .
Many other groups from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) are also included in the leak.
Thousands of personnel records include supervisors and subordinates, which enabled generating gigantic organizational charts automatically across these agencies.

Combine this with the groups (some officials tagged in dozens) and one can easily browse around the highest levels of activities, including thousands of groups dealing with surveillance, special operations, finance, social media, and much, much more.

The icepi.cx site includes more than 20 “CUC” groups (Active Directory / Okta workgroups) . (CUC is ICE jargon for “certified undercover” operations.) Each group can be checked for its individual members, which include leadership like assistant director and assistant special agents in charge, who are top personnel at individual field offices.
Top personnel are included in dozens of these software groups simultaneously.
For example groups called SG-AMO-EGIS-ITAK-TAK and SG-BEMS-EGIS-OFO-TAK would be used by 140 and 269 CBP personnel respectively for “Team Awareness Kit” access. (More on TAK below.)

The “Twitter.com” group includes not just “web communications,” multimedia and graphics design personnel, but many watch officers, “intelligence operations specialist” and National Operations Center (NOC) personnel. “Organizational Units” in that group include “Proxy Exceptions” which likely indicates their web traffic is handled in a special fashion — inside government agencies, data to external servers is often sent to specialized proxy computers that are controlled firewall gateways to the outside internet.
There are two entries in the database for “Christian Castro,” including an ICE agent stationed in Harlingen, Texas , where he was arrested.
The leaked groups are a kind of breadcrumb trail for software access controls and activities related to major websites like Twitter and Instagram.
The website highlights more than 50 ICE and HSI figures , including agents, officers, supervisors, managers and legal counsel based in Chicago.

extraction.body: Now posted on Internet: Officials in sensitive locations worldwide, thousands of groups, phone numbers, and countless other details cracked from Homeland Security login system Washington, DC — There’s been yet another major security breach among federal agencies. The Department of Homeland Security’s ‘single sign-on’ (SSO) login system was reportedly subverted by a hacker going by “Department of Peace” (DoP), which has revealed thousands upon thousands of federal employee records. Around one-fifth of Homeland Security’s personnel have been exposed. Offices and locations are identified in great detail, from Canadian airports to agents in U.S. embassies around the world. Groups assigned within the SSO system, going back at least to 2011, are also exposed, showing the names of globe-spanning activities, and management personnel handling undercover operations. Thousands of personnel records include supervisors and subordinates, which enabled generating gigantic organizational charts automatically across these agencies. Combine this with the groups (some officials tagged in dozens) and one can easily browse around the highest levels of activities, including thousands of groups dealing with surveillance, special operations, finance, social media, and much, much more. Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), a U.S.-based transparency nonprofit that “archives and publishes hacked and leaked documents in the public interest,” reported the records were provided by DoP and released on Wednesday, October 28, with help from a Swiss hacktivist and journalist, maia crimew . A searchable website called icepi.cx helps dig around this data which has “been enriched” with updates according to the FAQ ; the whole data set is now online . DoP said back in March amid a leak of “details of 6,681 organizations that applied for contracts” that state violence in Minnesota — the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti — had motivated hacking into Homeland Security. Both of Pretti’s killers appear to be in the leaked data. “Why hack the DHS? I can think of a couple Pretti Good reasons! I’m releasing this because the DHS is killing us and people deserve to know which companies support them and what they’re working on.” Many of the locations were not previously known as ICE or DHS offices. For example a suite on Parthenia Street in Northridge, California, has not been listed as an HSI office but is identified in the data . Keep in mind it could be inaccurate or out of date, but it is thought that journalists and local people will have a lot of places to check on. Jesus Ochoa was named as one of the agents who killed Alex Pretti, and a CBP “Supply chain security specialist” by that name based in Laredo, Texas is listed in the database, and is in various Laredo-related groups like SG-LAR029A-SEALS with more than 60 other Texas CBP personnel. Location 0000A2 , located at the Hidalgo/Pharr/Anzalduas Enrollment Center on South Stewart Road in Mission, Texas, is listed as the work site of Pretti’s other killer, Raymundo Gutierrez, who shared that space with four other “SRT OPERATOR” (an acronym for Special Response Team) and Special Operation Supervisors. A mosaic of Gutierrez’ access to DHS systems is revealed from his group memberships. For example groups called SG-AMO-EGIS-ITAK-TAK and SG-BEMS-EGIS-OFO-TAK would be used by 140 and 269 CBP personnel respectively for “Team Awareness Kit” access. (More on TAK below.) The site notes, “This is not a comprehensive list of all DHS employees. All data is provided as-is; inaccuracies are from source data and may be reproduced.” The icepi.cx site includes more than 20 “CUC” groups (Active Directory / Okta workgroups) . (CUC is ICE jargon for “certified undercover” operations.) Each group can be checked for its individual members, which include leadership like assistant director and assistant special agents in charge, who are top personnel at individual field offices. To name one example, the JKR HSI CUC , which would likely be a certified undercover operation group involving Homeland Security Investigations, shows personnel at “ JKR – ICE COLOCATION SAN ANTONIO ” which is likely an HSI office on Jackson Keller Road in the Texas city. 46 people are indexed at that location. This CUC activity also links to an office in Crystal City, Arlington, VA, called the “NGI – ARLINGTON OFFICE” with 50 people , many of whom are associated with technical programs with titles including R&D computer science, DevOps, senior data engineer, as the assigned workgroups show in exhaustive detail. (More on the Arlington office below.) There are 26 locations linked in Minnesota (filters by state are available). For example, the Grand Marais office at 518 E. HWY 61 is listed with five Customs and Border Protection personnel. 78 personnel associated to the Whipple Federal Building are listed at Fort Snelling, MN but one person’s records are erroneously under Saint Paul. This data could be significant in ongoing federal lawsuits since plaintiffs have named anonymous government officials as “John Doe,” including a lawsuit filed over Renée Good ‘s killing. Emma Best at DDoSecrets mentioned groups that stood out like “ERO-AD REMOVAL AWARD NOMINATION SR APPROVERS” which “hits hard” because their purpose is to congratulate ICE agents for deportations. There are more than 30 groups like this . The leaked groups are a kind of breadcrumb trail for software access controls and activities related to major websites like Twitter and Instagram. The “Twitter.com” group includes not just “web communications,” multimedia and graphics design personnel, but many watch officers, “intelligence operations specialist” and National Operations Center (NOC) personnel. “Organizational Units” in that group include “Proxy Exceptions” which likely indicates their web traffic is handled in a special fashion — inside government agencies, data to external servers is often sent to specialized proxy computers that are controlled firewall gateways to the outside internet. The 30 members in “NOC Twitter Access” appear similar in purpose, such as NOC desk officers and senior watch officers. Top personnel are included in dozens of these software groups simultaneously. A typical one is Citrix . Several groups include “WS1” (not to be confused with AWS, which likely means Amazon Web Services), such as “WS1-DHS-HQ-PROD-Sync-Users” . WS1 is a common federal abbreviation for Omnissa Workspace One . Major software packages are typically managed by service vendors. Just days ago Carahsoft obtained a nearly $2.7 billion blanket purchase agreement under a sole-source justification for dozens of vendors including Omnissa . Cellebrite is a cellphone data extraction vendor which is included in the Carahsoft sole-source agreement and mentioned in two groups. The SG-EDN006A-INTEL-CELLEBRITE group has 52 members , mostly CBP intelligence officers in Texas. The personnel index can be sorted by international locations as well, which are often five zeroes followed by a two-letter country code. In London, two CBP and three HSI personnel operate from the prominent, cube-shaped U.S. Embassy at 33 Nine Elms Lane . Some agents carry the title FSNI or “Foreign Service National Investigator” as ICE or its HSI subdivision; “Mission Support Specialist” is another common title. Three personnel, two of them investigators, are listed as in country “HN” , which is likely to mean Honduras, at the “TGK – U.S. EMBASSY” which likely means Tegucigalpa, the capital. Seven HSI investigators and other staff are listed at the BUE – Consular Section in Bangkok, Thailand. New Delhi, India has four HSI investigators listed. Three HSI investigators are listed in the ICE attache office in Phnom Penh, Thailand . Seven HSI personnel operate from the U.S. Embassy in Manila, the Philippines . In Canada, 13 CBP personnel are listed at the Calgary airport . 22 CBP personnel are listed at the Vancouver International Airport and 27 CBP personnel are listed at the international airport in Toronto. Two more HSI agents are listed at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto . Three HSI personnel are listed at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa . Ten CBP personnel are listed at an address near the airport in Nassau, the Bahamas . Six CBP personnel are listed at the Dublin airport in Ireland. A CBP officer specializing in “Container Security” is listed at a seaport address in Tokyo. Six agents (five HSI and one ICE-ERO Attache) are listed at the U.S. Embassy in Mexico City . The website highlights more than 50 ICE and HSI figures , including agents, officers, supervisors, managers and legal counsel based in Chicago. We reviewed a series of records about DHS agents in Chicago courtesy of Unraveled Press , who have been probing agents that turn up repeatedly. Martin Lagunas is in the Icepick data as a “supervisory detention deportation officer” based out of the ICE field office in Chicago. He’s listed on more than 30 groups, including “Broadview Mailbox Users” . Broadview is the notorious ICE detention facility near Chicago, and has seven other ICE agents listed , abbreviated as “BRV”. Indeed, Unraveled reporting confirmed Lagunas was highly active at Broadview . Lagunas is also assigned BRV_Home_Drive and BRV_Share groups, which would likely be linked with Broadview data. A few other entries matching Unraveled Press records: Alfredo Alvillar is listed in the records as a “1st Level Supervisor” in CBP based in Texas. He claimed to be assaulted in Chicago in an October 2025 incident . Michael Sveum, another CBP first level supervisor from El Paso, Texas, is listed ; he was at the site of Renée Good’s killing in Minneapolis alongside Greg Bovino. Edgar Vazquez, another Texas CBP agent at the site of the Good killing, seems to have two entries listed in different Texas cities, with different spellings for the email address. Sveum and Vazquez were both active in fighting protesters in Chicago as well. Note that the name search requires entering “%lagunas” to search for names ending that way – the % symbol is a wildcard. The leaks map out personnel, programs and systems at the highest levels of DHS & ICE technological research and implementation, which serves agents on American streets. A good example is deployment and development around the widely used Raven suite. “Raven” references a few products Homeland Security has developed internally, with major privacy implications for Americans . “RavenGo UEM Prod” has more than 3400 members including organizational units like “AI” within it. The “IC_raven_cloudbees_developers” group, while small, has several research & development computer science figures in it, and is colocated between the “NGI – ARLINGTON OFFICE” and Sandia National Laboratories in New Mexico. Cloudbees is an agentic coding vendor . Raven is short for Repository for Analytics in a Virtualized Environment, which is an AI-enhanced platform . (Additionally, per an attachment on contract award HSHQDC-12-D-00014 Raven is built on Blackberry United Endpoint Management (UEM).) Raven Compliance Automation Tool is another program in the suite. The Brennan Center investigated several vendors profiting from Raven development . There are nearly 20 “UEM” groups which include 4551 “UEM ERO Users” , who would likely be ICE deportation agents.) “UEM LEO Users” has more than 3700 members, including many deportation officers across the country. (LEO is a common acronym for Law Enforcement Organization.) There are two entries in the database for “Christian Castro,” including an ICE agent stationed in Harlingen, Texas , where he was arrested. The #ERO HARLINGEN FLD OFC group includes 160 members and there are 119 members in the HLG – HARLINGEN FIELD OFFICE ANNEX location . However the listed email address appears to have an N as a middle initial. A CBP Border Patrol Agent in Las Cruces with the same name is also listed , without any middle initial. Cyber groups : ICE-LSC Foxfire Users-SG, aws-dhs-uscis-acob-pentest-nonprod-Full-Access, BlackHat Coord, BOD 24-0X – Vulnerability Management, BOD 25-0X Known Exploited Configurations, Salt Typhoon Issue Team. Many other groups from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) are also included in the leak. Detention, asylum, removal groups : Many contain terms like DET, ERO, Removal, Detain, Detention. Including: #ERO HQ Removal, ICE-ERO-SLC-Removals-Escorts-SG, ICE-ERO-UT-Detainee-Requests-SG, DAL Detention and Removal, ICE-DET-DRO-Removals, ICE-DET-FlightOps, ICE-DET-SocialMedia, ICE-DET-Transport, Oklahoma Detained, AsylumCPMSCorrections-Full-Access. As locations, detention centers like the Moshannon Valley Correctional Facility in Philipsburg, PA are included with 8 personnel from ICE, mostly deportation officers.
