Keep in mind it could be inaccurate or out of date, but it is thought that journalists and local people will have a lot of places to check on.

Jesus Ochoa was named as one of the agents who killed Alex Pretti, and a CBP “Supply chain security specialist” by that name based in Laredo, Texas is listed in the database, and is in various Laredo-related groups like SG-LAR029A-SEALS with more than 60 other Texas CBP personnel.

Location 0000A2 , located at the Hidalgo/Pharr/Anzalduas Enrollment Center on South Stewart Road in Mission, Texas, is listed as the work site of Pretti’s other killer, Raymundo Gutierrez, who shared that space with four other “SRT OPERATOR” (an acronym for Special Response Team) and Special Operation Supervisors. A mosaic of Gutierrez’ access to DHS systems is revealed from his group memberships. For example groups called SG-AMO-EGIS-ITAK-TAK and SG-BEMS-EGIS-OFO-TAK would be used by 140 and 269 CBP personnel respectively for “Team Awareness Kit” access. (More on TAK below.)
The site notes, “This is not a comprehensive list of all DHS employees. All data is provided as-is; inaccuracies are from source data and may be reproduced.”

The icepi.cx site includes more than 20 “CUC” groups (Active Directory / Okta workgroups) . (CUC is ICE jargon for “certified undercover” operations.) Each group can be checked for its individual members, which include leadership like assistant director and assistant special agents in charge, who are top personnel at individual field offices.

To name one example, the JKR HSI CUC , which would likely be a certified undercover operation group involving Homeland Security Investigations, shows personnel at “ JKR – ICE COLOCATION SAN ANTONIO ” which is likely an HSI office on Jackson Keller Road in the Texas city. 46 people are indexed at that location. This CUC activity also links to an office in Crystal City, Arlington, VA, called the “NGI – ARLINGTON OFFICE” with 50 people , many of whom are associated with technical programs with titles including R&D computer science, DevOps, senior data engineer, as the assigned workgroups show in exhaustive detail. (More on the Arlington office below.)
There are 26 locations linked in Minnesota (filters by state are available). For example, the Grand Marais office at 518 E. HWY 61 is listed with five Customs and Border Protection personnel.

78 personnel associated to the Whipple Federal Building are listed at Fort Snelling, MN but one person’s records are erroneously under Saint Paul. This data could be significant in ongoing federal lawsuits since plaintiffs have named anonymous government officials as “John Doe,” including a lawsuit filed over Renée Good ‘s killing.

Emma Best at DDoSecrets mentioned groups that stood out like “ERO-AD REMOVAL AWARD NOMINATION SR APPROVERS” which “hits hard” because their purpose is to congratulate ICE agents for deportations. There are more than 30 groups like this .
The leaked groups are a kind of breadcrumb trail for software access controls and activities related to major websites like Twitter and Instagram.

The “Twitter.com” group includes not just “web communications,” multimedia and graphics design personnel, but many watch officers, “intelligence operations specialist” and National Operations Center (NOC) personnel. “Organizational Units” in that group include “Proxy Exceptions” which likely indicates their web traffic is handled in a special fashion — inside government agencies, data to external servers is often sent to specialized proxy computers that are controlled firewall gateways to the outside internet. The 30 members in “NOC Twitter Access” appear similar in purpose, such as NOC desk officers and senior watch officers.

Top personnel are included in dozens of these software groups simultaneously. A typical one is Citrix . Several groups include “WS1” (not to be confused with AWS, which likely means Amazon Web Services), such as “WS1-DHS-HQ-PROD-Sync-Users” . WS1 is a common federal abbreviation for Omnissa Workspace One . Major software packages are typically managed by service vendors. Just days ago Carahsoft obtained a nearly $2.7 billion blanket purchase agreement under a sole-source justification for dozens of vendors including Omnissa .

Cellebrite is a cellphone data extraction vendor which is included in the Carahsoft sole-source agreement and mentioned in two groups. The SG-EDN006A-INTEL-CELLEBRITE group has 52 members , mostly CBP intelligence officers in Texas.
The personnel index can be sorted by international locations as well, which are often five zeroes followed by a two-letter country code.

In London, two CBP and three HSI personnel operate from the prominent, cube-shaped U.S. Embassy at 33 Nine Elms Lane . Some agents carry the title FSNI or “Foreign Service National Investigator” as ICE or its HSI subdivision; “Mission Support Specialist” is another common title.
Three personnel, two of them investigators, are listed as in country “HN” , which is likely to mean Honduras, at the “TGK – U.S. EMBASSY” which likely means Tegucigalpa, the capital.

Seven HSI investigators and other staff are listed at the BUE – Consular Section in Bangkok, Thailand. New Delhi, India has four HSI investigators listed. Three HSI investigators are listed in the ICE attache office in Phnom Penh, Thailand . Seven HSI personnel operate from the U.S. Embassy in Manila, the Philippines .

In Canada, 13 CBP personnel are listed at the Calgary airport . 22 CBP personnel are listed at the Vancouver International Airport and 27 CBP personnel are listed at the international airport in Toronto. Two more HSI agents are listed at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto . Three HSI personnel are listed at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa .

Ten CBP personnel are listed at an address near the airport in Nassau, the Bahamas . Six CBP personnel are listed at the Dublin airport in Ireland. A CBP officer specializing in “Container Security” is listed at a seaport address in Tokyo. Six agents (five HSI and one ICE-ERO Attache) are listed at the U.S. Embassy in Mexico City .
The website highlights more than 50 ICE and HSI figures , including agents, officers, supervisors, managers and legal counsel based in Chicago.
We reviewed a series of records about DHS agents in Chicago courtesy of Unraveled Press , who have been probing agents that turn up repeatedly.

Martin Lagunas is in the Icepick data as a “supervisory detention deportation officer” based out of the ICE field office in Chicago. He’s listed on more than 30 groups, including “Broadview Mailbox Users” . Broadview is the notorious ICE detention facility near Chicago, and has seven other ICE agents listed , abbreviated as “BRV”. Indeed, Unraveled reporting confirmed Lagunas was highly active at Broadview .
Lagunas is also assigned BRV_Home_Drive and BRV_Share groups, which would likely be linked with Broadview data.

A few other entries matching Unraveled Press records: Alfredo Alvillar is listed in the records as a “1st Level Supervisor” in CBP based in Texas. He claimed to be assaulted in Chicago in an October 2025 incident . Michael Sveum, another CBP first level supervisor from El Paso, Texas, is listed ; he was at the site of Renée Good’s killing in Minneapolis alongside Greg Bovino. Edgar Vazquez, another Texas CBP agent at the site of the Good killing, seems to have two entries listed in different Texas cities, with different spellings for the email address. Sveum and Vazquez were both active in fighting protesters in Chicago as well. Note that the name search requires entering “%lagunas” to search for names ending that way – the % symbol is a wildcard.

The leaks map out personnel, programs and systems at the highest levels of DHS & ICE technological research and implementation, which serves agents on American streets. A good example is deployment and development around the widely used Raven suite. “Raven” references a few products Homeland Security has developed internally, with major privacy implications for Americans . “RavenGo UEM Prod” has more than 3400 members including organizational units like “AI” within it. The “IC_raven_cloudbees_developers” group, while small, has several research & development computer science figures in it, and is colocated between the “NGI – ARLINGTON OFFICE” and Sandia National Laboratories in New Mexico. Cloudbees is an agentic coding vendor .

Raven is short for Repository for Analytics in a Virtualized Environment, which is an AI-enhanced platform . (Additionally, per an attachment on contract award HSHQDC-12-D-00014 Raven is built on Blackberry United Endpoint Management (UEM).) Raven Compliance Automation Tool is another program in the suite. The Brennan Center investigated several vendors profiting from Raven development .

There are nearly 20 “UEM” groups which include 4551 “UEM ERO Users” , who would likely be ICE deportation agents.) “UEM LEO Users” has more than 3700 members, including many deportation officers across the country. (LEO is a common acronym for Law Enforcement Organization.)

There are two entries in the database for “Christian Castro,” including an ICE agent stationed in Harlingen, Texas , where he was arrested. The #ERO HARLINGEN FLD OFC group includes 160 members and there are 119 members in the HLG – HARLINGEN FIELD OFFICE ANNEX location . However the listed email address appears to have an N as a middle initial. A CBP Border Patrol Agent in Las Cruces with the same name is also listed , without any middle initial.

Cyber groups : ICE-LSC Foxfire Users-SG, aws-dhs-uscis-acob-pentest-nonprod-Full-Access, BlackHat Coord, BOD 24-0X – Vulnerability Management, BOD 25-0X Known Exploited Configurations, Salt Typhoon Issue Team. Many other groups from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) are also included in the leak.

Detention, asylum, removal groups : Many contain terms like DET, ERO, Removal, Detain, Detention. Including: #ERO HQ Removal, ICE-ERO-SLC-Removals-Escorts-SG, ICE-ERO-UT-Detainee-Requests-SG, DAL Detention and Removal, ICE-DET-DRO-Removals, ICE-DET-FlightOps, ICE-DET-SocialMedia, ICE-DET-Transport, Oklahoma Detained, AsylumCPMSCorrections-Full-Access. As locations, detention centers like the Moshannon Valley Correctional Facility in Philipsburg, PA are included with 8 personnel from ICE, mostly deportation officers.

extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro. DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.” Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security . He can be reached via encrypted message at zackwhittaker.1337 on Signal. You can also contact him by email, or to verify outreach, at [email protected] .

extraction.body: A previously undisclosed intrusion at the Department of Homeland Security has exposed the names, job titles, work email addresses, cell phone numbers and office locations of more than 41,000 employees, with the stolen records now circulating publicly online. The dataset covers roughly one-fifth of the department's approximately 220,000-strong workforce, spanning border and immigration agents, cybersecurity personnel and senior officials. A hacker using the handle "Department of Peace" claimed to have pulled the material from an Okta single sign-on system that DHS uses to let employees and contractors across its component agencies reach its central network. According to TechCrunch, which reviewed the data, more than half of the records -- about 21,000 -- belong to employees of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the agency that staffs airports and other ports of entry. Another 10,000 or so are tied to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, while just under 1,000 relate to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). Remaining records cover headquarters staff and other offices, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. Timestamps on the individual records suggest the directory was extracted around mid-August. The material was reportedly passed to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who shared a copy with DDoSecrets, a nonprofit collective that publishes leaked datasets in the public interest. The group is hosting the release under the name "Icepick." "They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs," the hacker wrote in a note accompanying the data. The department did not respond to requests for comment, and it remains unclear whether the vulnerability that permitted the access has been closed or whether officials were aware of the theft before it surfaced. Okta said it had reviewed the matter and found no sign of compromise on its side. "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised," a spokesperson said. Beyond personal details, the files shed light on how DHS organizes access to its internal systems. The records list membership in Active Directory user groups that govern which tools employees may use, including Microsoft 365, Adobe Acrobat and Citrix, along with third-party services. Some of those groups point to surveillance and monitoring products. About 4,500 accounts, including ICE agents and deportation officers, sit in a group labeled "Headspace_users," a reference to the online therapy provider that held an $82,500 federal contract with ICE ending in 2023. A Headspace spokesperson said the company has not served DHS or ICE since then. Dozens of other groups reference Penlink, a web surveillance firm whose technology is marketed as able to track location data from hundreds of millions of mobile devices and to capture real-time intelligence from calls, texts, web activity and social media. The groups range from a handful of users in local field offices to more than 2,000 across HSI nationally. Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One group links more than 200 CBP users to Mobile Fortify, a facial recognition application used by both CBP and ICE to identify individuals and verify immigration status. Others are associated with ChatGPT access, including for senior officials, and with investigative work on the China-linked intrusion sets known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. The incident is the second involving DHS this year, following the same hacker's earlier claim to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and private-sector vendors, including defense contractors and surveillance suppliers. It also adds to a run of federal breaches, among them the theft of personnel records for thousands of FBI agents and the personal data of millions of serving and former military personnel held by the Pentagon's human resources unit. Transparency advocates argue the exposed directory could open new avenues for oversight, particularly through public records requests that depend on pinpointing individual government email addresses. "Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results," said Ryan Shapiro, executive director of the nonprofit Property of the People. DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best described the release as a "catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests." The disclosure lands at a politically charged moment. DHS has moved to shield the identities of CBP and ICE personnel conducting immigration enforcement operations across the country, and the publication of agent contact details could complicate those efforts. The department's enforcement record has become a central issue for voters ahead of the midterm elections. For the cybersecurity industry, the episode puts fresh scrutiny on identity providers that serve as the front door to sprawling government networks. Okta's denial of any compromise shifts attention to how DHS configured and governed its own tenant, and to whether access controls around third-party applications were adequately segmented. Vendors named in the leaked user groups -- among them Penlink and Headspace -- now face questions about how their government customers manage account provisioning, even where the underlying contracts have lapsed. extraction.body: A leak website was published Wednesday, showcasing internal data on more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors after it was obtained by hackers who claimed to have breached an identity service used by the agency. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and the hacker maia arson crimew got the data from a hacktivist outfit known as the Department of Peace. ”The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in [its] simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government’s hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation — along with key personnel in DHS’s ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs,” said Emma Best, founder of DDoSecrets. CyberScoop was able to verify numerous current Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency employees are listed in the data, along with some former leadership members who left the agency years ago. The data goes back years, with various group names listed in the database making reference to COVID-19 planning and internal summits in 2023. The hacktivists said the breach was a response to the promise of stepped-up operations from Immigrations and Customs Enforcement by DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. ”On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was ’turning up the heat.’ This is what happens to ICE when you do that,” said a spokesperson for the Department of Peace. The spokesperson said they obtained the database from an Okta single sign-on service used at DHS. Okta said it was aware of the report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” an Okta spokesperson said. DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment. ”This dataset is massive in terms of both size and impact,” said crimew, a Swiss hacker and journalist who has been indicted in the United States over past leaks and who created a search tool for the DHS data. “It provides an unprecedented look into the Department of Homeland Security’s organizational structure, highlighting which people do what work across multiple DHS agencies, including ICE.” One researcher said the leak could prove valuable for Freedom of Information Act requests. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People, said. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent.” DHS has suffered notable breaches before, dating back to a 2014 breach that may have exposed the data of 390,000 then-current and former Homeland Security Department employees, job applicants and contractors. In 2018, DHS notified nearly 250,000 people of a breach at the department. Earlier this year, Security firm GitGuardian said it discovered a public GitHub repository that exposed credentials for privileged AWS GovCloud accounts and internal CISA systems dating back to November 2025.

extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro. DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.” Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security . He can be reached via encrypted message at zackwhittaker.1337 on Signal. You can also contact him by email, or to verify outreach, at [email protected] .

extraction.body: A leak website was published Wednesday, showcasing internal data on more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors after it was obtained by hackers who claimed to have breached an identity service used by the agency. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and the hacker maia arson crimew got the data from a hacktivist outfit known as the Department of Peace. ”The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in [its] simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government’s hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation — along with key personnel in DHS’s ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs,” said Emma Best, founder of DDoSecrets. CyberScoop was able to verify numerous current Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency employees are listed in the data, along with some former leadership members who left the agency years ago. The data goes back years, with various group names listed in the database making reference to COVID-19 planning and internal summits in 2023. The hacktivists said the breach was a response to the promise of stepped-up operations from Immigrations and Customs Enforcement by DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. ”On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was ’turning up the heat.’ This is what happens to ICE when you do that,” said a spokesperson for the Department of Peace. The spokesperson said they obtained the database from an Okta single sign-on service used at DHS. Okta said it was aware of the report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” an Okta spokesperson said. DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment. ”This dataset is massive in terms of both size and impact,” said crimew, a Swiss hacker and journalist who has been indicted in the United States over past leaks and who created a search tool for the DHS data. “It provides an unprecedented look into the Department of Homeland Security’s organizational structure, highlighting which people do what work across multiple DHS agencies, including ICE.” One researcher said the leak could prove valuable for Freedom of Information Act requests. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People, said. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent.” DHS has suffered notable breaches before, dating back to a 2014 breach that may have exposed the data of 390,000 then-current and former Homeland Security Department employees, job applicants and contractors. In 2018, DHS notified nearly 250,000 people of a breach at the department. Earlier this year, Security firm GitGuardian said it discovered a public GitHub repository that exposed credentials for privileged AWS GovCloud accounts and internal CISA systems dating back to November 2025.

passages: About 250 union watchmen at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach could strike as early as 5 p.m.
1, threatening cargo operations at the nation’s busiest container port complex if negotiators fail to reach a new labor agreement.
The potential disruption could extend well beyond the security workforce.
The employer group expects other ILWU members would honor picket lines, potentially halting vessel, yard and gate operations at affected facilities.

The strike threat comes as the LA–Long Beach complex is already contending with a backlog of containers awaiting inland rail transportation.

extraction.body: About 250 union watchmen at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach could strike as early as 5 p.m. Pacific time Sunday, Nov. 1, threatening cargo operations at the nation’s busiest container port complex if negotiators fail to reach a new labor agreement. Members of International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 have authorized a strike, according to the Pacific Maritime Association, which represents employers. The employers group said negotiations are continuing with the assistance of federal mediators. The potential disruption could extend well beyond the security workforce. PMA said the watchmen represent about 2% of ILWU workers at the two ports, but work at terminals handling roughly 85% of Long Beach’s cargo and 33% of Los Angeles’ cargo. The employer group expects other ILWU members would honor picket lines, potentially halting vessel, yard and gate operations at affected facilities. The watchmen’s previous agreement expired in July 2025, and employees have continued working under extensions. The latest extension expires Sunday, following more than a year of negotiations that have left the union and employers divided. PMA said significant differences remain but pledged to keep negotiating. “The Pacific Maritime Association remains committed to reaching a fair agreement with ILWU Local 26 at the bargaining table, and we will continue to negotiate in good faith through the November 1 deadline and beyond if necessary,” the association said in an email to FreightWaves. Employers said their offer includes wage increases and pension improvements. The local has not detailed its demands. The PMA said full-time watchmen currently earn an average of more than $170,000 annually, plus fully employer-paid health care and pension benefits. “The Port of Los Angeles encourages all parties to continue negotiating in good faith toward a mutually acceptable resolution,” the Port of Los Angeles said in an email to FreightWaves. “We recognize the importance of reaching an agreement that serves the interests of the parties involved while ensuring the continued movement of cargo through our port. We remain hopeful that an agreement can be reached without any disruption to operations.” The contract of Local 26 members is separate from the coastwide agreement covering ILWU longshore workers and marine clerks, which runs through 2028. The strike threat comes as the LA–Long Beach complex is already contending with a backlog of containers awaiting inland rail transportation. Terminal congestion and difficulties positioning enough rail equipment in Southern California have contributed to delays, raising concerns about the movement of holiday merchandise toward the eastern United States. This article was update Oct. 28 to add a comment from the Port of Los Angeles. Why it matters: A strike by just 250 watchmen could become a much larger cargo shutdown if other union dockworkers honor the local’s picket lines. extraction.body: Long Beach's most read source for local news, investigative reports, arts & culture, food, business, sports, and real-estate. The busiest year on record so far for the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach could run aground if bargaining between a small security workers union and shipping companies isn’t resolved. International Longshore and Warehouse Union’s Local 26, which represents about 250 watchmen who provide security at individual shipping terminals, has authorized a strike that could start at 5 p.m. Sunday. The union represents about 2% of ILWU’s workforce, but their work is spread across six terminals — split between Long Beach and Los Angeles — that handle more than half of the complex’s cargo, including 85% at the Long Beach seaport. If the strike is carried out, officials say thousands of other unionized dockworkers — the longshoremen, marine clerks and foremen — could honor the picket lines and not go to work. That would halt much of the work at the ports — which handle more than 31% of the nation’s containerized cargo — just as the heavy shipping season for holiday merchandise begins to gather steam. Negotiations have carried on since July 2025, after the contract expired between the union and Pacific Maritime Association, which represents the operators of all 12 terminals at the port complex. PMA said in a statement it has “put a strong economic package on the table,” that includes wage increases and pension improvements. But no deal has been struck and “significant differences remain.” “A timely agreement matters not only to the parties at the table, but to the entire Southern California supply chain and to the local, state and national economies that depend on it,” the statement read. “We urge Local 26 to work with us to reach an agreement that avoids a disruption at the nation’s two busiest ports.” A spokesperson for the union did not immediately respond to requests for comment or say when members voted to authorize the strike. In the meantime, the ports’ administrators said Wednesday they are closely watching negotiations and remain hopeful some resolution will come about ahead of the weekend. “Although the Port of Long Beach is not a party to the negotiations, we want to assure our customers that we remain committed to moving cargo through our port safely and reliably,” said Long Beach Port CEO Noel Hacegaba. Agreements for other unionized dockworkers expire in 2028. The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach are by far the nation’s largest container port complex, moving more than 20 million containers in 2025. That trade carried a value of more than $1.6 trillion last year. In Long Beach last month, the seaport saw a record 997,177 containers — 25% more than last September — in a jump that included 509,390, more than 31% higher than the same month last year. Hacegaba said that, “While the affected watchmen provide security within individual terminals, port-wide security provided by the Harbor Patrol and the Long Beach Police Department continues uninterrupted during negotiations.”

extraction.body: About 250 union watchmen at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach could strike as early as 5 p.m. Pacific time Sunday, Nov. 1, threatening cargo operations at the nation’s busiest container port complex if negotiators fail to reach a new labor agreement. Members of International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 have authorized a strike, according to the Pacific Maritime Association, which represents employers. The employers group said negotiations are continuing with the assistance of federal mediators. The potential disruption could extend well beyond the security workforce. PMA said the watchmen represent about 2% of ILWU workers at the two ports, but work at terminals handling roughly 85% of Long Beach’s cargo and 33% of Los Angeles’ cargo. The employer group expects other ILWU members would honor picket lines, potentially halting vessel, yard and gate operations at affected facilities. The watchmen’s previous agreement expired in July 2025, and employees have continued working under extensions. The latest extension expires Sunday, following more than a year of negotiations that have left the union and employers divided. PMA said significant differences remain but pledged to keep negotiating. “The Pacific Maritime Association remains committed to reaching a fair agreement with ILWU Local 26 at the bargaining table, and we will continue to negotiate in good faith through the November 1 deadline and beyond if necessary,” the association said in an email to FreightWaves. Employers said their offer includes wage increases and pension improvements. The local has not detailed its demands. The PMA said full-time watchmen currently earn an average of more than $170,000 annually, plus fully employer-paid health care and pension benefits. “The Port of Los Angeles encourages all parties to continue negotiating in good faith toward a mutually acceptable resolution,” the Port of Los Angeles said in an email to FreightWaves. “We recognize the importance of reaching an agreement that serves the interests of the parties involved while ensuring the continued movement of cargo through our port. We remain hopeful that an agreement can be reached without any disruption to operations.” The contract of Local 26 members is separate from the coastwide agreement covering ILWU longshore workers and marine clerks, which runs through 2028. The strike threat comes as the LA–Long Beach complex is already contending with a backlog of containers awaiting inland rail transportation. Terminal congestion and difficulties positioning enough rail equipment in Southern California have contributed to delays, raising concerns about the movement of holiday merchandise toward the eastern United States. This article was update Oct. 28 to add a comment from the Port of Los Angeles. Why it matters: A strike by just 250 watchmen could become a much larger cargo shutdown if other union dockworkers honor the local’s picket lines. extraction.body: Long Beach's most read source for local news, investigative reports, arts & culture, food, business, sports, and real-estate. The busiest year on record so far for the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach could run aground if bargaining between a small security workers union and shipping companies isn’t resolved. International Longshore and Warehouse Union’s Local 26, which represents about 250 watchmen who provide security at individual shipping terminals, has authorized a strike that could start at 5 p.m. Sunday. The union represents about 2% of ILWU’s workforce, but their work is spread across six terminals — split between Long Beach and Los Angeles — that handle more than half of the complex’s cargo, including 85% at the Long Beach seaport. If the strike is carried out, officials say thousands of other unionized dockworkers — the longshoremen, marine clerks and foremen — could honor the picket lines and not go to work. That would halt much of the work at the ports — which handle more than 31% of the nation’s containerized cargo — just as the heavy shipping season for holiday merchandise begins to gather steam. Negotiations have carried on since July 2025, after the contract expired between the union and Pacific Maritime Association, which represents the operators of all 12 terminals at the port complex. PMA said in a statement it has “put a strong economic package on the table,” that includes wage increases and pension improvements. But no deal has been struck and “significant differences remain.” “A timely agreement matters not only to the parties at the table, but to the entire Southern California supply chain and to the local, state and national economies that depend on it,” the statement read. “We urge Local 26 to work with us to reach an agreement that avoids a disruption at the nation’s two busiest ports.” A spokesperson for the union did not immediately respond to requests for comment or say when members voted to authorize the strike. In the meantime, the ports’ administrators said Wednesday they are closely watching negotiations and remain hopeful some resolution will come about ahead of the weekend. “Although the Port of Long Beach is not a party to the negotiations, we want to assure our customers that we remain committed to moving cargo through our port safely and reliably,” said Long Beach Port CEO Noel Hacegaba. Agreements for other unionized dockworkers expire in 2028. The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach are by far the nation’s largest container port complex, moving more than 20 million containers in 2025. That trade carried a value of more than $1.6 trillion last year. In Long Beach last month, the seaport saw a record 997,177 containers — 25% more than last September — in a jump that included 509,390, more than 31% higher than the same month last year. Hacegaba said that, “While the affected watchmen provide security within individual terminals, port-wide security provided by the Harbor Patrol and the Long Beach Police Department continues uninterrupted during negotiations.”

sources.title: Google tells platforms to noindex link-shared pages by default - PPC Land
passages: Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist.
The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp.
Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes.
Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link.
Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached.

Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records.
Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths.
It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document.
That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content.

A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content.
The new section does not discuss the interaction.
Google's own products fall within the categories as well.
Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.
Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable.

What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results.
Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website.
Google names no products, companies or technologies.
The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page.
A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage.
It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index.
The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule.
Google does not say which services prompted the change.
PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language.
The change also concerns publishers, SEO teams and marketers who build on those platforms or compete with pages hosted on them.

Research by security firm RedAccess, reported in May 2026, found more than 5,000 apps built with vibe coding tools such as Lovable, Replit, Base44 and Netlify that had essentially no authentication, along with phishing sites impersonating Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe's and McDonald's on Lovable's domain .

Google has a help page for websites that let the public post things, and today it said that tools where people make pages, apps or automatically generated content to share by link can be abused by spammers too. Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website. Google now says pages like that should be hidden from search by default, and that the companies running these tools should watch Search Console and their own numbers for sudden jumps in new public pages. The page is titled "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform." It sits in the "Preventing and monitoring abuse" part of Search Central's monitoring and debugging documentation, alongside guides on malware, phishing and deceptive sites, and the Google Safe Browsing Repeat Offenders Policy. Three passages are new or rewritten. Every other paragraph, from the reputation system for new accounts to an example about overnight traffic from Italian IP addresses on a site aimed at Japan, is unchanged word for word. The introduction previously warned that spammers exploit open comment forms, and that "hosting platforms may be similarly open to abuse," with spammers creating large numbers of sites that break Google's spam policies. The first asks services whose users create "shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools" to consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or "only accessed directly by people with a link." "When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default." Everything turns on the final two words. The guide does not tell platforms to keep shared content out of Search permanently, nor does it describe what should happen when a user wants a shared page to be found. It also names two Search Console reports, Page Indexing and Search performance, to be checked regularly for "unexpected spikes in indexed pages, impressions, or queries" that do not match what the platform is for. Neither item comes with a threshold. Google does not say what size of spike warrants attention, or what share of indexable URLs counts as "large." Platforms that tighten indexing defaults reduce one source of that competition. The guide's warning applies to every such service, whatever its current defaults.

The change also concerns publishers, SEO teams and marketers who build on those platforms or compete with pages hosted on them.

Where: On the "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform" page in the Search Central documentation, under monitoring and debugging, with the monitoring tools located in Search Console.

The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp.
Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes.
Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link.
Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached.

Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records.
Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths.
It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document.
That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content.

A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content.
The new section does not discuss the interaction.
Google's own products fall within the categories as well.
Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.
Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable.

What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results.
Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website.
Google names no products, companies or technologies.
The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page.
A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage.
It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index.
The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule.
Google does not say which services prompted the change.

The change also concerns publishers, SEO teams and marketers who build on those platforms or compete with pages hosted on them.

RedAccess located the apps by searching Google and Bing for the platforms' default domains.
The UGC Fresh Data Program offers a contrast with today's change.

Within one month, then, Google has documented a faster route into its systems for moderated public discussion, and a default route out of its index for user-created pages that were never meant to be searched.

The question of manual actions has been live for weeks.
The evidence was anecdotal, and Google did not comment.
That update was the fourth spam update of the year, following rollouts on March 24, June 24 and August 18 .

New spam guidance says to noindex or block crawling on pages made for sharing. Google's docs say a URL blocked in robots.txt can be indexed.

Google has recently created an additional “Only index content meant for Search” section within the spam guide it updated on Oct. 26. The new section advises websites with pages made for direct sharing, collaboration or utility to set a noindex tag or use a robots.txt directive to block crawlers by default for those pages.
According to Google’s changelog this is an addition relating to “blocking indexing of link-shared content.”
The new section includes a link to the introductory page about robots.txt , and according to that introductory page the robots.txt file “is not a mechanism for keeping a web page out of Google.”
Google’s new “Only index content meant for Search” section follows the guide’s advice on spotting spammy accounts and reads:

“If your service lets users create shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools, consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or only accessed directly by people with a link.”

“When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default.”

The guide’s opening paragraph said hosting platforms “may be similarly open to abuse.” The updated sentence adds “tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps,” and says spammers may create a large number of “pages or sites” where it used to say sites.
The previous version, last updated Dec. 10, 2025, already suggested noindex on posts from new users until they build a reputation on the platform. That advice is unchanged.

Google’s robots.txt introduction says a page “that’s disallowed in robots.txt can still be indexed if linked to from other sites.” Google won’t crawl the blocked content in that case, but the URL and possibly the anchor text of links pointing to it can appear in results, without a description.

Google’s page on noindex says the rule only works when robots.txt isn’t blocking the page, because otherwise “the crawler will never see the noindex rule.” Google’s “Control what you share” page , updated Oct. 21, lists robots.txt as applicable to “images and video” and noindex as applicable to “all content types.”

On July 27, I confirmed that Claude’s share path was blocked by a “Disallow” directive in robots.txt. In addition, the share pages also returned a “none” value for the X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header. Google treats “none” as equal to both noindex and nofollow according to its documentation of robots meta tags . I have been unable to determine what Google saw when it initially found those links.

The new spam guide from Google states you should be verifying your website or subdomain through Search Console for your platform to receive emails when it gets a manual action or has a security issue. It further suggests you check the Page Indexing report and Search performance report on an ongoing basis for “unexpected spikes” of indexed pages, impressions or queries which do not align with your platform’s intent.

A new bullet under the guide’s monitoring advice suggests tracking creation and indexing at the platform level, with alerts for spikes in newly published public pages or “a small number of users generating a large share of indexable URLs.”
Google’s changelog says its Oct. 26 update to the spam guide aims to help platforms “keep user-created pages that aren’t meant for Search out of the index and detect spam earlier.”
For share links, generated outputs, and app pages, check that any noindex can reach Googlebot. A robots.txt rule that blocks Googlebot from those pages means Google never reads it.

The Page Indexing report that Google’s new monitoring advice points to has a status called “Indexed, though blocked by robots.txt.” Google’s help for that status says to remove the block and use noindex. Share URLs that Google indexes despite a robots.txt block can appear under that status in Search Console.

coreStoryFacts.text: Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist.
The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp.
Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes.
Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link.
Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached.

Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records.
Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths.
It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document.
That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content.

A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content.
The new section does not discuss the interaction.
Google's own products fall within the categories as well.
Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.
Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable.

What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results.
Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website.
Google names no products, companies or technologies.
The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page.
A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage.
It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index.
The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule.
Google does not say which services prompted the change.
PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language.

That means days of adjustment instead of months of retraining.

extraction.body: Web app builders and generated-content tools now sit in the spam guide, next to new Search Console alerts. Will those platforms switch their indexing defaults? Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist. The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp. Google has a help page for websites that let the public post things, and today it said that tools where people make pages, apps or automatically generated content to share by link can be abused by spammers too. Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website. Google now says pages like that should be hidden from search by default, and that the companies running these tools should watch Search Console and their own numbers for sudden jumps in new public pages. The page is titled "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform." It sits in the "Preventing and monitoring abuse" part of Search Central's monitoring and debugging documentation, alongside guides on malware, phishing and deceptive sites, and the Google Safe Browsing Repeat Offenders Policy. Three passages are new or rewritten. Every other paragraph, from the reputation system for new accounts to an example about overnight traffic from Italian IP addresses on a site aimed at Japan, is unchanged word for word. The introduction previously warned that spammers exploit open comment forms, and that "hosting platforms may be similarly open to abuse," with spammers creating large numbers of sites that break Google's spam policies. The revised sentence reads: "Hosting platforms and tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps may be similarly open to abuse; spammers may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies and add little or no value to the web." Two edits sit inside that sentence. The first adds a category of service defined by what its users can publish - shared pages, generated content and web apps - rather than by whether it sells hosting. The second changes the unit of abuse from "sites" to "pages or sites," which brings individual URLs, not just whole sites, within the scope of the warning. Google names no products, companies or technologies. The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page. passages: The timing matters because the traffic data is already moving.

Over the past month I've watched websites with heavy concentrations of AI-generated content, the kind Ahrefs now flags as "Very high" on its AI Content Level metric, begin sliding in Google organic search.
This also lines up with the rollout of Google’s latest June 2026 spam update that recently finished rolling out.
But when declines cluster around a specific site profile right as Google publishes both an algorithm update and research on detecting that exact profile, it deserves attention.
Google's 2023 guidance rewards content for quality regardless of production method; enforcement targets scaled content abuse, meaning high-volume, low-value pages built mainly to manipulate rankings.
A content classifier scans for repetitive, templated narratives and for high-frequency publishing behavior that no human schedule produces.
An infrastructure component ties accounts back to a common source.
When enough accounts in a cluster show the same AI-generated templates, Google removes the whole cluster at once rather than penalizing individual pages.
Automation has been part of publishing for decades, from sports scores to weather forecasts.
The risk calculus for AI-heavy SEO & AEO has changed shape.
The question used to be whether a single page looked low quality.
The question now includes whether your templates, publishing cadence, infrastructure and content similarities make your operation resemble a coordinated spam network.
Gabe's read: Google will not let companies spam their way into AI search , and marketers should expect stronger automated systems plus manual actions.
Traditional quality filters evaluate one piece of content at a time.
Google's researchers acknowledge that generative AI broke that model.
Spammers can now produce endless variations of what the paper calls functionally identical content: every page technically unique, every page effectively the same.
At volume, that flood is built to swamp content-level filters.
SBERT has existed since 2019, and Montti points out the SEO industry has rarely discussed it as a spam-detection mechanism.
Its appearance in a Google paper about catching synthetic spam suggests it may have been put to that use only recently.
One more detail worth knowing: speed of adaptation.
The paper describes using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) to retune classifiers when spammers move to new generative models.
That means days of adjustment instead of months of retraining.
When the next model ships and spam operations migrate, Google can follow almost immediately.
The paper, covered by Roger Montti at Search Engine Journal and shared widely by Glenn Gabe on X , describes the Scalable Cluster Termination System.

Google has recently created an additional “Only index content meant for Search” section within the spam guide it updated on Oct. 26. The new section advises websites with pages made for direct sharing, collaboration or utility to set a noindex tag or use a robots.txt directive to block crawlers by default for those pages. According to Google’s changelog this is an addition relating to “blocking indexing of link-shared content.” The new section includes a link to the introductory page about robots.txt , and according to that introductory page the robots.txt file “is not a mechanism for keeping a web page out of Google.” Google’s new “Only index content meant for Search” section follows the guide’s advice on spotting spammy accounts and reads: “If your service lets users create shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools, consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or only accessed directly by people with a link.” “When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default.” The guide’s opening paragraph said hosting platforms “may be similarly open to abuse.” The updated sentence adds “tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps,” and says spammers may create a large number of “pages or sites” where it used to say sites. The previous version, last updated Dec. 10, 2025, already suggested noindex on posts from new users until they build a reputation on the platform. That advice is unchanged. Google’s robots.txt introduction says a page “that’s disallowed in robots.txt can still be indexed if linked to from other sites.” Google won’t crawl the blocked content in that case, but the URL and possibly the anchor text of links pointing to it can appear in results, without a description. Google’s page on noindex says the rule only works when robots.txt isn’t blocking the page, because otherwise “the crawler will never see the noindex rule.” Google’s “Control what you share” page , updated Oct. 21, lists robots.txt as applicable to “images and video” and noindex as applicable to “all content types.” On July 27, I confirmed that Claude’s share path was blocked by a “Disallow” directive in robots.txt. In addition, the share pages also returned a “none” value for the X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header. Google treats “none” as equal to both noindex and nofollow according to its documentation of robots meta tags . I have been unable to determine what Google saw when it initially found those links. The new spam guide from Google states you should be verifying your website or subdomain through Search Console for your platform to receive emails when it gets a manual action or has a security issue. It further suggests you check the Page Indexing report and Search performance report on an ongoing basis for “unexpected spikes” of indexed pages, impressions or queries which do not align with your platform’s intent. A new bullet under the guide’s monitoring advice suggests tracking creation and indexing at the platform level, with alerts for spikes in newly published public pages or “a small number of users generating a large share of indexable URLs.” Google’s changelog says its Oct. 26 update to the spam guide aims to help platforms “keep user-created pages that aren’t meant for Search out of the index and detect spam earlier.” For share links, generated outputs, and app pages, check that any noindex can reach Googlebot. A robots.txt rule that blocks Googlebot from those pages means Google never reads it. The Page Indexing report that Google’s new monitoring advice points to has a status called “Indexed, though blocked by robots.txt.” Google’s help for that status says to remove the block and use noindex. Share URLs that Google indexes despite a robots.txt block can appear under that status in Search Console. Follow on YouTube. Matt G.
