sources.title: Amazon unveils new Echo devices, powered by its AI, Alexa+ - TechCrunch
passages: To showcase the AI’s capabilities, Amazon is releasing four new Echo devices with improved processing power and memory: the Echo Dot Max, Echo Studio, Echo Show 8, and Echo Show 11.

At its annual hardware event, Amazon introduced a new lineup of Echo devices, built specifically for its AI assistant, Alexa+, which has already rolled out to millions of customers through its early access program.
This will later include an Alexa+ Store, where users can explore services from brands like Fandango, GrubHub, Lyft, Priceline, Taskrabbit, Thumbtack, and Yahoo Sports.
The devices will also be able to manage new or existing subscriptions with Amazon’s own services like Amazon Music, Amazon Kids+, or Alexa Emergency Assist and customize their Alexa experience.

With this feature, the devices allow Alexa to act on events happening in the home, like delivering a reminder when a particular person walks in the room or alerting you to an open garage door before you go to bed at night.
Plus, Amazon is teaming up with smart ring maker Oura to bring personalized health and wellness suggestions to Alexa devices.
This could help do things like add workout reminders or nudges to head to bed to get the best sleep.
The $219.99 Echo Studio, meanwhile, features a new spherical design, allowing it to be 40% smaller than the original, says Amazon.
The chip also improves detection of the wake word by over 50%, Amazon claims.

As Alexa devices with a screen, the displays also work well for accessing entertainment, like streaming audio and video, managing home organization and family activities, and managing household shopping needs.
The latter integrates with Amazon, Whole Foods, and Amazon Fresh to make reordering favorites and delivery tracking easier.

Key to the devices are the Alexa+ integrations, allowing the speakers to respond to more queries than earlier models, offering support for natural language conversations, more complex questions, and soon, more add-ons and capabilities.

extraction.body: At its annual hardware event, Amazon introduced a new lineup of Echo devices, built specifically for its AI assistant, Alexa+, which has already rolled out to millions of customers through its early access program. To showcase the AI’s capabilities, Amazon is releasing four new Echo devices with improved processing power and memory: the Echo Dot Max, Echo Studio, Echo Show 8, and Echo Show 11. Key to the devices are the Alexa+ integrations, allowing the speakers to respond to more queries than earlier models, offering support for natural language conversations, more complex questions, and soon, more add-ons and capabilities. This will later include an Alexa+ Store, where users can explore services from brands like Fandango, GrubHub, Lyft, Priceline, Taskrabbit, Thumbtack, and Yahoo Sports. The devices will also be able to manage new or existing subscriptions with Amazon’s own services like Amazon Music, Amazon Kids+, or Alexa Emergency Assist and customize their Alexa experience. The new Echo devices launching today run on Amazon’s custom-designed silicon chips, the AZ3 and AZ3 Pro, which include an AI Accelerator designed to run AI edge models. The AZ3 enables better conversation detection on the Echo Dot, letting people talk to the device from anywhere in the room, while still filtering out background noise. The chip also improves detection of the wake word by over 50%, Amazon claims. The other three devices — the Studio, Show 8, and 11 — use the AZ3 Pro, which adds support for advanced language models and vision transformers. Plus, the AZ3 Pro-enabled devices include Ominisense, a custom sensor platform for ambient AI that uses the 13-megapixel camera on new Echo Show devices, audio, ultrasound, Wi-Fi radar, accelerometer, and Wi-Fi channel state information (CSI). With this feature, the devices allow Alexa to act on events happening in the home, like delivering a reminder when a particular person walks in the room or alerting you to an open garage door before you go to bed at night. The new Echo Dot Max, $99.99, adds nearly three times the bass for better sound. The two-way speaker includes a woofer for the deep bass and a custom tweeter for the high notes. The $219.99 Echo Studio, meanwhile, features a new spherical design, allowing it to be 40% smaller than the original, says Amazon. The Echo Studio also includes a high-excursion woofer, spatial audio, and Dolby Atmos, and an upgraded light ring for better visual understanding of what Alexa is doing or processing. The company notes consumers can connect up to five Echo Studio or Echo Dot Max devices with compatible Fire TV sticks for an immersive sound system in their home, and it plans to sell products in Alexa Home Theater bundles. Also new are two smart displays, the Echo Show 8 ($179.99) and Echo Show 11 ($219.99), which both have a new design, improved picture quality, a 13-megapixel camera, a larger screen area, new front-facing stereo speakers, a custom woofer, and Alexa+ powered features. The AI assistant will run a new smart home experience called Alexa+ Home, which combines things like event summaries from Ring camera feeds and a smart home hub that supports Matter, Thread, and Zigbee. As Alexa devices with a screen, the displays also work well for accessing entertainment, like streaming audio and video, managing home organization and family activities, and managing household shopping needs. The latter integrates with Amazon, Whole Foods, and Amazon Fresh to make reordering favorites and delivery tracking easier. Plus, Amazon is teaming up with smart ring maker Oura to bring personalized health and wellness suggestions to Alexa devices. This could help do things like add workout reminders or nudges to head to bed to get the best sleep. Other devices from Withings and Wyze will be supported in the future. sources.title: Amazon unveils its newest lineup of Alexa+ devices - About Amazon Australia
passages: Today, Amazon announced the latest generation of Alexa devices , each designed for Alexa+ and purpose-built for the moments and tasks customers turn to Alexa for most.
The next-generation Echo Dot is designed for everywhere you can imagine and packs even more into its compact form factor.

For the first time, it includes a built-in smart home hub, so Alexa connects to hundreds of compatible devices such as lights, locks, thermostats right out of the box, plus a built-in eero Wi-Fi extender that adds up to 93 square metres of coverage to your existing network.
At its core is Amazon’s custom AZ3 silicon, with a new AI Accelerator built for on-device AI that sharpens conversational detection and filters out background noise.
Music, audiobooks, and podcasts sound great on the new Echo Dot, with crisp vocals and 50% more bass than its predecessor.
Echo Studio with Home Camera takes Amazon's best-sounding speaker and gives it a richer understanding of the room around it, making Alexa even more useful.
The camera enables a new Adaptive Volume feature that optimises playback as you move throughout the room.

What's new is context: with more awareness of its surroundings, Alexa can help in real time —explaining the rules on a board game box you hold up, recognizing a box of cereal to help you reorder it, or letting you check in on the room from the Alexa app while you're away.
Privacy is built into every Echo device from the ground up, and customers are in control of their experience.
There are clear visual indicators when Alexa is listening, and a dedicated privacy button turns the microphones off completely.

The camera enables a new Adaptive Volume feature that optimises playback as you move throughout the room. What's new is context: with more awareness of its surroundings, Alexa can help in real time —explaining the rules on a board game box you hold up, recognizing a box of cereal to help you reorder it, or letting you check in on the room from the Alexa app while you're away.

story.title: Amazon unveils its newest lineup of Alexa devices - About Amazon

facts.text: Amazon on Thursday debuted a set of new, pricier Alexa tablets and said it's ditching its budget-friendly Fire lineup, marking a significant shift in the e-commerce juggernaut's devices strategy.
Amazon denied that rising memory costs played a role in its decision to charge more for the Alexa tablet.
But Panos Panay, the company's devices boss, acknowledged that the shortage made it "quite tricky" to build a premium tablet at a reasonable price without making any "trade-offs."
Alexa is front and center in the new tablets, via a "dynamic tab" on the home screen that offers recommendations and lets users quickly pick up where they left off reading or watching a TV show.
Users can say "Alexa" or tap the "Ask Alexa" button to ask questions.
The Fire lineup includes a 10-inch and 8-inch model as well as two versions targeted for kids.
The $550 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro costs more than double the price of the $155 Fire HD 10, Amazon's base model, and puts it more in line with Apple 's iPad, which runs from $449 to $1,199.
Amazon added a sleeker, sturdier aluminum backing, higher resolution display and faster processors.
The launch comes as Amazon and other device makers are grappling with a historic surge in memory prices .
Amazon in August boosted prices on Echos, Kindles, Fire TVs and other hardware, citing the memory crunch.
In a demo, Panay showed how users could watch a TikTok clip of someone cooking on a grill and ask Alexa to shop for a burger press used in the video.
Users can also pull up a game schedule and add every date to their calendar, Amazon said.

Amazon has historically sold its devices at or near the cost of manufacturing them, partly to undercut competitors with extremely cheap prices, but also with the goal of promoting its other products and services.
It's hoped that for every $80 Echo smart speaker it sells, users will purchase movies, audiobook subscriptions or items from its sprawling webstore, which tend to have higher margins.
The company has recently taken steps to make more money from its devices business under CEO Andy Jassy , who succeeded founder Jeff Bezos in 2021.
Last year, it introduced pricier versions of its Echo smart speakers and began charging non-Prime members a subscription for Alexa+ , the souped-up version of its digital assistant.
"I think the team did a good job designing without making that trade," Panay told CNBC in an interview.
"They gave you the full craftsmanship of a product, but are able to keep it at that price point."
To showcase the AI’s capabilities, Amazon is releasing four new Echo devices with improved processing power and memory: the Echo Dot Max, Echo Studio, Echo Show 8, and Echo Show 11.

At its annual hardware event, Amazon introduced a new lineup of Echo devices, built specifically for its AI assistant, Alexa+, which has already rolled out to millions of customers through its early access program.
This will later include an Alexa+ Store, where users can explore services from brands like Fandango, GrubHub, Lyft, Priceline, Taskrabbit, Thumbtack, and Yahoo Sports.
The devices will also be able to manage new or existing subscriptions with Amazon’s own services like Amazon Music, Amazon Kids+, or Alexa Emergency Assist and customize their Alexa experience.

With this feature, the devices allow Alexa to act on events happening in the home, like delivering a reminder when a particular person walks in the room or alerting you to an open garage door before you go to bed at night.
Plus, Amazon is teaming up with smart ring maker Oura to bring personalized health and wellness suggestions to Alexa devices.
This could help do things like add workout reminders or nudges to head to bed to get the best sleep.
The $219.99 Echo Studio, meanwhile, features a new spherical design, allowing it to be 40% smaller than the original, says Amazon.
The chip also improves detection of the wake word by over 50%, Amazon claims.

As Alexa devices with a screen, the displays also work well for accessing entertainment, like streaming audio and video, managing home organization and family activities, and managing household shopping needs.
The latter integrates with Amazon, Whole Foods, and Amazon Fresh to make reordering favorites and delivery tracking easier.

Key to the devices are the Alexa+ integrations, allowing the speakers to respond to more queries than earlier models, offering support for natural language conversations, more complex questions, and soon, more add-ons and capabilities.

sources.title: Amazon debuts the Alexa Photo Frame and Echo Time smart clock, plus other upgraded devices
passages: Amazon unveiled five new Alexa devices today, including two new kinds of hardware: the Alexa Photo Frame , a smart picture frame, and the Echo Time, a smart alarm clock.
Finally, Amazon unveiled the new Echo Show 16, which includes a 16-inch display.
Amazon says the device has a 10% larger viewing area than its predecessor, but with a 40% smaller frame.
It has Fire TV built in, plus Smart Home tools like Family Organizer.
It can also function like a digital photo frame.
The device is said to be specifically calibrated for sharing photos, featuring a semi-matte, anti-glare display that makes it look more like a Samsung Frame TV than a laptop screen.

“Millions of customers start and end their days with Alexa — checking the weather and turning on the lights from bed in the morning or winding down with white noise at night,” Amazon wrote. “But the bedroom asks for something different from a device than the kitchen or living room does — so we designed an Echo specifically for it.”
Amazon’s new device, though, adds the value of integration with users’ existing Amazon accounts.
Prime members get unlimited storage on Amazon Photos, and Alexa+ is supposed to intelligently choose how and when to display photos.
Amazon also showed off updates to its existing lines of devices.

“Alexa can also see and understand what’s in front of the camera and help you in real time,” Amazon explained. “Pull out a board game box and ask Alexa+ to explain the rules or hold up a cereal box and Alexa can recognize it and help you reorder more flavors.”

“It knows to choose photos where you’re smiling and the lighting is right, and it matches the season you’re in, so you see last year’s family Halloween costumes in October instead of the middle of spring.
It also knows what to skip, like screenshots and receipts,” Amazon said in a press release.
You can also add voice notes to photos, and images sync automatically as you take them.
Amazon says its most advanced speaker, however, is the Echo Studio with Home Camera.
This speaker doubles as a camera so you can check on your home while you’re out, and also has visual intelligence features.

It also knows what to skip, like screenshots and receipts,” Amazon said in a press release. You can also add voice notes to photos, and images sync automatically as you take them. sources.title: Apple readies touch-screen MacBook Pro for 2026, reversing decade-long anti-touch stance
passages: Bloomberg News first reported in January 2023 that Apple was working on a touch-screen MacBook Pro.
For the revamped MacBook Pro, Apple is retiring the “notch” — the cutout at the top of the screen that houses the camera.
The current MacBook Pro design dates back to 2021, though Apple refreshed the 14-inch base version with an M5 chip on Wednesday.
The late Jobs, then Apple’s chief executive officer, said in 2010 that “touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical,” suggesting that they wouldn’t make sense for a computer screen.
As of now, Apple isn’t actively developing additional touch-screen Macs.
There have been concerns within Apple that touch-screen computers would cannibalize sales of iPads.
While the $999 MacBook Air remains the company’s bestselling laptop, a high-end touch-enabled MacBook Pro might entice customers to trade up — or switch from a Windows PC.
Apple’s iPad Magic Keyboard, introduced in 2020, also showed that customers were interested in combining a touch display with a traditional keyboard and trackpad.
Apple is exploring another major Mac change as well: a shift from the Touch ID fingerprint scanner to Face ID.
Apple shares pared their losses Thursday after Bloomberg reported on the plans.
The company is planning M5 Pro and M5 Max iterations for early 2026 that retain the current look, Bloomberg News has reported.
The company has also developed a reinforced hinge and screen hardware to prevent the display from bouncing back or moving when touched, a common drawback of existing touch PCs.
This follows a typical strategy for Apple, which offers new features on its top-end devices before bringing them down-market.
But tablet growth has already slowed in recent years, and touch screens have increasingly become must-have features for PCs.

extraction.body: Apple Inc. is preparing to finally launch a touch-screen version of its Mac computer, reversing course on a stance that dates back to co-founder Steve Jobs. The company is readying a revamped MacBook Pro with a touch display for late 2026 or early 2027, according to people with knowledge of the matter. In making the move, Apple is following the rest of the computing industry, which embraced touch-screen laptops more than a decade ago. The company has taken years to formulate its approach to the market, aiming to improve on current designs. Bloomberg News first reported in January 2023 that Apple was working on a touch-screen MacBook Pro. The new laptops will feature displays with OLED technology — short for organic light-emitting diode — the same standard used in iPhones and iPad Pros, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the products haven’t been announced. A spokesperson for Cupertino, Calif.a-based Apple declined to comment. Apple shares pared their losses Thursday after Bloomberg reported on the plans. The touch-screen MacBook Pro will retain a full trackpad and keyboard — mirroring the approach of PC makers like Dell Technologies Inc., Acer Inc., Lenovo Group Ltd. and Microsoft Corp. That means users won’t have to rely on the touch display if they don’t want to. For the revamped MacBook Pro, Apple is retiring the “notch” — the cutout at the top of the screen that houses the camera. In its place, the company will adopt a so-called hole-punch design that leaves a display area around the sensor. The company has also developed a reinforced hinge and screen hardware to prevent the display from bouncing back or moving when touched, a common drawback of existing touch PCs. Because of the pricier components, the new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros are likely to cost a few hundred dollars more than current versions. Today’s non-touch models with high-end chips start at $1,999 for the 14-inch version and $2,499 for the larger one. The current MacBook Pro design dates back to 2021, though Apple refreshed the 14-inch base version with an M5 chip on Wednesday. The company is planning M5 Pro and M5 Max iterations for early 2026 that retain the current look, Bloomberg News has reported. As of now, Apple isn’t actively developing additional touch-screen Macs. Instead, it’s waiting to see the market’s reaction to the touch version of the MacBook Pro, the people said. This follows a typical strategy for Apple, which offers new features on its top-end devices before bringing them down-market. For years, Apple resisted the idea of touch-screen Macs, arguing that PCs with the feature were difficult to use and not ergonomic. It instead pushed users who want touch interfaces to buy iPads. The late Jobs, then Apple’s chief executive officer, said in 2010 that “touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical,” suggesting that they wouldn’t make sense for a computer screen. Apple tried a compromise in 2016 with the Touch Bar, a touch-screen strip that sat above the keyboard. There have been concerns within Apple that touch-screen computers would cannibalize sales of iPads. But tablet growth has already slowed in recent years, and touch screens have increasingly become must-have features for PCs. And Apple has bridged the gap between iPads and Macs in other ways: The devices now have unified interfaces, processors and app ecosystems. Apple’s iPad Magic Keyboard, introduced in 2020, also showed that customers were interested in combining a touch display with a traditional keyboard and trackpad. The accessory has become central to the iPad Pro’s sales pitch, letting users easily shift between touch and traditional controls. Adding a touch screen to the MacBook Pro could push users upmarket, creating new revenue opportunities for Apple. While the $999 MacBook Air remains the company’s bestselling laptop, a high-end touch-enabled MacBook Pro might entice customers to trade up — or switch from a Windows PC. Other new Macs in development include updated MacBook Airs with the M5 chip. The company is also working on a refreshed Mac Studio, Mac mini, and a pair of external Mac monitors dubbed J427 and J527. Apple is exploring another major Mac change as well: a shift from the Touch ID fingerprint scanner to Face ID.

extraction.body: (Bloomberg) -- After two decades of spurning the idea, Apple Inc. unveiled an overhauled MacBook Pro that includes a touch screen, giving its flagship laptop a feature that has become a must-have in the personal computer industry. The thinner and lighter machine, which comes in 14- and 16-inch sizes, is also the first Mac with OLED — short for organic light-emitting diode — a display technology used on recent iPhones, iPads and other Apple devices. It’s also the first Mac with a Dynamic Island, the screen element familiar to iPhone users.The computer has a redesigned software interface optimized for touch and is offered with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. The 14-inch version is priced from $2,899, while the 16-inch model starts at $3,399. A maxed-out version with 16 terabytes of storage and 128 gigabytes of memory costs $14,549.Johny Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer, called the new machine a “monumental step forward for the Mac.” It was introduced on stage by new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus, who took the reins from Tim Cook last month. Customers have been prodding the company for years to embrace touch displays, which the iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch helped popularize. But Apple had to overcome some deep-seated opposition that has existed for nearly two decades. Co-founder Steve Jobs famously lambasted touch Macs in the later stages of his career, once calling them “ergonomically terrible.” Cook, his successor, said combining a laptop and tablet would be like merging a fridge and toaster. Other company executives laughed at the idea in interviews.But about four years ago Cook and Ternus became proponents of ditching past orthodoxy and moving to a touch display on the MacBook Pro, Bloomberg News has reported. The hope is to give the Mac new momentum and raise revenue with higher prices driven by more premium features.Still, Apple is releasing the new machines at a turbulent time for the laptop market. Higher memory chip prices have increased computer prices and hurt demand, sending the industry into a downward spiral. Global PC shipments tumbled 20% in the third quarter, according to researcher IDC. Apple suffered its own decline in the period, though it wasn’t as severe as the industry average.The new 14-inch MacBook Pro weighs 3 pounds, down from 3.5 on the non-touch model, while the 16-inch version now comes in at 4 pounds. That’s down from 4.7 pounds on the prior generation. It also has an Apple logo that lights up on the back, marking the return of an old feature. Bloomberg News first reported in January 2023 on Apple’s plans to bring touch screens to the MacBook Pro and subsequently detailed the new displays, software interface, processors, pricing and design changes.Earlier this week, Apple launched a new low-end MacBook Pro with an M6 chip and 14-inch screen, an updated iMac and an overhauled iPad mini with an OLED screen and higher price. The launches cap a strong new product year for Apple, which put the iPhone Duo on sale last Friday. (Updated with more product details starting in third paragraph.)More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

extraction.body: Apple unveiled the first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen in Mac history. After 20 years of refusing to add a touchscreen since the MacBook's 2006 launch, Apple changed course under new CEO John Turnus. Apple founder Steve Jobs once said, "Touchscreen notebooks are ergonomically terrible." On the 28th (local time), Apple held a product launch event in Los Angeles, California, and unveiled 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros equipped with a touchscreen and M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. CEO Turnus said, "That's right. We are bringing touch to the Mac for the first time." Johny Srouji, Apple's chief hardware officer (CHO), said, "By introducing touch to MacBook Pro, we created a completely new way for pro users to interact with content." Apple had long been negative about adding touchscreens to laptops. At the "Back to the Mac" event in Oct. 2010, founder Jobs said, "Touch surfaces don't want to be vertical," adding, "After a short period, you start to fatigue, and after an extended period, your arm wants to fall off." He called them "ergonomically terrible" and kept touchscreens off the Mac. Bloomberg reported, "Former CEO Tim Cook and CEO Turnus thought customers had begun to expect a touchscreen on the Mac," adding, "But Apple's industrial design team still opposed the idea." It said the touchscreen MacBook ultimately emerged as a compromise: keeping the keyboard and trackpad as the primary input while using touch as a secondary method when needed. Apple said it reduced latency by integrating the touch sensor into the panel itself rather than placing it on top of the display. The 14-inch model of the touchscreen MacBook Pro weighs 1.38 kg, down 220 g from its predecessor, and the 16-inch model weighs 1.82 kg, 320 g lighter, improving portability. Battery life is up to 24 hours. Unified memory goes up to 128GB, and storage up to 16TB. Prices start at $2,899 for the 14-inch M5 Pro model and $3,399 for the 16-inch. The M5 Max model starts at $4,499 for the 14-inch and $4,799 for the 16-inch. Apple will begin preorders today in 30 countries, including the United States, and on the 30th in Korea. It goes on sale on Nov. 6.

coreStoryFacts.text: Bloomberg News first reported in January 2023 that Apple was working on a touch-screen MacBook Pro.
For the revamped MacBook Pro, Apple is retiring the “notch” — the cutout at the top of the screen that houses the camera.
The current MacBook Pro design dates back to 2021, though Apple refreshed the 14-inch base version with an M5 chip on Wednesday.
The late Jobs, then Apple’s chief executive officer, said in 2010 that “touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical,” suggesting that they wouldn’t make sense for a computer screen.
As of now, Apple isn’t actively developing additional touch-screen Macs.
There have been concerns within Apple that touch-screen computers would cannibalize sales of iPads.
While the $999 MacBook Air remains the company’s bestselling laptop, a high-end touch-enabled MacBook Pro might entice customers to trade up — or switch from a Windows PC.
Apple’s iPad Magic Keyboard, introduced in 2020, also showed that customers were interested in combining a touch display with a traditional keyboard and trackpad.
Apple is exploring another major Mac change as well: a shift from the Touch ID fingerprint scanner to Face ID.
Apple shares pared their losses Thursday after Bloomberg reported on the plans.
The company is planning M5 Pro and M5 Max iterations for early 2026 that retain the current look, Bloomberg News has reported.
The company has also developed a reinforced hinge and screen hardware to prevent the display from bouncing back or moving when touched, a common drawback of existing touch PCs.
This follows a typical strategy for Apple, which offers new features on its top-end devices before bringing them down-market.
But tablet growth has already slowed in recent years, and touch screens have increasingly become must-have features for PCs.

After two decades of spurning the idea, Apple Inc. unveiled an overhauled MacBook Pro that includes a touch screen, giving its flagship laptop a feature that has become a must-have in the personal computer industry.

passages: (Bloomberg) -- After two decades of spurning the idea, Apple Inc. unveiled an overhauled MacBook Pro that includes a touch screen, giving its flagship laptop a feature that has become a must-have in the personal computer industry.

Co-founder Steve Jobs famously lambasted touch Macs in the later stages of his career, once calling them “ergonomically terrible.” Cook, his successor, said combining a laptop and tablet would be like merging a fridge and toaster.
Customers have been prodding the company for years to embrace touch displays, which the iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch helped popularize.

It’s also the first Mac with a Dynamic Island, the screen element familiar to iPhone users.The computer has a redesigned software interface optimized for touch and is offered with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

The launches cap a strong new product year for Apple, which put the iPhone Duo on sale last Friday. (Updated with more product details starting in third paragraph.)More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

extraction.body: (Bloomberg) -- After two decades of spurning the idea, Apple Inc. unveiled an overhauled MacBook Pro that includes a touch screen, giving its flagship laptop a feature that has become a must-have in the personal computer industry. The thinner and lighter machine, which comes in 14- and 16-inch sizes, is also the first Mac with OLED — short for organic light-emitting diode — a display technology used on recent iPhones, iPads and other Apple devices. It’s also the first Mac with a Dynamic Island, the screen element familiar to iPhone users.The computer has a redesigned software interface optimized for touch and is offered with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. The 14-inch version is priced from $2,899, while the 16-inch model starts at $3,399. A maxed-out version with 16 terabytes of storage and 128 gigabytes of memory costs $14,549.Johny Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer, called the new machine a “monumental step forward for the Mac.” It was introduced on stage by new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus, who took the reins from Tim Cook last month. Customers have been prodding the company for years to embrace touch displays, which the iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch helped popularize. But Apple had to overcome some deep-seated opposition that has existed for nearly two decades. Co-founder Steve Jobs famously lambasted touch Macs in the later stages of his career, once calling them “ergonomically terrible.” Cook, his successor, said combining a laptop and tablet would be like merging a fridge and toaster. Other company executives laughed at the idea in interviews.But about four years ago Cook and Ternus became proponents of ditching past orthodoxy and moving to a touch display on the MacBook Pro, Bloomberg News has reported. The hope is to give the Mac new momentum and raise revenue with higher prices driven by more premium features.Still, Apple is releasing the new machines at a turbulent time for the laptop market. Higher memory chip prices have increased computer prices and hurt demand, sending the industry into a downward spiral. Global PC shipments tumbled 20% in the third quarter, according to researcher IDC. Apple suffered its own decline in the period, though it wasn’t as severe as the industry average.The new 14-inch MacBook Pro weighs 3 pounds, down from 3.5 on the non-touch model, while the 16-inch version now comes in at 4 pounds. That’s down from 4.7 pounds on the prior generation. It also has an Apple logo that lights up on the back, marking the return of an old feature. Bloomberg News first reported in January 2023 on Apple’s plans to bring touch screens to the MacBook Pro and subsequently detailed the new displays, software interface, processors, pricing and design changes.Earlier this week, Apple launched a new low-end MacBook Pro with an M6 chip and 14-inch screen, an updated iMac and an overhauled iPad mini with an OLED screen and higher price. The launches cap a strong new product year for Apple, which put the iPhone Duo on sale last Friday. (Updated with more product details starting in third paragraph.)More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

passages: Apple unveiled the first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen in Mac history.
After 20 years of refusing to add a touchscreen since the MacBook's 2006 launch, Apple changed course under new CEO John Turnus.
Apple founder Steve Jobs once said, "Touchscreen notebooks are ergonomically terrible."
Apple had long been negative about adding touchscreens to laptops.

2010, founder Jobs said, "Touch surfaces don't want to be vertical," adding, "After a short period, you start to fatigue, and after an extended period, your arm wants to fall off." He called them "ergonomically terrible" and kept touchscreens off the Mac.
The 14-inch model of the touchscreen MacBook Pro weighs 1.38 kg, down 220 g from its predecessor, and the 16-inch model weighs 1.82 kg, 320 g lighter, improving portability.
Unified memory goes up to 128GB, and storage up to 16TB.
Apple will begin preorders today in 30 countries, including the United States, and on the 30th in Korea.
Apple said it reduced latency by integrating the touch sensor into the panel itself rather than placing it on top of the display.

extraction.body: Apple unveiled the first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen in Mac history. After 20 years of refusing to add a touchscreen since the MacBook's 2006 launch, Apple changed course under new CEO John Turnus. Apple founder Steve Jobs once said, "Touchscreen notebooks are ergonomically terrible." On the 28th (local time), Apple held a product launch event in Los Angeles, California, and unveiled 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros equipped with a touchscreen and M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. CEO Turnus said, "That's right. We are bringing touch to the Mac for the first time." Johny Srouji, Apple's chief hardware officer (CHO), said, "By introducing touch to MacBook Pro, we created a completely new way for pro users to interact with content." Apple had long been negative about adding touchscreens to laptops. At the "Back to the Mac" event in Oct. 2010, founder Jobs said, "Touch surfaces don't want to be vertical," adding, "After a short period, you start to fatigue, and after an extended period, your arm wants to fall off." He called them "ergonomically terrible" and kept touchscreens off the Mac. Bloomberg reported, "Former CEO Tim Cook and CEO Turnus thought customers had begun to expect a touchscreen on the Mac," adding, "But Apple's industrial design team still opposed the idea." It said the touchscreen MacBook ultimately emerged as a compromise: keeping the keyboard and trackpad as the primary input while using touch as a secondary method when needed. Apple said it reduced latency by integrating the touch sensor into the panel itself rather than placing it on top of the display. The 14-inch model of the touchscreen MacBook Pro weighs 1.38 kg, down 220 g from its predecessor, and the 16-inch model weighs 1.82 kg, 320 g lighter, improving portability. Battery life is up to 24 hours. Unified memory goes up to 128GB, and storage up to 16TB. Prices start at $2,899 for the 14-inch M5 Pro model and $3,399 for the 16-inch. The M5 Max model starts at $4,499 for the 14-inch and $4,799 for the 16-inch. Apple will begin preorders today in 30 countries, including the United States, and on the 30th in Korea. It goes on sale on Nov. 6.

extraction.body: Steve Jobs famously called touchscreen laptops “ergonomically terrible,” and for over a decade, Apple stridently refused to make one. Today that all changes with the MacBook Pro — the company’s first laptop to embrace a touch interface. While it’s unlikely that Apple can fix all the “terrible” ergonomics of having to lift your arm up and touch a laptop screen, the company has put some effort into making macOS more touch-friendly. The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display weighs just 3 pounds, which is noticeably lighter than the current generation of non-touch MacBook Pros, which start at 3.4 pounds for the newly introduced M6 models. The difference is even bigger when you jump to the 16-inch model, which clocks in at 4 pounds, while the M5 Pro version without a touchscreen is 4.7. It still has heft, but it feels better balanced when picking it up from a corner with one hand. Putting it side by side with a current 16-inch MacBook Pro, you see that it’s slightly thinner and has a footprint a smidge smaller. It’s a seemingly minor feature, but one that definitely got the audience excited during the introduction, and marks the return of a bit of flair to the MacBook lineup, which, let’s be fair, has grown a bit utilitarian-looking over the years. Touch works almost exactly like you’d expect it to with Apple’s first-party apps. That said, anyone who has tried to “click” a tiny button in an app with their finger knows it’s a pretty fiddly experience at best and infuriating at worst. Apple is trying to address this, at least slightly, by magnifying some controls when you poke at them — like the red, yellow, and green traffic light buttons in the top left corner of windows to close, minimize, and maximize an app. And while MacBook Pro hinges are pretty solid, yes, you can make it wobble pretty easily with some firm taps toward the top of the screen. The OLED is punchy, bright, contrasty, and saturated. Without more time to do side-by-side comparisons, it’s hard to tell just how much of an improvement the OLED XDR display is. On first impression, at least, the touchscreen doesn’t seem likely to revolutionize the MacBook. That’s why it’s just a MacBook Pro variant and not an entirely new product line. Unsurprisingly, there is a price premium for the new MacBook Pro PROLED XDR. The touchscreen OLED model starts at $2,899, $400 more than the otherwise similarly-specced M5 Pro MacBook Pro.

passages: I’m looking forward to spending more time with the new MacBook Pro, but for right now, it seems to follow in the lineup’s existing tradition: impressively high-end components like an outstanding OLED panel, but a very steep price to match.
Though after well over a decade of speculation and back-and-forth, you’d be forgiven for being surprised that the touchscreen thing actually finally happened.
But while it’s not about the touchscreen capability for me, I was impressed by the OLED screen itself—and I’m quite the display snob, if I’m being honest.
The peak brightness, absolute blacks, well-balanced color, and dynamic range were genuinely remarkable.

When the credible reports emerged that the MacBook Pro would get a touchscreen, I imagined a convertible with Apple Pencil support—something you could use as a large iPad or drawing tablet, essentially.

extraction.body: It’s not as different from the previous model as you might have expected. LOS ANGELES—For about five minutes on an extremely crowded showroom floor, I got to take pictures of the new MacBook Pro and test out some of its new features. First impressions: It’s not as much of a departure from the previous design as I expected, but the outstanding OLED display steals the show regardless. The first thing I noticed was that it’s lighter. My daily driver is a 14-inch MacBook Pro (M1 Max), and it’s a bit weighty for a 14-incher. Picking up the new model, I could immediately tell it was lighter. It’s not like it’s in a different general weight class, but it’s a noticeable difference. The next thing I noticed was the Dynamic Island. Given the larger screen real estate of a laptop, it’s much less dominant on the screen than it is on an iPhone. I do worry about what will happen with fullscreen games, which I wasn’t able to test today. The notch MacBook Pro has an option to maximize apps or games to just below the notch, so it doesn’t cut into the image. I’m curious to test in the full review whether that remains the case with this little cutout. And lastly, the Apple logo on the back glows again! Some find this tacky, some find it essential. I just think it’s a little bit nostalgic. Of course, you might make the case that the most notable thing about this laptop is not its weight or the Dynamic Island. For years, people have debated whether Apple should introduce a touchscreen laptop. Steve Jobs was famously against it. A few years ago—there were reports that under Tim Cook and now John Ternus—Apple decided to move ahead with the idea. I played with it a bit, and it works just about exactly as you expect for a laptop touchscreen. A few of the things I did with the touchscreen during my brief time with the laptop: All of that is nice to have, I guess, but there’s not much you can do with it that you couldn’t already do with trackpad gestures, at least at the OS level; some creative apps, like finger painting on the screen, seemed to offer a bit more. When the credible reports emerged that the MacBook Pro would get a touchscreen, I imagined a convertible with Apple Pencil support—something you could use as a large iPad or drawing tablet, essentially. That’s not what this is; it only takes the usual laptop shape, and I was told it does not support the Apple Pencil. It’s just a MacBook Pro, in its normal form factor, but you can use your fingers on the screen to do things like drag files around, swipe between desktop spaces, or pinch-to-zoom on maps or images. But while it’s not about the touchscreen capability for me, I was impressed by the OLED screen itself—and I’m quite the display snob, if I’m being honest. The peak brightness, absolute blacks, well-balanced color, and dynamic range were genuinely remarkable. It’s an enormous upgrade over the MiniLED screen in the previous MacBook Pro. It took far too long for OLED to come to the MacBook Pro, but unsurprisingly, Apple spared no expense and cut no immediately obvious corners on quality. I was also happy to see that the cutout near the top of the screen that has replaced the camera notch is what Apple calls a Dynamic Island; it can resize to show live activities and other information on the fly. That’s one of my favorite features on the iPhone, as I’ve been impressed with Apple’s ability to turn something that should be an albatross into an appealing feature. Based on my time with the device and today’s announcement, the screen seems to be the main draw (though it’s nice that it noticeably weighs less, too), but the price is the real barrier. A 16-inch model with an M5 Max, 64 GB of RAM, and 2 TB of storage is currently priced at $5,799. Sure, that’s a high-end spec, but that’s some serious cash. Much of that is due to the storage and memory; upgrading from 64GB to 128GB adds a whopping $1,600 to that. Sure, most people don’t need anywhere near that much RAM—but some might for future-proofing for local AI workflows. I’m looking forward to spending more time with the new MacBook Pro, but for right now, it seems to follow in the lineup’s existing tradition: impressively high-end components like an outstanding OLED panel, but a very steep price to match. No surprises here! Though after well over a decade of speculation and back-and-forth, you’d be forgiven for being surprised that the touchscreen thing actually finally happened. The first touchscreen MacBook Pro is finally here When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . I'll be honest. I'm not a fan of the name. "MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display" is a mouthful. But this laptop, starting at $2,899, definitely made my jaw drop. 24GB or 48GB (M5 Pro with 16-core GPU), 24GB, 48GB or 64GB (M5 Pro with 20-core GPU), 36GB (M5 Max with 32-core GPU), 48GB, 64GB or 128GB (M5 Max with 40-core GPU) 24GB, 48GB or 64GB (M5 Pro with 20-core GPU), 36GB (M5 Max with 32-core GPU), 48GB, 64GB or 128GB (M5 Max with 40-core GPU) 1TB, 2TB or 4TB (M5 Pro with 16-core or 20-core GPU), 2TB, 4TB, 8TB or 16TB (M5 Max with 32-core or 40-core GPU) 1TB, 2TB or 4TB (M5 Pro with 20-core GPU), 2TB, 4TB, 8TB or 16TB (M5 Max with 32-core or 40-core GPU) The first thing I noticed was the colorful tandem OLED panel. At 2,000 nits, this screen is so bright we had to turn down our camera to record it. The colors really pop off the display. The screen offers a 120Hz refresh rate and a 10 million to 1 contrast ratio, which Apple says is industry leading — and I believe it. The second thing that hit me is that the notch is gone, replaced by a smaller Dynamic Island. When playing music, for example, the music player will shrink in a little window at the top of the display, and you bring it back with a tap. And that brings me to perhaps the biggest upgrade overall, as it's a first for MacBooks: touch. I found the touchscreen support to be pretty smooth as I navigated between apps. I could draw using my finger with ease, though there's no Apple Pencil support to speak of. As you would expect, pinch-to-zoom works well, and I could easily drag and drop video clips in a timeline. I also played a virtual keyboard (complete with chords) and interacted with a 3D model by spinning it around. We'll have to see how well touch works with third-party apps, but Apple already promises support for Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Office, Adobe Lightroom and more. All of this is wrapped up in a design that's only 3 pounds, which is less than the MacBook Pro with M6 at 3.4 pounds. I could easily see myself carrying this as my everyday laptop — if I had the budget. Another design highlight is that Apple has brought back the glowing Apple logo, so everyone will know from across the room that you have the touchscreen Mac. Powering the MacBook Pro with PROLED is the M5 Pro and M5 Max chip, which should offer swift performance for creative pros and coders. And this new MacBook Pro will hopefully sound as good as it looks, thanks to a new woofer design with 50% more bass. The port selection is robust, with three Thunderbolt 5 ports, HDMI, SDXC card, MagSafe and a headphone jack. And you get both Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support. Starting at $2,899 for the 14-inch version and $3,399 for the 16-inch, this is one pricey laptop. But if you want the very best display quality it could be worth the premium. Anyone who works with photos and video on a daily basis I think will love this panel. I would say the touch interface is more of a bonus, and I'd like to see Apple offer it across the lineup just to give people more options. The first touchscreen MacBook Pro is finally here
When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works .
I'll be honest. I'm not a fan of the name. "MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display" is a mouthful. But this laptop, starting at $2,899, definitely made my jaw drop.

The first thing I noticed was the colorful tandem OLED panel. At 2,000 nits, this screen is so bright we had to turn down our camera to record it. The colors really pop off the display. The screen offers a 120Hz refresh rate and a 10 million to 1 contrast ratio, which Apple says is industry leading — and I believe it.

The second thing that hit me is that the notch is gone, replaced by a smaller Dynamic Island. When playing music, for example, the music player will shrink in a little window at the top of the display, and you bring it back with a tap.
And that brings me to perhaps the biggest upgrade overall, as it's a first for MacBooks: touch.
I found the touchscreen support to be pretty smooth as I navigated between apps. I could draw using my finger with ease, though there's no Apple Pencil support to speak of.

As you would expect, pinch-to-zoom works well, and I could easily drag and drop video clips in a timeline. I also played a virtual keyboard (complete with chords) and interacted with a 3D model by spinning it around.
We'll have to see how well touch works with third-party apps, but Apple already promises support for Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Office, Adobe Lightroom and more.

All of this is wrapped up in a design that's only 3 pounds, which is less than the MacBook Pro with M6 at 3.4 pounds. I could easily see myself carrying this as my everyday laptop — if I had the budget.
Another design highlight is that Apple has brought back the glowing Apple logo, so everyone will know from across the room that you have the touchscreen Mac.
Powering the MacBook Pro with PROLED is the M5 Pro and M5 Max chip, which should offer swift performance for creative pros and coders.
And this new MacBook Pro will hopefully sound as good as it looks, thanks to a new woofer design with 50% more bass.
The port selection is robust, with three Thunderbolt 5 ports, HDMI, SDXC card, MagSafe and a headphone jack. And you get both Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support.

Starting at $2,899 for the 14-inch version and $3,399 for the 16-inch, this is one pricey laptop. But if you want the very best display quality it could be worth the premium. Anyone who works with photos and video on a daily basis I think will love this panel.
I would say the touch interface is more of a bonus, and I'd like to see Apple offer it across the lineup just to give people more options.

extraction.body: A great-sounding display, but Apple seems out of touch for the touchscreen. Senior Editor / Computers and Gaming Hardware Surpassed only by the iPhone Duo , this year’s most anticipated Apple announcement is its launch of both a 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen display — the company’s last-to-the-party use of both technologies in one of its laptops. And despite the awful name, it’s more than just a fancy new display. It’s really a complete design overhaul that, at least on paper, brings its feature set up to the front of the class for professional content creation, albeit with the same processor options and ports as the other MacBook Pros. Aside from a screen that brings its capabilities more in line with the Studio Display XDR , the new model adds: It doesn’t come cheap, though; as predicted, you pay a $400 premium over the standard models. The 14-inch M5 Pro model starts at $2,899 compared with $2,499 for the same non-OLED version, and the M5 Max model begins at $4,499 compared with $4,099. If you want to upgrade to 16TB, you have to bump to the M5 Max — that’s a minimum buy-in of $11,499 with only 36GB of memory. Preorders started on Wednesday, and systems are slated to start shipping Nov. 6. One of the most popular changes won’t be the whizzy features, but the drop in weight to 3 pounds for the 14-inch model (down from 3.4 pounds) and to 4 pounds (down from 4.7 pounds) for the 16-inch. Also, while Apple updated its sound system to deliver better bass and incorporated Dolby Atmos support to its spatial audio, one of the more notable enhancements is the claimed improvements to the sound when the MacBook is closed. A lot of the traditional advantages of OLED over alternatives like IPS with array backlights — such as a wider color gamut and true blacks — are less pronounced than they used to be. That’s even more true for the current MacBook Pro’s mini-LED-backlit Liquid Retina XDR screens: They already deliver excellent deep blacks and 100% P3 gamut coverage, along with great color accuracy sufficient for prosumer creative work. But the PROLED XDR screen sounds top-notch. While I take Apple’s claim of a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio with 10,000,000 grains of salt — the arithmetic ratio of peak brightness to minimum black isn’t really meaningful, especially beyond about a million — the display has an expanded gamut that covers the Adobe RGB color space and more of Rec. 2020, a space for mastering video. The latter is still only 80%, but at the moment, that’s the best you can get in a laptop display. Peak brightness is also similar to the desktop display at 2,000 nits. As with the current screens, though, you can set the SDR brightness only up to 1,000 nits; above that, it’s automated to compensate only for bright sunlight. That can get frustrating for people like me who find auto- brightness distracting. The display can do 1,000 nits full screen in both SDR and HDR, though. Microsoft’s recently shipped Surface Laptop Ultra also hits 2,000 nits, the first Windows laptop that does, but uses mini-LED. Oddly, Apple still quotes a 1-nit minimum brightness spec, similar to its mini-LED screens, though OLED’s native minimum is a lot lower: Theoretically, it’s zero, but professional colorimeters have measured it a lot lower. That may be because Apple has adopted it as a standard, and possibly clamped it, to tonally match its mini-LED models. Apple also refers to its panel technology generically as “tandem OLED,” which is a little annoying, since there is a raft of tandem OLED types. But it is “state of the art!” There are a couple of potential disappointments, though. For one, the battery life is unchanged. While the MacBook Pro’s battery life has always been good, it’s clear that the OLED display didn’t provide any power savings, or at least savings that weren’t spent elsewhere in the system. Touch looks like the biggest mixed bag, though. The hardware is only a small aspect of the implementation; operating system interfaces like those of iOS and iPadOS are built around considerations like your finger is bigger and fatter than a cursor. Simply porting the mobile interfaces to a laptop isn’t necessarily a solution, either. We use laptops in part because a hardware keyboard is sometimes the best input choice, and even navigating the mobile devices via touch can get annoying, so those interfaces don’t necessarily translate optimally. The point is, a lot is riding on how Apple has adapted MacOS for touch. For instance, the Touch Bar floundered in part because it felt grafted on rather than integral to the OS’ interface, as well as arguably superfluous. And since Apple didn’t launch the capability with MacOS 27 at its developer conference, WWDC , this year, it sounds like the applications will be behind. That’s not something you beta test on a pro-level production system. Pros rely heavily on muscle memory. It should really have launched with a MacBook Air. Plus, to adapt to touchscreen use, Apple had to stiffen the hinge — poking the screen makes that necessary — and add image stabilization to the webcam in case you poke the screen during video calls. Apple seemed like it was really stretching to find meaningful uses for touch. Playing piano on a screen that forces your hand to an awkward angle? No thanks. The one application that sounded like it might be OK was for developers to simulate mobile app interfaces. I was also kind of hoping for increased refresh rates beyond 120Hz or the ability to manually set it above 60Hz. Apple seems to position ProMotion as a power-saving technology rather than for gaming. Apple also seems to think 60fps is a great frame rate, so it’s not surprising. © 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

Surpassed only by the iPhone Duo , this year’s most anticipated Apple announcement is its launch of both a 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen display — the company’s last-to-the-party use of both technologies in one of its laptops. And despite the awful name, it’s more than just a fancy new display. It’s really a complete design overhaul that, at least on paper, brings its feature set up to the front of the class for professional content creation, albeit with the same processor options and ports as the other MacBook Pros.
Aside from a screen that brings its capabilities more in line with the Studio Display XDR , the new model adds:

It doesn’t come cheap, though; as predicted, you pay a $400 premium over the standard models. The 14-inch M5 Pro model starts at $2,899 compared with $2,499 for the same non-OLED version, and the M5 Max model begins at $4,499 compared with $4,099. If you want to upgrade to 16TB, you have to bump to the M5 Max — that’s a minimum buy-in of $11,499 with only 36GB of memory. Preorders started on Wednesday, and systems are slated to start shipping Nov. 6.

One of the most popular changes won’t be the whizzy features, but the drop in weight to 3 pounds for the 14-inch model (down from 3.4 pounds) and to 4 pounds (down from 4.7 pounds) for the 16-inch. Also, while Apple updated its sound system to deliver better bass and incorporated Dolby Atmos support to its spatial audio, one of the more notable enhancements is the claimed improvements to the sound when the MacBook is closed.
A lot of the traditional advantages of OLED over alternatives like IPS with array backlights — such as a wider color gamut and true blacks — are less pronounced than they used to be.

That’s even more true for the current MacBook Pro’s mini-LED-backlit Liquid Retina XDR screens: They already deliver excellent deep blacks and 100% P3 gamut coverage, along with great color accuracy sufficient for prosumer creative work.

But the PROLED XDR screen sounds top-notch. While I take Apple’s claim of a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio with 10,000,000 grains of salt — the arithmetic ratio of peak brightness to minimum black isn’t really meaningful, especially beyond about a million — the display has an expanded gamut that covers the Adobe RGB color space and more of Rec. 2020, a space for mastering video.
The latter is still only 80%, but at the moment, that’s the best you can get in a laptop display.

Peak brightness is also similar to the desktop display at 2,000 nits. As with the current screens, though, you can set the SDR brightness only up to 1,000 nits; above that, it’s automated to compensate only for bright sunlight. That can get frustrating for people like me who find auto- brightness distracting.
The display can do 1,000 nits full screen in both SDR and HDR, though. Microsoft’s recently shipped Surface Laptop Ultra also hits 2,000 nits, the first Windows laptop that does, but uses mini-LED.

Oddly, Apple still quotes a 1-nit minimum brightness spec, similar to its mini-LED screens, though OLED’s native minimum is a lot lower: Theoretically, it’s zero, but professional colorimeters have measured it a lot lower. That may be because Apple has adopted it as a standard, and possibly clamped it, to tonally match its mini-LED models.
Apple also refers to its panel technology generically as “tandem OLED,” which is a little annoying, since there is a raft of tandem OLED types. But it is “state of the art!”

There are a couple of potential disappointments, though. For one, the battery life is unchanged. While the MacBook Pro’s battery life has always been good, it’s clear that the OLED display didn’t provide any power savings, or at least savings that weren’t spent elsewhere in the system.

Touch looks like the biggest mixed bag, though. The hardware is only a small aspect of the implementation; operating system interfaces like those of iOS and iPadOS are built around considerations like your finger is bigger and fatter than a cursor. Simply porting the mobile interfaces to a laptop isn’t necessarily a solution, either.

We use laptops in part because a hardware keyboard is sometimes the best input choice, and even navigating the mobile devices via touch can get annoying, so those interfaces don’t necessarily translate optimally.

The point is, a lot is riding on how Apple has adapted MacOS for touch. For instance, the Touch Bar floundered in part because it felt grafted on rather than integral to the OS’ interface, as well as arguably superfluous.

And since Apple didn’t launch the capability with MacOS 27 at its developer conference, WWDC , this year, it sounds like the applications will be behind. That’s not something you beta test on a pro-level production system. Pros rely heavily on muscle memory. It should really have launched with a MacBook Air.
Plus, to adapt to touchscreen use, Apple had to stiffen the hinge — poking the screen makes that necessary — and add image stabilization to the webcam in case you poke the screen during video calls.

Apple seemed like it was really stretching to find meaningful uses for touch. Playing piano on a screen that forces your hand to an awkward angle? No thanks. The one application that sounded like it might be OK was for developers to simulate mobile app interfaces.

I was also kind of hoping for increased refresh rates beyond 120Hz or the ability to manually set it above 60Hz. Apple seems to position ProMotion as a power-saving technology rather than for gaming. Apple also seems to think 60fps is a great frame rate, so it’s not surprising.

coreStoryFacts.text: The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display weighs just 3 pounds, which is noticeably lighter than the current generation of non-touch MacBook Pros, which start at 3.4 pounds for the newly introduced M6 models.
Touch works almost exactly like you’d expect it to with Apple’s first-party apps.
Steve Jobs famously called touchscreen laptops “ergonomically terrible,” and for over a decade, Apple stridently refused to make one.
Today that all changes with the MacBook Pro — the company’s first laptop to embrace a touch interface.
That’s why it’s just a MacBook Pro variant and not an entirely new product line.
And while MacBook Pro hinges are pretty solid, yes, you can make it wobble pretty easily with some firm taps toward the top of the screen.
While it’s unlikely that Apple can fix all the “terrible” ergonomics of having to lift your arm up and touch a laptop screen, the company has put some effort into making macOS more touch-friendly.

Apple is trying to address this, at least slightly, by magnifying some controls when you poke at them — like the red, yellow, and green traffic light buttons in the top left corner of windows to close, minimize, and maximize an app.
On first impression, at least, the touchscreen doesn’t seem likely to revolutionize the MacBook.

I’m looking forward to spending more time with the new MacBook Pro, but for right now, it seems to follow in the lineup’s existing tradition: impressively high-end components like an outstanding OLED panel, but a very steep price to match.
Though after well over a decade of speculation and back-and-forth, you’d be forgiven for being surprised that the touchscreen thing actually finally happened.
But while it’s not about the touchscreen capability for me, I was impressed by the OLED screen itself—and I’m quite the display snob, if I’m being honest.
The peak brightness, absolute blacks, well-balanced color, and dynamic range were genuinely remarkable.

When the credible reports emerged that the MacBook Pro would get a touchscreen, I imagined a convertible with Apple Pencil support—something you could use as a large iPad or drawing tablet, essentially.

extraction.body: Steve Jobs famously called touchscreen laptops “ergonomically terrible,” and for over a decade, Apple stridently refused to make one. Today that all changes with the MacBook Pro — the company’s first laptop to embrace a touch interface. While it’s unlikely that Apple can fix all the “terrible” ergonomics of having to lift your arm up and touch a laptop screen, the company has put some effort into making macOS more touch-friendly. The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display weighs just 3 pounds, which is noticeably lighter than the current generation of non-touch MacBook Pros, which start at 3.4 pounds for the newly introduced M6 models. The difference is even bigger when you jump to the 16-inch model, which clocks in at 4 pounds, while the M5 Pro version without a touchscreen is 4.7. It still has heft, but it feels better balanced when picking it up from a corner with one hand. Putting it side by side with a current 16-inch MacBook Pro, you see that it’s slightly thinner and has a footprint a smidge smaller. It’s a seemingly minor feature, but one that definitely got the audience excited during the introduction, and marks the return of a bit of flair to the MacBook lineup, which, let’s be fair, has grown a bit utilitarian-looking over the years. Touch works almost exactly like you’d expect it to with Apple’s first-party apps. That said, anyone who has tried to “click” a tiny button in an app with their finger knows it’s a pretty fiddly experience at best and infuriating at worst. Apple is trying to address this, at least slightly, by magnifying some controls when you poke at them — like the red, yellow, and green traffic light buttons in the top left corner of windows to close, minimize, and maximize an app. And while MacBook Pro hinges are pretty solid, yes, you can make it wobble pretty easily with some firm taps toward the top of the screen. The OLED is punchy, bright, contrasty, and saturated. Without more time to do side-by-side comparisons, it’s hard to tell just how much of an improvement the OLED XDR display is. On first impression, at least, the touchscreen doesn’t seem likely to revolutionize the MacBook. That’s why it’s just a MacBook Pro variant and not an entirely new product line. Unsurprisingly, there is a price premium for the new MacBook Pro PROLED XDR. The touchscreen OLED model starts at $2,899, $400 more than the otherwise similarly-specced M5 Pro MacBook Pro.

extraction.body: It’s not as different from the previous model as you might have expected. LOS ANGELES—For about five minutes on an extremely crowded showroom floor, I got to take pictures of the new MacBook Pro and test out some of its new features. First impressions: It’s not as much of a departure from the previous design as I expected, but the outstanding OLED display steals the show regardless. The first thing I noticed was that it’s lighter. My daily driver is a 14-inch MacBook Pro (M1 Max), and it’s a bit weighty for a 14-incher. Picking up the new model, I could immediately tell it was lighter. It’s not like it’s in a different general weight class, but it’s a noticeable difference. The next thing I noticed was the Dynamic Island. Given the larger screen real estate of a laptop, it’s much less dominant on the screen than it is on an iPhone. I do worry about what will happen with fullscreen games, which I wasn’t able to test today. The notch MacBook Pro has an option to maximize apps or games to just below the notch, so it doesn’t cut into the image. I’m curious to test in the full review whether that remains the case with this little cutout. And lastly, the Apple logo on the back glows again! Some find this tacky, some find it essential. I just think it’s a little bit nostalgic. Of course, you might make the case that the most notable thing about this laptop is not its weight or the Dynamic Island. For years, people have debated whether Apple should introduce a touchscreen laptop. Steve Jobs was famously against it. A few years ago—there were reports that under Tim Cook and now John Ternus—Apple decided to move ahead with the idea. I played with it a bit, and it works just about exactly as you expect for a laptop touchscreen. A few of the things I did with the touchscreen during my brief time with the laptop: All of that is nice to have, I guess, but there’s not much you can do with it that you couldn’t already do with trackpad gestures, at least at the OS level; some creative apps, like finger painting on the screen, seemed to offer a bit more. When the credible reports emerged that the MacBook Pro would get a touchscreen, I imagined a convertible with Apple Pencil support—something you could use as a large iPad or drawing tablet, essentially. That’s not what this is; it only takes the usual laptop shape, and I was told it does not support the Apple Pencil. It’s just a MacBook Pro, in its normal form factor, but you can use your fingers on the screen to do things like drag files around, swipe between desktop spaces, or pinch-to-zoom on maps or images. But while it’s not about the touchscreen capability for me, I was impressed by the OLED screen itself—and I’m quite the display snob, if I’m being honest. The peak brightness, absolute blacks, well-balanced color, and dynamic range were genuinely remarkable. It’s an enormous upgrade over the MiniLED screen in the previous MacBook Pro. It took far too long for OLED to come to the MacBook Pro, but unsurprisingly, Apple spared no expense and cut no immediately obvious corners on quality. I was also happy to see that the cutout near the top of the screen that has replaced the camera notch is what Apple calls a Dynamic Island; it can resize to show live activities and other information on the fly. That’s one of my favorite features on the iPhone, as I’ve been impressed with Apple’s ability to turn something that should be an albatross into an appealing feature. Based on my time with the device and today’s announcement, the screen seems to be the main draw (though it’s nice that it noticeably weighs less, too), but the price is the real barrier. A 16-inch model with an M5 Max, 64 GB of RAM, and 2 TB of storage is currently priced at $5,799. Sure, that’s a high-end spec, but that’s some serious cash. Much of that is due to the storage and memory; upgrading from 64GB to 128GB adds a whopping $1,600 to that. Sure, most people don’t need anywhere near that much RAM—but some might for future-proofing for local AI workflows. I’m looking forward to spending more time with the new MacBook Pro, but for right now, it seems to follow in the lineup’s existing tradition: impressively high-end components like an outstanding OLED panel, but a very steep price to match. No surprises here! Though after well over a decade of speculation and back-and-forth, you’d be forgiven for being surprised that the touchscreen thing actually finally happened. But this laptop, starting at $2,899, definitely made my jaw drop. 24GB or 48GB (M5 Pro with 16-core GPU), 24GB, 48GB or 64GB (M5 Pro with 20-core GPU), 36GB (M5 Max with 32-core GPU), 48GB, 64GB or 128GB (M5 Max with 40-core GPU) 24GB, 48GB or 64GB (M5 Pro with 20-core GPU), 36GB (M5 Max with 32-core GPU), 48GB, 64GB or 128GB (M5 Max with 40-core GPU) 1TB, 2TB or 4TB (M5 Pro with 16-core or 20-core GPU), 2TB, 4TB, 8TB or 16TB (M5 Max with 32-core or 40-core GPU) 1TB, 2TB or 4TB (M5 Pro with 20-core GPU), 2TB, 4TB, 8TB or 16TB (M5 Max with 32-core or 40-core GPU) The first thing I noticed was the colorful tandem OLED panel. At 2,000 nits, this screen is so bright we had to turn down our camera to record it. The colors really pop off the display. The screen offers a 120Hz refresh rate and a 10 million to 1 contrast ratio, which Apple says is industry leading — and I believe it. The second thing that hit me is that the notch is gone, replaced by a smaller Dynamic Island. When playing music, for example, the music player will shrink in a little window at the top of the display, and you bring it back with a tap. And that brings me to perhaps the biggest upgrade overall, as it's a first for MacBooks: touch. I found the touchscreen support to be pretty smooth as I navigated between apps. I could draw using my finger with ease, though there's no Apple Pencil support to speak of. As you would expect, pinch-to-zoom works well, and I could easily drag and drop video clips in a timeline. I also played a virtual keyboard (complete with chords) and interacted with a 3D model by spinning it around. We'll have to see how well touch works with third-party apps, but Apple already promises support for Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Office, Adobe Lightroom and more. All of this is wrapped up in a design that's only 3 pounds, which is less than the MacBook Pro with M6 at 3.4 pounds. I could easily see myself carrying this as my everyday laptop — if I had the budget. Another design highlight is that Apple has brought back the glowing Apple logo, so everyone will know from across the room that you have the touchscreen Mac. Powering the MacBook Pro with PROLED is the M5 Pro and M5 Max chip, which should offer swift performance for creative pros and coders. And this new MacBook Pro will hopefully sound as good as it looks, thanks to a new woofer design with 50% more bass. The port selection is robust, with three Thunderbolt 5 ports, HDMI, SDXC card, MagSafe and a headphone jack. And you get both Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support. Starting at $2,899 for the 14-inch version and $3,399 for the 16-inch, this is one pricey laptop. But if you want the very best display quality it could be worth the premium. Anyone who works with photos and video on a daily basis I think will love this panel. I would say the touch interface is more of a bonus, and I'd like to see Apple offer it across the lineup just to give people more options. We'll have to see how well touch works with third-party apps, but Apple already promises support for Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Office, Adobe Lightroom and more.

All of this is wrapped up in a design that's only 3 pounds, which is less than the MacBook Pro with M6 at 3.4 pounds. I could easily see myself carrying this as my everyday laptop — if I had the budget.
Another design highlight is that Apple has brought back the glowing Apple logo, so everyone will know from across the room that you have the touchscreen Mac.
Powering the MacBook Pro with PROLED is the M5 Pro and M5 Max chip, which should offer swift performance for creative pros and coders.
And this new MacBook Pro will hopefully sound as good as it looks, thanks to a new woofer design with 50% more bass.
The port selection is robust, with three Thunderbolt 5 ports, HDMI, SDXC card, MagSafe and a headphone jack. And you get both Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support.

Starting at $2,899 for the 14-inch version and $3,399 for the 16-inch, this is one pricey laptop. But if you want the very best display quality it could be worth the premium. Anyone who works with photos and video on a daily basis I think will love this panel.
I would say the touch interface is more of a bonus, and I'd like to see Apple offer it across the lineup just to give people more options.
