sources.title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3 Diarization Open-Weight Speaker Model - Unite.AI
passages: NVIDIA on September 23, 2026 released Nemotron 3 Diarization, an open-weight speaker diarization model that identifies up to eight speakers in live or recorded audio, and Baseten announced same-day serving support with batch, streaming, and diarized-transcription presets that each run on one RTX PRO 6000 GPU.

Speaker diarization segments an audio stream by when each distinct speaker is talking, outputs timings for each voice, and assigns every span a consistent label; paired with transcription, it attributes transcribed words to the person who said them.

Nemotron 3 Diarization is available on Hugging Face under the repository nvidia/Nemotron-3-Diarization and in Baseten’s Model Library, with NeMo Framework v3.0 integration and support for NVIDIA Ampere, Ada Lovelace, Hopper, and Blackwell GPUs.

NVIDIA’s model card reports diarization error rate, speaker counting accuracy, and speaker counting mean absolute error against the diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1 baseline, with overlapping speech included and a zero-second collar on every benchmark except CALLHOME-Part2, which uses a 0.25-second collar.
The Batch Diarization preset is an HTTP endpoint for recorded audio that returns speaker turns with a per-request latency profile.

Streaming Diarized Transcription pairs the diarizer with NVIDIA’s Parakeet V2 speech recognition model, a 600-million-parameter system, and returns speaker-tagged words with timings, per-speaker partials, and overlap flags.
Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI , focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence.

His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind.

For streaming, the model uses the Arrival-Order Speaker Cache and FIFO queue introduced in NVIDIA’s Streaming Sortformer work: the cache retains speaker information from earlier chunks so the first voice heard keeps its label, while the queue provides recent frame context for each processing step.

extraction.body: NVIDIA on September 23, 2026 released Nemotron 3 Diarization, an open-weight speaker diarization model that identifies up to eight speakers in live or recorded audio, and Baseten announced same-day serving support with batch, streaming, and diarized-transcription presets that each run on one RTX PRO 6000 GPU. Speaker diarization segments an audio stream by when each distinct speaker is talking, outputs timings for each voice, and assigns every span a consistent label; paired with transcription, it attributes transcribed words to the person who said them. Baseten’s announcement describes Nemotron 3 Diarization as an open, end-to-end model that replaces the usual segmentation-plus-embedding pipeline and its tuning with a single pass, labeling speakers at a configurable interval as low as every 320 milliseconds. According to NVIDIA’s model card , the model is designed to determine “who spoke when” in real-world audio, supports both streaming and offline inference, and is ready for commercial or non-commercial use. It is a 100-million-parameter, 31-layer Transformer encoder with Rotary Positional Embeddings. Incoming 16 kHz single-channel audio is converted into 10-millisecond mel-spectrogram frames, downsampled by a factor of eight to an 80-millisecond encoder frame rate, and a Conv1D layer above the encoder upsamples predictions back to the 10-millisecond input resolution. The model outputs a tensor of per-speaker activity probabilities with shape T, 8, and its eight speaker channels are ordered by each speaker’s first arrival in the audio. For streaming, the model uses the Arrival-Order Speaker Cache and FIFO queue introduced in NVIDIA’s Streaming Sortformer work: the cache retains speaker information from earlier chunks so the first voice heard keeps its label, while the queue provides recent frame context for each processing step. The design requires no embeddings or clustering, and chunked inference places no fixed limit on audio duration. A single checkpoint serves four recommended latency configurations: 0.32, 0.64, and 1.04 seconds, plus an offline-style 30.4-second input buffer. The card defines this latency as input buffer latency — chunk length plus right context, multiplied by 80 milliseconds — and notes that the figure excludes computational processing time. The checkpoint can run with a buffer as low as 80 milliseconds, though 0.32 seconds is the lowest recommended configuration, and output frame resolution is configurable in multiples of 10 milliseconds. NVIDIA’s model card reports diarization error rate, speaker counting accuracy, and speaker counting mean absolute error against the diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1 baseline, with overlapping speech included and a zero-second collar on every benchmark except CALLHOME-Part2, which uses a 0.25-second collar. On DIHARD III, the card reports a full-set error rate of 12.73 at the 30.4-second profile and 13.55 at 0.32 seconds, versus 19.09 and 19.85 for the baseline. On NOTSOFAR1 single-channel recordings it reports 11.00 versus 30.49 at the offline profile; on AMI Test SDM, 11.14 versus 21.42; on AliMeeting Test Near, 6.40 versus 11.57; and on CALLHOME-Part2, 9.10 versus 10.32. The card states that its AMI, AliMeeting, and NOTSOFAR1 scores were computed with forced-alignment reference labels and that results scored against different reference annotations are not directly comparable. A speed table in the card reports real-time-factor speedup, defined as total audio duration divided by total processing time, of 1,340 in eager mode and 4,385 compiled at batch size one on the offline profile, measured on an RTX PRO 5000 at BF16 precision. At the 0.32-second profile, the corresponding figures are 12.5 and 54. Baseten ran its own evaluation, also scoring error rate with overlapping speech included and no collar. It reports a 9.8 percent error rate on AISHELL-4 at the low latency profile against 27.2 percent for Streaming Sortformer v2.1, and says that moving from the 30-second offline profile to the 0.32-second ultra-low profile raises the error rate by only one to two points. Baseten reports the model outperformed Meta Muse Voice Transcribe on every dataset it tested, at even the ultra-low configuration, and lost to pyannote community-1 only on AMI. The model card lists roughly 10,000 hours of real conversations (including Fisher English, the AMI and ICSI meeting corpora, VoxConverse, AISHELL-4, AliMeeting, the third DIHARD challenge, CALLHOME, NOTSOFAR1, the DISPLACE sets, licensed David AI recordings, and a pseudo-labeled YODAS-v2 subset) alongside 82,611 hours of multi-talker mixtures simulated with the FastMSS toolkit from about 28,000 hours of single-speaker recordings. Training initialized from a NEST self-supervised checkpoint and ran on eight nodes of eight A100-80GB GPUs in two stages: offline training on simulated data, followed by streaming fine-tuning on a combination of real and simulated audio. Use of the model is governed by the OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1. Baseten exposes the model through three presets, each running on one RTX PRO 6000 behind a CUDA-graph engine built around NVIDIA’s NeMo streaming loop, according to its Model Library listing , which also describes the model as the successor to Streaming Sortformer v2.1. The Batch Diarization preset is an HTTP endpoint for recorded audio that returns speaker turns with a per-request latency profile. Streaming Diarization is a WebSocket endpoint for live audio that carries speaker identity across a conversation without re-clustering. Streaming Diarized Transcription pairs the diarizer with NVIDIA’s Parakeet V2 speech recognition model, a 600-million-parameter system, and returns speaker-tagged words with timings, per-speaker partials, and overlap flags. Baseten says this preset feeds per-speaker activity vectors directly into Parakeet’s initial encoder layers so overlapped speech is transcribed in a single pass, with speaker labels final on arrival and committed words never revised. Baseten reports that one RTX PRO 6000 sustains more than 500 concurrent hour-long diarization streams at the 1.04-second profile, 200 streams at the 0.32-second profile, and 190 hour-long streams when transcription is added, while the batch preset processes 200 six-minute audio files per minute. Using identical files and hardware, Baseten reports that its optimized preset delivered roughly 1.35 times higher batch throughput than the NVIDIA reference setup it tested, under k6-generated load inside the cluster with a one-stream control on an idle replica. Baseten also says the model’s per-speaker activity signal, tracked in 10-millisecond increments, can drive voice activity detection, speaker-specific end-of-turn detection, and turn-taking and interruption handling, responding in roughly 300 milliseconds on ultra-low latency settings. Nemotron 3 Diarization is available on Hugging Face under the repository nvidia/Nemotron-3-Diarization and in Baseten’s Model Library, with NeMo Framework v3.0 integration and support for NVIDIA Ampere, Ada Lovelace, Hopper, and Blackwell GPUs. Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI , focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind. With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models. coreStoryFacts.text: SAN FRANCISCO, July 21, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )-- Deepgram today announced an initiative to bring enterprise-grade speech recognition directly onto PCs powered by Snapdragon® processors.

By optimizing Deepgram's Nova-3 speech-to-text model on the Qualcomm® Hexagon™ NPU in the Snapdragon X Series platform, Deepgram is enabling developers and device manufacturers to deliver real-time voice experiences with greater speed, privacy, and reliability, without relying on a cloud connection.
This effort opens the door to further integration of voice into a new generation of intelligent applications across automotive, mobile, AI PC, XR, industrial edge, IoT, and wearable devices.
"We recognize that voice AI technologies serve different needs.

That's why we value our work with Deepgram – because accuracy, latency, reliability, and scalability matter for developers building automotive systems, healthcare applications, industrial solutions, and other mission-critical experiences," said Upendra Kulkarni, Vice President Product Management, Qualcomm Technologies, Inc.
Deepgram's voice-native foundation models, accessed through cloud APIs or as self-hosted/on-premises APIs, deliver unmatched accuracy, low latency, and competitive pricing.
Having processed over 50,000 years of audio and transcribed over 1 trillion words, there is no organization in the world that understands voice better than Deepgram.

"The future of voice-first interaction is about meeting users wherever they are — in a vehicle, on a factory floor, inside an XR headset — without compromising on accuracy or responsiveness," said Abe Pursell, Vice President, Business Development and Partnerships, Deepgram.

We're bringing Deepgram Nova-3 directly to the ecosystem of PCs with Snapdragon, providing a foundation to build voice into products that work wherever people happen to be, regardless of network conditions."
It is the first voice AI model to offer real-time multilingual transcription.
Qualcomm, Hexagon and Snapdragon are trademarks or registered trademarks of Qualcomm Incorporated.

Still, the company promises Transcribe, at 30 billion parameters, can run on a single chip, from the Jetson AGX Thor robotics controller and DGX Spark chip powering new laptops , to Blackwell datacenter chips.
It joins Nvidia’s open-weight voice models, including the super small yet powerful Parakeet (1.1 billion parameters).
Nvidia on Wednesday released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe , a free, open-weight model that transcribes audio in up to 40 languages.
It also released version 2 of Granary, its open source speech dataset.
These tools target developers building apps for business meetings and medical transcription, two of AI’s most established footholds in the workplace.
Nvidia says developers can use the model, the updated Granary dataset, and tools like its NeMo Speech model to customize apps to recognize an industry’s jargon in each language.
One drawback: Transcribe works with recorded audio, not livestreams.

NVIDIA on September 23, 2026 released Nemotron 3 Diarization, an open-weight speaker diarization model that identifies up to eight speakers in live or recorded audio, and Baseten announced same-day serving support with batch, streaming, and diarized-transcription presets that each run on one RTX PRO 6000 GPU.

Speaker diarization segments an audio stream by when each distinct speaker is talking, outputs timings for each voice, and assigns every span a consistent label; paired with transcription, it attributes transcribed words to the person who said them.

Nemotron 3 Diarization is available on Hugging Face under the repository nvidia/Nemotron-3-Diarization and in Baseten’s Model Library, with NeMo Framework v3.0 integration and support for NVIDIA Ampere, Ada Lovelace, Hopper, and Blackwell GPUs.

NVIDIA’s model card reports diarization error rate, speaker counting accuracy, and speaker counting mean absolute error against the diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1 baseline, with overlapping speech included and a zero-second collar on every benchmark except CALLHOME-Part2, which uses a 0.25-second collar.
The Batch Diarization preset is an HTTP endpoint for recorded audio that returns speaker turns with a per-request latency profile.

Streaming Diarized Transcription pairs the diarizer with NVIDIA’s Parakeet V2 speech recognition model, a 600-million-parameter system, and returns speaker-tagged words with timings, per-speaker partials, and overlap flags.

extraction.body: Deepgram's Nova-3 speech-to-text model on PCs powered by Snapdragon ® delivers real-time voice experiences with greater speed, privacy, and reliability SAN FRANCISCO, July 21, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )-- Deepgram today announced an initiative to bring enterprise-grade speech recognition directly onto PCs powered by Snapdragon® processors. By optimizing Deepgram's Nova-3 speech-to-text model on the Qualcomm® Hexagon™ NPU in the Snapdragon X Series platform, Deepgram is enabling developers and device manufacturers to deliver real-time voice experiences with greater speed, privacy, and reliability, without relying on a cloud connection. This effort opens the door to further integration of voice into a new generation of intelligent applications across automotive, mobile, AI PC, XR, industrial edge, IoT, and wearable devices. Many voice AI solutions have historically relied on a cloud-based architecture. Before a response could be delivered, each interaction required audio to leave the device, travel to the cloud, be processed somewhere else, and then return. With this approach, delays and privacy concerns are sometimes introduced, which limit where voice AI can realistically be deployed. Deepgram is fundamentally changing that model, enabling speech recognition to happen directly on the device itself. The result is an entirely new world of applications and user experiences that feel like a natural conversation, whether it is running in a vehicle, on an AI PC, inside an XR headset, or at the edge of a network where connectivity cannot be guaranteed. "We recognize that voice AI technologies serve different needs. That's why we value our work with Deepgram – because accuracy, latency, reliability, and scalability matter for developers building automotive systems, healthcare applications, industrial solutions, and other mission-critical experiences," said Upendra Kulkarni, Vice President Product Management, Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. "The on-device AI capabilities of Snapdragon processors combined with Deepgram's enterprise-class voice AI uniquely bring those requirements together in a way that opens new possibilities for real-time voice experiences across the device ecosystem." "The future of voice-first interaction is about meeting users wherever they are — in a vehicle, on a factory floor, inside an XR headset — without compromising on accuracy or responsiveness," said Abe Pursell, Vice President, Business Development and Partnerships, Deepgram. "To make that possible, you need enterprise-grade speech recognition that can deliver within the constraints of a device. We're bringing Deepgram Nova-3 directly to the ecosystem of PCs with Snapdragon, providing a foundation to build voice into products that work wherever people happen to be, regardless of network conditions." Nova-3 advances Deepgram's industry-leading accuracy, extending its capabilities to a broader range of real-world enterprise use cases and challenging audio conditions. It is the first voice AI model to offer real-time multilingual transcription. Deepgram is also the first to provide users with demonstrably effective and highly accurate self-serve customization – enabling instant vocabulary adaptation without model retraining. Superior accuracy: Nova-3 leads transcription accuracy with a 6.89% word error rate on real-world production audio, a 24.7% lower error rate than the next-best competitor. Deepgram is the real-time AI infrastructure company underpinning the Voice AI economy. Today, more than 200,000 developers and 1,400 organizations are Powered by Deepgram . Its voice AI platform offers speech-to-text (STT), text-to-speech (TTS), and full speech-to-speech (STS) capabilities, all powered by its enterprise-grade runtime. Deepgram's voice-native foundation models, accessed through cloud APIs or as self-hosted/on-premises APIs, deliver unmatched accuracy, low latency, and competitive pricing. Customers include technology ISVs building voice products or platforms, co-sell partners working with large enterprises, and enterprises solving internal use cases. Having processed over 50,000 years of audio and transcribed over 1 trillion words, there is no organization in the world that understands voice better than Deepgram. sources.title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3 Diarization Open-Weight Speaker Model - Unite.AI
passages: NVIDIA on September 23, 2026 released Nemotron 3 Diarization, an open-weight speaker diarization model that identifies up to eight speakers in live or recorded audio, and Baseten announced same-day serving support with batch, streaming, and diarized-transcription presets that each run on one RTX PRO 6000 GPU.

Speaker diarization segments an audio stream by when each distinct speaker is talking, outputs timings for each voice, and assigns every span a consistent label; paired with transcription, it attributes transcribed words to the person who said them.

Nemotron 3 Diarization is available on Hugging Face under the repository nvidia/Nemotron-3-Diarization and in Baseten’s Model Library, with NeMo Framework v3.0 integration and support for NVIDIA Ampere, Ada Lovelace, Hopper, and Blackwell GPUs.

NVIDIA’s model card reports diarization error rate, speaker counting accuracy, and speaker counting mean absolute error against the diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1 baseline, with overlapping speech included and a zero-second collar on every benchmark except CALLHOME-Part2, which uses a 0.25-second collar.
The Batch Diarization preset is an HTTP endpoint for recorded audio that returns speaker turns with a per-request latency profile.

Streaming Diarized Transcription pairs the diarizer with NVIDIA’s Parakeet V2 speech recognition model, a 600-million-parameter system, and returns speaker-tagged words with timings, per-speaker partials, and overlap flags.
Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI , focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence.

His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind.

For streaming, the model uses the Arrival-Order Speaker Cache and FIFO queue introduced in NVIDIA’s Streaming Sortformer work: the cache retains speaker information from earlier chunks so the first voice heard keeps its label, while the queue provides recent frame context for each processing step.

extraction.body: NVIDIA on September 23, 2026 released Nemotron 3 Diarization, an open-weight speaker diarization model that identifies up to eight speakers in live or recorded audio, and Baseten announced same-day serving support with batch, streaming, and diarized-transcription presets that each run on one RTX PRO 6000 GPU. Speaker diarization segments an audio stream by when each distinct speaker is talking, outputs timings for each voice, and assigns every span a consistent label; paired with transcription, it attributes transcribed words to the person who said them. Baseten’s announcement describes Nemotron 3 Diarization as an open, end-to-end model that replaces the usual segmentation-plus-embedding pipeline and its tuning with a single pass, labeling speakers at a configurable interval as low as every 320 milliseconds. According to NVIDIA’s model card , the model is designed to determine “who spoke when” in real-world audio, supports both streaming and offline inference, and is ready for commercial or non-commercial use. It is a 100-million-parameter, 31-layer Transformer encoder with Rotary Positional Embeddings. Incoming 16 kHz single-channel audio is converted into 10-millisecond mel-spectrogram frames, downsampled by a factor of eight to an 80-millisecond encoder frame rate, and a Conv1D layer above the encoder upsamples predictions back to the 10-millisecond input resolution. The model outputs a tensor of per-speaker activity probabilities with shape T, 8, and its eight speaker channels are ordered by each speaker’s first arrival in the audio. For streaming, the model uses the Arrival-Order Speaker Cache and FIFO queue introduced in NVIDIA’s Streaming Sortformer work: the cache retains speaker information from earlier chunks so the first voice heard keeps its label, while the queue provides recent frame context for each processing step. The design requires no embeddings or clustering, and chunked inference places no fixed limit on audio duration. A single checkpoint serves four recommended latency configurations: 0.32, 0.64, and 1.04 seconds, plus an offline-style 30.4-second input buffer. The card defines this latency as input buffer latency — chunk length plus right context, multiplied by 80 milliseconds — and notes that the figure excludes computational processing time. The checkpoint can run with a buffer as low as 80 milliseconds, though 0.32 seconds is the lowest recommended configuration, and output frame resolution is configurable in multiples of 10 milliseconds. NVIDIA’s model card reports diarization error rate, speaker counting accuracy, and speaker counting mean absolute error against the diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1 baseline, with overlapping speech included and a zero-second collar on every benchmark except CALLHOME-Part2, which uses a 0.25-second collar. On DIHARD III, the card reports a full-set error rate of 12.73 at the 30.4-second profile and 13.55 at 0.32 seconds, versus 19.09 and 19.85 for the baseline. On NOTSOFAR1 single-channel recordings it reports 11.00 versus 30.49 at the offline profile; on AMI Test SDM, 11.14 versus 21.42; on AliMeeting Test Near, 6.40 versus 11.57; and on CALLHOME-Part2, 9.10 versus 10.32. The card states that its AMI, AliMeeting, and NOTSOFAR1 scores were computed with forced-alignment reference labels and that results scored against different reference annotations are not directly comparable. A speed table in the card reports real-time-factor speedup, defined as total audio duration divided by total processing time, of 1,340 in eager mode and 4,385 compiled at batch size one on the offline profile, measured on an RTX PRO 5000 at BF16 precision. At the 0.32-second profile, the corresponding figures are 12.5 and 54. Baseten ran its own evaluation, also scoring error rate with overlapping speech included and no collar. It reports a 9.8 percent error rate on AISHELL-4 at the low latency profile against 27.2 percent for Streaming Sortformer v2.1, and says that moving from the 30-second offline profile to the 0.32-second ultra-low profile raises the error rate by only one to two points. Baseten reports the model outperformed Meta Muse Voice Transcribe on every dataset it tested, at even the ultra-low configuration, and lost to pyannote community-1 only on AMI. The model card lists roughly 10,000 hours of real conversations (including Fisher English, the AMI and ICSI meeting corpora, VoxConverse, AISHELL-4, AliMeeting, the third DIHARD challenge, CALLHOME, NOTSOFAR1, the DISPLACE sets, licensed David AI recordings, and a pseudo-labeled YODAS-v2 subset) alongside 82,611 hours of multi-talker mixtures simulated with the FastMSS toolkit from about 28,000 hours of single-speaker recordings. Training initialized from a NEST self-supervised checkpoint and ran on eight nodes of eight A100-80GB GPUs in two stages: offline training on simulated data, followed by streaming fine-tuning on a combination of real and simulated audio. Use of the model is governed by the OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1. Baseten exposes the model through three presets, each running on one RTX PRO 6000 behind a CUDA-graph engine built around NVIDIA’s NeMo streaming loop, according to its Model Library listing , which also describes the model as the successor to Streaming Sortformer v2.1. The Batch Diarization preset is an HTTP endpoint for recorded audio that returns speaker turns with a per-request latency profile. Streaming Diarization is a WebSocket endpoint for live audio that carries speaker identity across a conversation without re-clustering. Streaming Diarized Transcription pairs the diarizer with NVIDIA’s Parakeet V2 speech recognition model, a 600-million-parameter system, and returns speaker-tagged words with timings, per-speaker partials, and overlap flags. Baseten says this preset feeds per-speaker activity vectors directly into Parakeet’s initial encoder layers so overlapped speech is transcribed in a single pass, with speaker labels final on arrival and committed words never revised. Baseten reports that one RTX PRO 6000 sustains more than 500 concurrent hour-long diarization streams at the 1.04-second profile, 200 streams at the 0.32-second profile, and 190 hour-long streams when transcription is added, while the batch preset processes 200 six-minute audio files per minute. Using identical files and hardware, Baseten reports that its optimized preset delivered roughly 1.35 times higher batch throughput than the NVIDIA reference setup it tested, under k6-generated load inside the cluster with a one-stream control on an idle replica. Baseten also says the model’s per-speaker activity signal, tracked in 10-millisecond increments, can drive voice activity detection, speaker-specific end-of-turn detection, and turn-taking and interruption handling, responding in roughly 300 milliseconds on ultra-low latency settings. Nemotron 3 Diarization is available on Hugging Face under the repository nvidia/Nemotron-3-Diarization and in Baseten’s Model Library, with NeMo Framework v3.0 integration and support for NVIDIA Ampere, Ada Lovelace, Hopper, and Blackwell GPUs. Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI , focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind. With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models. extraction.body: NVIDIA released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe on October 28, 2026. It is an open speech model that handles transcription, speaker attribution, translation and audio question answering in one set of weights. Coverage from SiliconANGLE, TechCrunch, AI Insider and Technology Org put the launch at the top of today’s AI news. The pitch is simple. Instead of chaining a speech recognizer, a diarization tool, a translation engine and a text model, a developer points one model at an audio file and tells it what to do in plain language. The reports describe a single model that covers 40 languages for transcription, 31 languages for translation to or from English, and speaker attribution in 13 languages. This piece sorts what the announcement confirms from what it leaves open. It also places the release next to NVIDIA’s earlier Nemotron 3.5 open models and the wider fight over open-weight AI. The Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe name matters here, because the “all-in-one adaptable” wording floating around headlines is not confirmed as official NVIDIA language. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The official product name found in the reporting is NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe. NVIDIA describes it as an open speech LLM built for intelligent transcription. In practice that means an open-weight model that listens to audio and produces text, but also reasons about what it heard. The “speech LLM” label is the key. Classic automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems turn sound into words and stop there. A speech LLM accepts audio as input to a language model, which lets it follow instructions. Ask it for a verbatim transcript and it keeps the stumbles and filler words. Ask for written form and it cleans the text up. Ask a question about the recording and it answers. Every figure below comes from the verified launch details. Anything the sources do not state, such as accuracy scores, parameter counts or licensing terms, stays out of the table on purpose. Read the three language counts together. Forty languages for plain transcription is the widest net. Translation narrows to 31 languages, and every one of those pairs touches English. Speaker attribution narrows again to 13. The model does more in some languages than in others, and buyers should plan around that gradient. The headline capability is consolidation. NVIDIA says one model covers four jobs that teams usually split across separate tools. Those jobs are transcription, speaker attribution, translation and question answering over audio. Transcription style is a real product decision. A court reporter wants every false start preserved. A podcast editor wants a clean paragraph. Most speech systems force that choice at build time through separate models or post-processing rules. According to the reports, Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe makes it a runtime instruction, so the same weights serve both audiences. Speaker attribution answers the question of who said what. The model identifies up to eight speakers in a recording and supports this in 13 languages. Word timestamps tie each word to a position in the audio, which makes it possible to jump from a transcript line straight to the sound, build subtitles, or search a long meeting. What a unified model does offer with certainty is fewer moving parts. One deployment, one set of weights to version, one failure surface to monitor. For small teams that alone can decide the build-versus-buy math. The language numbers deserve a slower read than the headline gives them. A claim of 40 languages tells you the model can transcribe in 40. It does not tell you the quality is equal across all of them, and the sources publish no per-language accuracy figures. Translation is anchored on English. The 31 languages are described as to or from English, so a Spanish-to-Japanese request would not be a listed direction. Teams that need direct pairs would have to route through English, which can compound errors, or test the model themselves. Speaker attribution is the narrowest at 13 languages. If your audio is Hindi, Swahili or Vietnamese, check the model card before you promise speaker labels to a customer. Transcription may work while attribution does not. Voice products in fast-growing markets feel this gap most. Our earlier look at India’s voice AI latency budget shows how tight real-time speech constraints get once multilingual audio enters the picture. The reports say the model handles recordings up to one hour and identifies up to eight speakers. Those are practical limits, and they map neatly onto real workloads. A board meeting, a lecture, a podcast episode or a customer call all fit inside an hour. A full-day deposition or a conference keynote with a long Q&A does not. None of this is a flaw, just a boundary. Stating the ceiling openly helps teams scope pilots honestly. A model that promises unlimited length usually hides its limits in quality drift. A model with a stated one-hour cap at least tells you where to look. The sources list no price for Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe. That is consistent with an open-weight release distributed through Hugging Face and ModelScope, where the model files are the product. A team running thousands of hours of audio a month can trade a recurring vendor invoice for GPU time it already owns. A team with a few hours of audio a month may still prefer a hosted API, since idle GPUs cost money too. Education and enterprise meetings. Lectures and team calls fit inside the one-hour cap. Searchable, speaker-labeled transcripts with translation help multilingual classrooms and global teams. NVIDIA enters a crowded field. OpenAI open-sourced Whisper in 2022, and that release made open-weight transcription a baseline expectation. Cloud providers sell managed speech APIs with transcription, diarization and translation as separate or bundled features. Specialist vendors compete on accuracy and latency. NVIDIA’s own earlier speech work, including its Parakeet and Canary model families, also shaped expectations before this launch. The new angle is bundling. A single open model that does all four jobs, at least on paper, targets the gap between those two options. The broader open-weight race adds pressure. Chinese labs have pushed hard on open releases, a trend we tracked in our DeepSeek, Qwen and Mistral comparison . NVIDIA’s decision to list the model on ModelScope as well as Hugging Face suggests it wants a seat in that ecosystem too. story.title: Voice AI in vogue: Nvidia releases new open transcription model

facts.text: SAN FRANCISCO, July 21, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )-- Deepgram today announced an initiative to bring enterprise-grade speech recognition directly onto PCs powered by Snapdragon® processors.

By optimizing Deepgram's Nova-3 speech-to-text model on the Qualcomm® Hexagon™ NPU in the Snapdragon X Series platform, Deepgram is enabling developers and device manufacturers to deliver real-time voice experiences with greater speed, privacy, and reliability, without relying on a cloud connection.
This effort opens the door to further integration of voice into a new generation of intelligent applications across automotive, mobile, AI PC, XR, industrial edge, IoT, and wearable devices.
"We recognize that voice AI technologies serve different needs.

That's why we value our work with Deepgram – because accuracy, latency, reliability, and scalability matter for developers building automotive systems, healthcare applications, industrial solutions, and other mission-critical experiences," said Upendra Kulkarni, Vice President Product Management, Qualcomm Technologies, Inc.
Deepgram's voice-native foundation models, accessed through cloud APIs or as self-hosted/on-premises APIs, deliver unmatched accuracy, low latency, and competitive pricing.
Having processed over 50,000 years of audio and transcribed over 1 trillion words, there is no organization in the world that understands voice better than Deepgram.

"The future of voice-first interaction is about meeting users wherever they are — in a vehicle, on a factory floor, inside an XR headset — without compromising on accuracy or responsiveness," said Abe Pursell, Vice President, Business Development and Partnerships, Deepgram.

We're bringing Deepgram Nova-3 directly to the ecosystem of PCs with Snapdragon, providing a foundation to build voice into products that work wherever people happen to be, regardless of network conditions."
It is the first voice AI model to offer real-time multilingual transcription.
Qualcomm, Hexagon and Snapdragon are trademarks or registered trademarks of Qualcomm Incorporated.

Still, the company promises Transcribe, at 30 billion parameters, can run on a single chip, from the Jetson AGX Thor robotics controller and DGX Spark chip powering new laptops , to Blackwell datacenter chips.
It joins Nvidia’s open-weight voice models, including the super small yet powerful Parakeet (1.1 billion parameters).
Nvidia on Wednesday released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe , a free, open-weight model that transcribes audio in up to 40 languages.
It also released version 2 of Granary, its open source speech dataset.
These tools target developers building apps for business meetings and medical transcription, two of AI’s most established footholds in the workplace.
Nvidia says developers can use the model, the updated Granary dataset, and tools like its NeMo Speech model to customize apps to recognize an industry’s jargon in each language.
One drawback: Transcribe works with recorded audio, not livestreams.

NVIDIA on September 23, 2026 released Nemotron 3 Diarization, an open-weight speaker diarization model that identifies up to eight speakers in live or recorded audio, and Baseten announced same-day serving support with batch, streaming, and diarized-transcription presets that each run on one RTX PRO 6000 GPU.

Speaker diarization segments an audio stream by when each distinct speaker is talking, outputs timings for each voice, and assigns every span a consistent label; paired with transcription, it attributes transcribed words to the person who said them.

NVIDIA’s model card reports diarization error rate, speaker counting accuracy, and speaker counting mean absolute error against the diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1 baseline, with overlapping speech included and a zero-second collar on every benchmark except CALLHOME-Part2, which uses a 0.25-second collar.
The Batch Diarization preset is an HTTP endpoint for recorded audio that returns speaker turns with a per-request latency profile.

Streaming Diarized Transcription pairs the diarizer with NVIDIA’s Parakeet V2 speech recognition model, a 600-million-parameter system, and returns speaker-tagged words with timings, per-speaker partials, and overlap flags.

Having processed over 50,000 years of audio and transcribed over 1 trillion words, there is no organization in the world that understands voice better than Deepgram.

"The future of voice-first interaction is about meeting users wherever they are — in a vehicle, on a factory floor, inside an XR headset — without compromising on accuracy or responsiveness," said Abe Pursell, Vice President, Business Development and Partnerships, Deepgram.

We're bringing Deepgram Nova-3 directly to the ecosystem of PCs with Snapdragon, providing a foundation to build voice into products that work wherever people happen to be, regardless of network conditions."
It is the first voice AI model to offer real-time multilingual transcription.

Still, the company promises Transcribe, at 30 billion parameters, can run on a single chip, from the Jetson AGX Thor robotics controller and DGX Spark chip powering new laptops , to Blackwell datacenter chips.
It joins Nvidia’s open-weight voice models, including the super small yet powerful Parakeet (1.1 billion parameters).
Nvidia on Wednesday released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe , a free, open-weight model that transcribes audio in up to 40 languages.
It also released version 2 of Granary, its open source speech dataset.
These tools target developers building apps for business meetings and medical transcription, two of AI’s most established footholds in the workplace.
Nvidia says developers can use the model, the updated Granary dataset, and tools like its NeMo Speech model to customize apps to recognize an industry’s jargon in each language.
One drawback: Transcribe works with recorded audio, not livestreams.

NVIDIA on September 23, 2026 released Nemotron 3 Diarization, an open-weight speaker diarization model that identifies up to eight speakers in live or recorded audio, and Baseten announced same-day serving support with batch, streaming, and diarized-transcription presets that each run on one RTX PRO 6000 GPU.

Speaker diarization segments an audio stream by when each distinct speaker is talking, outputs timings for each voice, and assigns every span a consistent label; paired with transcription, it attributes transcribed words to the person who said them.

NVIDIA’s model card reports diarization error rate, speaker counting accuracy, and speaker counting mean absolute error against the diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1 baseline, with overlapping speech included and a zero-second collar on every benchmark except CALLHOME-Part2, which uses a 0.25-second collar.
The Batch Diarization preset is an HTTP endpoint for recorded audio that returns speaker turns with a per-request latency profile.

Streaming Diarized Transcription pairs the diarizer with NVIDIA’s Parakeet V2 speech recognition model, a 600-million-parameter system, and returns speaker-tagged words with timings, per-speaker partials, and overlap flags.
Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI , focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence.

His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind.

NVIDIA released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe on October 28, 2026.
It is an open speech model that handles transcription, speaker attribution, translation and audio question answering in one set of weights.
Coverage from SiliconANGLE, TechCrunch, AI Insider and Technology Org put the launch at the top of today’s AI news.
Is “all-in-one adaptable” NVIDIA’s official description?
That wording is not confirmed as official NVIDIA language.
This piece sorts what the announcement confirms from what it leaves open.
The next shift joined speech to large language models.
Once a language model can ingest audio, it can follow instructions about that audio.
Transcription becomes one skill among several rather than the whole product.
NVIDIA has used it for a line of open models, and the 3.5 label ties this speech release to that family.
The sources do not describe how the speech model was trained or how it relates to its siblings, so that connection stays at the level of naming and timing.
Instead of chaining a speech recognizer, a diarization tool, a translation engine and a text model, a developer points one model at an audio file and tells it what to do in plain language.
Transcription style is a real product decision.
A court reporter wants every false start preserved.
Most speech systems force that choice at build time through separate models or post-processing rules.
That is consistent with an open-weight release distributed through Hugging Face and ModelScope, where the model files are the product.
The cited reports do not spell out the license, so check the model card for commercial-use terms before you build on it.
The language numbers deserve a slower read than the headline gives them.
A claim of 40 languages tells you the model can transcribe in 40.
It does not tell you the quality is equal across all of them, and the sources publish no per-language accuracy figures.
Reports list 40 languages for transcription, 31 languages for translation to or from English, and 13 languages for speaker attribution.
NVIDIA says one model covers four jobs that teams usually split across separate tools.
OpenAI open-sourced Whisper in 2022, and that release made open-weight transcription a baseline expectation.
NVIDIA packaged them into one open model and put it where developers already shop for weights.

extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro. DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.” Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security . He can be reached via encrypted message at zackwhittaker.1337 on Signal. You can also contact him by email, or to verify outreach, at [email protected] .

coreStoryFacts.text: This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit .
TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database.
The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff .
Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE.
A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.
We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected.
We will update the public when more information is available.”
The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access.
Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years.
One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media.

One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status .

The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest.
“They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen.
The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out.
Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch.
More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S.
Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry.

The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon.

Around 21,000 records pertain to CBP employees, and nearly 7,000 belong to staff at ICE.
This leak comes just weeks after hackers stole data from the FBI on its employees and job applicants.

The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database.
The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff .
Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE.
A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.
We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected.
We will update the public when more information is available.”
The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access.
Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years.
One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media.

One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status .

The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest.
“They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen.
The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out.
Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch.
More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S.
Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry.

The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon.
A hacker stole a trove of personal information from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
Around 21,000 records pertain to CBP employees, and nearly 7,000 belong to staff at ICE.
This leak comes just weeks after hackers stole data from the FBI on its employees and job applicants.
A hacker using the name "Department of Peace" stole personal information on about 40,000 employees of the U.S.
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and posted it online, TechCrunch reported on Oct.

Distributed Denial of Secrets hosted the leak in a database named Icepick and shared it through a website hosted by Distributed Denial of Secrets, and the BBC said the Wednesday leak marked the third time in recent weeks a government agency had been targeted by leaks or hacks.

TechCrunch reported that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, were members of a group called "Headspace_users," and it said Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund "mental health software required for ERO employees."

In addition, a newly designed hinge provides greater stability while using Touch, and advanced video stabilization automatically smooths the camera feed in real time while using Touch on a video call.
Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 provide fast, reliable wireless connectivity, and Touch ID enables a quick, easy, and secure login experience.

As with all Apple products, its paper packaging is 100 percent fiber-based 10 and designed to be recycled.
Both deliver phenomenal single- and multithreaded CPU performance, along with faster unified memory, giving users blazing speed for the most demanding workflows.

M5 Pro offers game-changing performance for scientists, engineers, software developers, and creative pros tackling intensive projects, accelerating everything from compiling code and running AI tasks to sequencing DNA and editing multiple streams of 8K ProRes video.

With M5 Max, pros can run LLMs with hundreds of billions of parameters entirely on device and accelerate intense workflows across detailed visual effects, 3D animation projects, film scores, and 8K video post-production.
