extraction.body: Apple announced its first touchscreen laptop on October 28, 2026, and the price tag landed as loudly as the feature. The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch, according to Ars Technica’s launch coverage . Both sizes use Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, and both go on sale November 6, 2026. For a company that spent more than a decade steering Mac owners toward the keyboard and trackpad, this is a real reversal. We tracked the build-up in our earlier look at the Pro and tell launch expectations , and the final product matches the broad outline. This analysis covers what Apple confirmed, what it left open, how the pricing compares with the rest of the market, and what the touchscreen MacBook Pro means for buyers, developers and rival laptop makers. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Apple calls the product the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, and coverage identifies it as the company’s first laptop with a touch-sensitive screen. It ships in two sizes, 14 inches and 16 inches. Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips power the lineup. The company showed the machines at its “Pro and tell” event, where John Ternus, identified in coverage as Apple’s CEO, unveiled the touchscreen MacBooks. The headline feature is simple to state. You can now touch the Mac’s screen and expect it to respond. The harder question is what that changes in daily use. Apple has not turned the MacBook Pro into a tablet. The hardware stays a clamshell laptop with a keyboard and trackpad, and the touch layer sits on top of the existing Mac experience. How deeply macOS adapts to fingers, and which apps get touch-native controls on day one, remain open points that the announcement coverage does not settle. The Verge published the reveal video for the touchscreen MacBook Pro , which gives the clearest first look at how Apple chose to present the change. CNN Business framed the news more bluntly, with a headline that called it Apple’s first-ever MacBook with a touchscreen. Reuters, Ars Technica and other outlets reached the same conclusion. The story is not that Apple copied a Windows feature. The story is that Apple moved at all. Three facts anchor everything else in this piece. First, the display technology is new to the MacBook Pro line. Second, the price floor sits well above where most people expect a laptop to start. Third, the on-sale date is only nine days away, so Apple has little time to let rumor fill the gaps. Those three facts shape the rest of the analysis below. The 14-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899. The 16-inch starts at $3,399. The gap between the two sizes is exactly $500, or roughly 17% on top of the smaller model’s base price. Apple has not published a wider configuration list in the material we verified, so those two numbers are the only prices we can state with confidence. BNN Bloomberg’s report on the first touchscreen laptops arriving amid a product blitz placed the launch inside a busy stretch for Apple, and that context matters for pricing. When a company launches several products in a short window, it usually prices the newest halo item high and lets cheaper models absorb the volume. A $2,899 entry point reads as a halo price, aimed at buyers who already pay for top-end Pro hardware. Pricing tells you who Apple expects to buy first. At these levels the customer is a working professional, a studio, or a company that buys machines in batches and writes them off. Casual users who want a touchscreen laptop for browsing and video calls have cheaper options on the Windows side. Apple appears comfortable ceding that segment for now. The panel is where the money goes. Apple’s reported specifications describe a tandem OLED display with up to 2,000 nits of brightness, a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. Tandem OLED stacks two emissive layers, which generally lets a panel reach higher brightness and last longer than a single-layer design. Apple has not, in the verified material, published lifetime or burn-in data for the new panel, so treat durability as an open question. Pairing a touch layer with OLED also creates engineering tradeoffs that Apple has not discussed in the verified coverage. Touch sensors, a protective surface and a glare-control finish all affect how a screen looks under bright light. Reviewers will test those tradeoffs once units reach them. Until then, the spec sheet tells you the ceiling and the review bench will tell you the reality. Apple chose its M5 Pro and M5 Max chips for the new machines. We have no verified CPU or GPU core counts, memory ceilings, storage ceilings or battery-life numbers, so this section sticks to what is solid. The pairing signals that Apple sees the touchscreen MacBook Pro as a premium creative and engineering tool rather than a general-purpose entry laptop. Chip choice also frames the competition. Our own Apple Silicon vs Intel MacBook Pro comparison looked at how the M5 Max stacks up against Intel’s top mobile part, and the memory bandwidth gap was a central point. Apple’s advantage in efficiency per watt has shaped laptop buying for several years. Adding a touchscreen does not change that equation, but it does raise the question of what the new panel costs in battery life, a number Apple has not confirmed. The wider architecture story is covered in our ARM vs x86 analysis . The short version is that Apple’s unified memory design and its controlled software stack let it tune hardware and macOS together. That control becomes more important with touch, because input latency depends on the screen, the sensor, the chip and the operating system acting as one pipeline. Windows laptop makers assemble that pipeline from parts supplied by many companies. Apple builds it in house. Coverage names John Ternus as the Apple executive who unveiled the touchscreen MacBooks, and identifies him as the company’s CEO. His role in the presentation carries weight. Putting the chief executive on stage for a hardware reversal this large sends a message about how much weight Apple places on the change. The event name, “Pro and tell,” also hints at the framing. The name points to a professional-first pitch. That fits the pricing and the chip selection, and it fits the way Apple has historically introduced new display technology on its highest-priced models before spreading it down the range. Past launches, from the first Retina MacBook Pro to the mini-LED displays, followed a similar path. Apple did experiment. In 2016 it added the Touch Bar, a thin touch strip above the keyboard on some MacBook Pro models, as a way to bring touch to the Mac without touching the main screen. The idea never became a staple of daily use for most owners, and Apple dropped it from the redesigned Pro line in 2021. The episode showed Apple was willing to try touch but unwilling to put it on the display itself. For years the iPad served as Apple’s answer to anyone who wanted touch with serious software. Add a keyboard case and the tablet behaves like a small laptop. That strategy kept the product lines distinct, with the Mac for desktop-class work and the iPad for touch. The new MacBook Pro blurs the line. Our coverage of the iPad mini’s move to OLED shows Apple pushing OLED across touch devices at the same time, which suggests a broader display strategy rather than a one-off experiment. CNN’s report on the first-ever MacBook with a touchscreen underlines how much the company’s position has shifted. Whatever Apple’s internal reasoning, the market pressure is plain. Buyers who use pen input, tablets and phones all day increasingly expect a screen to respond to a tap. Apple appears to have decided that holding out cost more than conceding. The gaps in the announcement are as useful to know as the specs. Several details that buyers will want before spending $2,899 or more are not in the verified record. We list them here so readers do not mistake rumor for fact. Battery life deserves special attention. OLED panels draw different power than LCD panels depending on what is on screen, and a touch layer adds its own overhead. Apple’s claims will matter, and independent testing will matter more. If you plan to buy on November 6, wait for reviews that run the same workload on the old and new models. Repair cost is another unknown. OLED screens cost more to replace than LCD panels, and a touch OLED sits in a more exposed position because people will now press on it. Our report on Apple replacing iPhone Duo inner displays covers a $999 fix, and while that product differs, it shows how steep a premium display repair can run. No verified source has yet given a screen repair price for the touchscreen MacBook Pro. Apple enters a market that has long offered touch. Windows makers from Lenovo to Dell to HP ship touchscreen laptops at nearly every price point, and many of them flip into tablet modes. Apple’s entry is narrower. It sells one family at the high end and does not offer a convertible hinge in the verified details. That makes the comparison less about features and more about philosophy. The table highlights Apple’s strategic bet. It does not compete on price. It competes on display quality, chip efficiency and software integration. If those advantages show up in testing, buyers who value them will accept the premium. If they do not, Windows rivals with lower prices and years of touch refinement will pitch themselves as the smarter value. TechCrunch’s write-up of Apple launching its new touchscreen MacBook Pro reported the release as a product launch, and the market read-through follows from that. Component suppliers that make OLED panels and touch sensors for large laptop screens gain a major volume customer if Apple scales production. Rival laptop makers lose one of their long-standing talking points, because a touchscreen no longer separates a Windows machine from a Mac. Retailers and resellers face a trickier picture. A $2,899 starting price narrows the pool of buyers compared with a mid-priced laptop. At the same time, higher average selling prices help Apple’s revenue per unit. Investors will watch the November 6 launch window and the following quarter for signs of whether premium Mac demand holds. We will track the broader hardware picture in our hardware coverage hub as sales data arrives. Three buyer types make sense for a first-wave purchase. The first is the creative professional who already pays for top Pro hardware and wants a better display for color-critical work. The second is the developer or designer who splits time between a Mac and an iPad and wants one device that covers both habits. The third is the business buyer upgrading a fleet and willing to pay for the newest panel. Everyone else has reasons to wait. First-generation hardware tends to carry quirks, and Apple has not shown battery-life, thermal or repair data. Waiting a few weeks for independent reviews costs little and could save a lot. If your current Mac works well, the touchscreen alone rarely justifies the jump. If you are choosing between sizes, the $500 step up to the 16-inch buys screen area, and you should weigh whether you carry the machine daily. A practical checklist helps. Confirm the configuration you need before launch day, because Apple has not published every option in the verified material. Check return terms in case touch feels awkward in your workflow. Apple calls the product the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, and coverage identifies it as the company’s first laptop with a touch-sensitive screen. It ships in two sizes, 14 inches and 16 inches. Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips power the lineup. The company showed the machines at its “Pro and tell” event, where John Ternus, identified in coverage as Apple’s CEO, unveiled the touchscreen MacBooks.

The headline feature is simple to state. You can now touch the Mac’s screen and expect it to respond. The harder question is what that changes in daily use. Apple has not turned the MacBook Pro into a tablet. The hardware stays a clamshell laptop with a keyboard and trackpad, and the touch layer sits on top of the existing Mac experience. How deeply macOS adapts to fingers, and which apps get touch-native controls on day one, remain open points that the announcement coverage does not settle.

The Verge published the reveal video for the touchscreen MacBook Pro , which gives the clearest first look at how Apple chose to present the change. CNN Business framed the news more bluntly, with a headline that called it Apple’s first-ever MacBook with a touchscreen. Reuters, Ars Technica and other outlets reached the same conclusion. The story is not that Apple copied a Windows feature. The story is that Apple moved at all.

Three facts anchor everything else in this piece. First, the display technology is new to the MacBook Pro line. Second, the price floor sits well above where most people expect a laptop to start. Third, the on-sale date is only nine days away, so Apple has little time to let rumor fill the gaps. Those three facts shape the rest of the analysis below.

The 14-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899. The 16-inch starts at $3,399. The gap between the two sizes is exactly $500, or roughly 17% on top of the smaller model’s base price. Apple has not published a wider configuration list in the material we verified, so those two numbers are the only prices we can state with confidence.

BNN Bloomberg’s report on the first touchscreen laptops arriving amid a product blitz placed the launch inside a busy stretch for Apple, and that context matters for pricing. When a company launches several products in a short window, it usually prices the newest halo item high and lets cheaper models absorb the volume. A $2,899 entry point reads as a halo price, aimed at buyers who already pay for top-end Pro hardware.

Pricing tells you who Apple expects to buy first. At these levels the customer is a working professional, a studio, or a company that buys machines in batches and writes them off. Casual users who want a touchscreen laptop for browsing and video calls have cheaper options on the Windows side. Apple appears comfortable ceding that segment for now.

The panel is where the money goes. Apple’s reported specifications describe a tandem OLED display with up to 2,000 nits of brightness, a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. Tandem OLED stacks two emissive layers, which generally lets a panel reach higher brightness and last longer than a single-layer design. Apple has not, in the verified material, published lifetime or burn-in data for the new panel, so treat durability as an open question.

Pairing a touch layer with OLED also creates engineering tradeoffs that Apple has not discussed in the verified coverage. Touch sensors, a protective surface and a glare-control finish all affect how a screen looks under bright light. Reviewers will test those tradeoffs once units reach them. Until then, the spec sheet tells you the ceiling and the review bench will tell you the reality.

Apple chose its M5 Pro and M5 Max chips for the new machines. We have no verified CPU or GPU core counts, memory ceilings, storage ceilings or battery-life numbers, so this section sticks to what is solid. The pairing signals that Apple sees the touchscreen MacBook Pro as a premium creative and engineering tool rather than a general-purpose entry laptop.

Chip choice also frames the competition. Our own Apple Silicon vs Intel MacBook Pro comparison looked at how the M5 Max stacks up against Intel’s top mobile part, and the memory bandwidth gap was a central point. Apple’s advantage in efficiency per watt has shaped laptop buying for several years. Adding a touchscreen does not change that equation, but it does raise the question of what the new panel costs in battery life, a number Apple has not confirmed.

The wider architecture story is covered in our ARM vs x86 analysis . The short version is that Apple’s unified memory design and its controlled software stack let it tune hardware and macOS together. That control becomes more important with touch, because input latency depends on the screen, the sensor, the chip and the operating system acting as one pipeline. Windows laptop makers assemble that pipeline from parts supplied by many companies. Apple builds it in house.

Coverage names John Ternus as the Apple executive who unveiled the touchscreen MacBooks, and identifies him as the company’s CEO. His role in the presentation carries weight. Putting the chief executive on stage for a hardware reversal this large sends a message about how much weight Apple places on the change.

The event name, “Pro and tell,” also hints at the framing. The name points to a professional-first pitch. That fits the pricing and the chip selection, and it fits the way Apple has historically introduced new display technology on its highest-priced models before spreading it down the range. Past launches, from the first Retina MacBook Pro to the mini-LED displays, followed a similar path.

Apple did experiment. In 2016 it added the Touch Bar, a thin touch strip above the keyboard on some MacBook Pro models, as a way to bring touch to the Mac without touching the main screen. The idea never became a staple of daily use for most owners, and Apple dropped it from the redesigned Pro line in 2021. The episode showed Apple was willing to try touch but unwilling to put it on the display itself.

For years the iPad served as Apple’s answer to anyone who wanted touch with serious software. Add a keyboard case and the tablet behaves like a small laptop. That strategy kept the product lines distinct, with the Mac for desktop-class work and the iPad for touch. The new MacBook Pro blurs the line. Our coverage of the iPad mini’s move to OLED shows Apple pushing OLED across touch devices at the same time, which suggests a broader display strategy rather than a one-off experiment.

CNN’s report on the first-ever MacBook with a touchscreen underlines how much the company’s position has shifted. Whatever Apple’s internal reasoning, the market pressure is plain. Buyers who use pen input, tablets and phones all day increasingly expect a screen to respond to a tap. Apple appears to have decided that holding out cost more than conceding.

Apple’s claims will matter, and independent testing will matter more. If you plan to buy on November 6, wait for reviews that run the same workload on the old and new models.

Repair cost is another unknown. OLED screens cost more to replace than LCD panels, and a touch OLED sits in a more exposed position because people will now press on it. Our report on Apple replacing iPhone Duo inner displays covers a $999 fix, and while that product differs, it shows how steep a premium display repair can run. No verified source has yet given a screen repair price for the touchscreen MacBook Pro.

Apple enters a market that has long offered touch. Windows makers from Lenovo to Dell to HP ship touchscreen laptops at nearly every price point, and many of them flip into tablet modes. Apple’s entry is narrower. It sells one family at the high end and does not offer a convertible hinge in the verified details. That makes the comparison less about features and more about philosophy.

The table highlights Apple’s strategic bet. It does not compete on price. It competes on display quality, chip efficiency and software integration. If those advantages show up in testing, buyers who value them will accept the premium. If they do not, Windows rivals with lower prices and years of touch refinement will pitch themselves as the smarter value.

Component suppliers that make OLED panels and touch sensors for large laptop screens gain a major volume customer if Apple scales production. Rival laptop makers lose one of their long-standing talking points, because a touchscreen no longer separates a Windows machine from a Mac.

Retailers and resellers face a trickier picture. A $2,899 starting price narrows the pool of buyers compared with a mid-priced laptop. At the same time, higher average selling prices help Apple’s revenue per unit. Investors will watch the November 6 launch window and the following quarter for signs of whether premium Mac demand holds. extraction.body: Apple once scoffed at the idea of a laptop with a touchscreen. But that all changed on Wednesday when the tech giant announced the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, its first laptop with a touch-sensitive display. For years, PC makers have been releasing touchscreen computers in an attempt to modernize laptops for the mobile era. Apple is late to the game, but is betting its touchscreen laptop will appeal to the MacBook Pro’s core audience of creative professionals and app developers. Today’s announcement marks the latest in a blitz of new Apple products to launch during John Ternus’ first two months as the company’s CEO. The touchscreen MacBook – along with other Apple firsts like the iPhone Duo and HomeView home hub – will test whether Apple can still develop hit products that anticipate users’ needs. Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook The new touchscreen MacBook Pro, which launches on November 6, will come in 14-inch and 16-inch versions and runs on Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips. The smaller model starts at $2,899, the bigger at $3,399. Apple is touting the touchscreen as being useful for dragging and dropping slides between presentations, allowing developers to directly test on their computers how their apps work. It also highlighted its usefulness for graphic designers and musicians, saying they’ll be able to draw sketches and play virtual instruments with just a touch of the screen. The company also claims many existing apps will work with the touchscreen right away because the software will register touches as clicks. The Dynamic Island, or the pill-shaped carveout topping iPhone screens with information and the front camera, will also be included on the new laptop. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display also includes additions aimed at creatives, like higher peak brightness than non-touch versions and Adobe’s RGB color space. The company says the touch sensor is built into the display itself rather than layered on top of it, which it claims will reduce latency when swiping and scrolling. Struggles of early touchscreen laptops Touchscreen laptops have existed for more than a decade. Microsoft made a major push to shift the industry in this direction with the release of Windows 8 in 2012. That software featured a new design with larger tile-shaped icons meant to resemble phones and tablets. The hardware also needed work; early touchscreen laptops were clunky, expensive and awkward to use as tablets. PC makers struggled to keep pace with the rise of smartphones and tablets. “Our competition is different, they’re confused,” Tim Cook, Apple’s then-CEO who is now executive chair of its board of directors, said during a 2013 event. He said rival laptop makers were trying to “make PCs into tablets and tablets into PCs. Who knows what they will do next?” Despite those early gripes, touchscreen laptops have improved over the years thanks to lower component costs, lighter designs and enhancements to Windows. Even Apple, which previously criticized hybrid computers, has been inching in its products in this direction for years. It overhauled the iPad’s software in 2019 with more productivity features, like the ability to use more than one app at once. Yet touchscreen devices only accounted for 16.3% of global laptop shipments in 2025, according to market research from the International Data Corporation. That’s largely because touchscreens aren’t popular with commercial buyers since most workers just plug their laptop into a monitor when they’re at their desk, according to Ryan Reith, group vice president for the IDC. Apple previously tried incorporating touch technology into the MacBook Pro in 2016 with the introduction of the Touch Bar, a touch-sensitive strip located above the keyboard for accessing app controls and other shortcuts. But it largely flopped with consumers because its utility didn’t justify the additional cost. Apple’s next era Apple is known for being late to technologies – usually for good reason. It wasn’t the first company to launch MP3 players, tablets or smartwatches, but it made those products popular with consumers by making its devices simpler and easier to use. The touchscreen MacBook Pro is the latest of several recent examples to follow this playbook. The company introduced its HomeView smart home hub earlier this month, attempting to challenge Amazon’s dominance in the smart home industry. And last week, Apple’s first foldable iPhone went on sale, debuting long after chief rival Samsung established a lead in that market. Apple has long faced pressure to come up with new blockbuster products, especially given Ternus’s background in hardware compared to Cook’s operations expertise. Wall Street will be watching for signs of how Apple’s new products are being received on the company’s earnings call next week, especially following reports of broken iPhone Duo screens. Still, some analysts think Apple’s new laptop will raise the bar for Windows rivals.

extraction.body: Apple once scoffed at the idea of a laptop with a touchscreen. But that all changed on Wednesday when the tech giant announced the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, its first laptop with a touch-sensitive display. For years, PC makers have been releasing touchscreen computers in an attempt to modernize laptops for the mobile era. Apple is late to the game, but is betting its touchscreen laptop will appeal to the MacBook Pro’s core audience of creative professionals and app developers. Today’s announcement marks the latest in a blitz of new Apple products to launch during John Ternus’ first two months as the company’s CEO. The touchscreen MacBook – along with other Apple firsts like the iPhone Duo and HomeView home hub – will test whether Apple can still develop hit products that anticipate users’ needs. Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook The new touchscreen MacBook Pro, which launches on November 6, will come in 14-inch and 16-inch versions and runs on Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips. The smaller model starts at $2,899, the bigger at $3,399. Apple is touting the touchscreen as being useful for dragging and dropping slides between presentations, allowing developers to directly test on their computers how their apps work. It also highlighted its usefulness for graphic designers and musicians, saying they’ll be able to draw sketches and play virtual instruments with just a touch of the screen. The company also claims many existing apps will work with the touchscreen right away because the software will register touches as clicks. The Dynamic Island, or the pill-shaped carveout topping iPhone screens with information and the front camera, will also be included on the new laptop. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display also includes additions aimed at creatives, like higher peak brightness than non-touch versions and Adobe’s RGB color space. The company says the touch sensor is built into the display itself rather than layered on top of it, which it claims will reduce latency when swiping and scrolling. Struggles of early touchscreen laptops Touchscreen laptops have existed for more than a decade. Microsoft made a major push to shift the industry in this direction with the release of Windows 8 in 2012. That software featured a new design with larger tile-shaped icons meant to resemble phones and tablets. The hardware also needed work; early touchscreen laptops were clunky, expensive and awkward to use as tablets. PC makers struggled to keep pace with the rise of smartphones and tablets. “Our competition is different, they’re confused,” Tim Cook, Apple’s then-CEO who is now executive chair of its board of directors, said during a 2013 event. He said rival laptop makers were trying to “make PCs into tablets and tablets into PCs. Who knows what they will do next?” Despite those early gripes, touchscreen laptops have improved over the years thanks to lower component costs, lighter designs and enhancements to Windows. Even Apple, which previously criticized hybrid computers, has been inching in its products in this direction for years. It overhauled the iPad’s software in 2019 with more productivity features, like the ability to use more than one app at once. Yet touchscreen devices only accounted for 16.3% of global laptop shipments in 2025, according to market research from the International Data Corporation. That’s largely because touchscreens aren’t popular with commercial buyers since most workers just plug their laptop into a monitor when they’re at their desk, according to Ryan Reith, group vice president for the IDC. Apple previously tried incorporating touch technology into the MacBook Pro in 2016 with the introduction of the Touch Bar, a touch-sensitive strip located above the keyboard for accessing app controls and other shortcuts. But it largely flopped with consumers because its utility didn’t justify the additional cost. Apple’s next era Apple is known for being late to technologies – usually for good reason. It wasn’t the first company to launch MP3 players, tablets or smartwatches, but it made those products popular with consumers by making its devices simpler and easier to use. The touchscreen MacBook Pro is the latest of several recent examples to follow this playbook. The company introduced its HomeView smart home hub earlier this month, attempting to challenge Amazon’s dominance in the smart home industry. And last week, Apple’s first foldable iPhone went on sale, debuting long after chief rival Samsung established a lead in that market. Apple has long faced pressure to come up with new blockbuster products, especially given Ternus’s background in hardware compared to Cook’s operations expertise. Wall Street will be watching for signs of how Apple’s new products are being received on the company’s earnings call next week, especially following reports of broken iPhone Duo screens. Still, some analysts think Apple’s new laptop will raise the bar for Windows rivals.

Today’s announcement marks the latest in a blitz of new Apple products to launch during John Ternus’ first two months as the company’s CEO.
The touchscreen MacBook – along with other Apple firsts like the iPhone Duo and HomeView home hub – will test whether Apple can still develop hit products that anticipate users’ needs.
Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook The new touchscreen MacBook Pro, which launches on November 6, will come in 14-inch and 16-inch versions and runs on Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips.
The smaller model starts at $2,899, the bigger at $3,399.
Apple is touting the touchscreen as being useful for dragging and dropping slides between presentations, allowing developers to directly test on their computers how their apps work.
It also highlighted its usefulness for graphic designers and musicians, saying they’ll be able to draw sketches and play virtual instruments with just a touch of the screen.
The company also claims many existing apps will work with the touchscreen right away because the software will register touches as clicks.
The Dynamic Island, or the pill-shaped carveout topping iPhone screens with information and the front camera, will also be included on the new laptop.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display also includes additions aimed at creatives, like higher peak brightness than non-touch versions and Adobe’s RGB color space.
The company says the touch sensor is built into the display itself rather than layered on top of it, which it claims will reduce latency when swiping and scrolling.
Struggles of early touchscreen laptops Touchscreen laptops have existed for more than a decade.
Microsoft made a major push to shift the industry in this direction with the release of Windows 8 in 2012.
That software featured a new design with larger tile-shaped icons meant to resemble phones and tablets.
The hardware also needed work; early touchscreen laptops were clunky, expensive and awkward to use as tablets.
PC makers struggled to keep pace with the rise of smartphones and tablets.
“Our competition is different, they’re confused,” Tim Cook, Apple’s then-CEO who is now executive chair of its board of directors, said during a 2013 event.
He said rival laptop makers were trying to “make PCs into tablets and tablets into PCs.
Who knows what they will do next?” Despite those early gripes, touchscreen laptops have improved over the years thanks to lower component costs, lighter designs and enhancements to Windows.
Even Apple, which previously criticized hybrid computers, has been inching in its products in this direction for years.
It overhauled the iPad’s software in 2019 with more productivity features, like the ability to use more than one app at once.
Yet touchscreen devices only accounted for 16.3% of global laptop shipments in 2025, according to market research from the International Data Corporation.

That’s largely because touchscreens aren’t popular with commercial buyers since most workers just plug their laptop into a monitor when they’re at their desk, according to Ryan Reith, group vice president for the IDC.

Apple previously tried incorporating touch technology into the MacBook Pro in 2016 with the introduction of the Touch Bar, a touch-sensitive strip located above the keyboard for accessing app controls and other shortcuts.
But it largely flopped with consumers because its utility didn’t justify the additional cost.
Apple’s next era Apple is known for being late to technologies – usually for good reason.
It wasn’t the first company to launch MP3 players, tablets or smartwatches, but it made those products popular with consumers by making its devices simpler and easier to use.
The touchscreen MacBook Pro is the latest of several recent examples to follow this playbook.
The company introduced its HomeView smart home hub earlier this month, attempting to challenge Amazon’s dominance in the smart home industry.
And last week, Apple’s first foldable iPhone went on sale, debuting long after chief rival Samsung established a lead in that market.
Apple has long faced pressure to come up with new blockbuster products, especially given Ternus’s background in hardware compared to Cook’s operations expertise.
Wall Street will be watching for signs of how Apple’s new products are being received on the company’s earnings call next week, especially following reports of broken iPhone Duo screens.
Still, some analysts think Apple’s new laptop will raise the bar for Windows rivals.

sources.title: Robinhood Shares Fall 8.7% as Q3 Revenue Miss and Crypto Trading Decline Weigh on Outlook - Yahoo Finance
passages: Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ:HOOD) shares declined 8.7% in pre-market trading on Wednesday after the online brokerage reported third-quarter 2026 revenue below analyst expectations, despite exceeding adjusted earnings forecasts.
A substantial decline in cryptocurrency trading revenue, higher operating expenses and management's comments about fourth-quarter trading spreads contributed to the market reaction.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Following the pre-market decline, Robinhood shares were indicated at approximately $86.31.
Robinhood reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.60, exceeding the consensus estimate of $0.55.
Robinhood reported cryptocurrency transaction revenue of $120 million, representing a decline of 55% compared with the same period last year.
Comments from Robinhood's management during the earnings conference call added to concerns about the company's near-term revenue outlook.
Cryptocurrency trading volume decreased 38% year over year, reducing the revenue generated from digital asset transactions.
The results indicated continued annual revenue growth, although the company faced weaker performance in certain trading activities and higher operating costs.
Robinhood also reported an increase in operating expenses that exceeded its rate of revenue growth.
The figures demonstrate the continued influence of cryptocurrency trading activity on Robinhood's financial results.

passages: Oct 28 (Reuters) - Robinhood's shares fell 8% in premarket trading on Wednesday after a prolonged chill in crypto markets dragged the trading platform's third-quarter profit below Wall Street expectations.

Crypto markets have been under pressure this year due to shifting expectations for US interest rates, outflows from bitcoin exchange-traded funds and bouts of risk aversion that have unsettled investors and sparked waves of selling.
• Robinhood's cryptocurrencies revenue fell 55% in the third quarter to $120 million
• Rising oil prices and geopolitical tensions have added to market jitters, while heightened volatility has prompted retail traders to pull back from speculative bets
• Robinhood's per-share quarterly profit declined 16% to 51 cents and missed Street expectations of 55 cents, according to estimates compiled by LSEG
• Bitcoin, the world's largest digital asset by market cap, has fallen nearly 28% over the past 3 months
• Despite the quarter's volatility, Wall Street analysts remain optimistic about Robinhood's long-term growth prospects
• "We see Robinhood's legacy brokerage business continuing to perform well in what we see as a near-perfect environment for retail traders," J.P. Morgan's Kenneth Worthington wrote in a note

• The company, once heavily reliant on market-sensitive transaction revenue and retail trader sentiment, has rapidly expanded its product offerings in recent years, broadening its business into a full-service financial services firm
• Its total net revenue increased 12% in the third quarter to $1.42 billion
(Reporting by Manya Saini in Bengaluru; Editing by Shinjini Ganguli)

Shares of the company fell 4.2% in ‌after-hours trading. The trading platform’s transaction-based revenue from cryptocurrencies fell 55% to $120 million from a year earlier. Crypto markets have come under pressure this year amid heightened volatility and persistent outflows, as inflationary pressures and higher interest ‌rates ​make bonds and other traditional investments ⁠more attractive than speculative ⁠assets. Bitcoin, the world’s largest cryptocurrency, has fallen as much as 8% year to date as geopolitical tensions and rising oil prices add to market uncertainty. Meanwhile, Middle East tensions rattled ​markets globally, prompting investors to buy, sell or rebalance positions more frequently. Robinhood’s overall transaction-based revenue rose about 19% to $867 ⁠million, driven by a more ⁠than sixfold increase in event-contracts revenue and a ​31% jump in options revenue. The company’s operating expenses rose 16% to $739 ​million, driven by higher credit-loss provisions, spending on ‌new businesses such as Trump Accounts and Rothera, and increased marketing. Robinhood CFO Shiv Verma said that prediction markets emerged as an important growth driver for the company. “Prediction markets is almost a $500-million-a-year ⁠business already, and so growing incredibly nicely, and it’s less than two years old because it came out at the start ⁠of the 2024 ‌election,” Verma told journalists over a call. He said ⁠both sports and non-sports event contracts were ​growing ‌strongly, with non-sports contracts accounting for a larger ​share of ⁠overall trading volume. The Menlo Park, California-based company reported a profit of 51 cents per share, below analysts’ expectations of a profit of 55 cents per share, according to estimates compiled by LSEG. (Reporting by Prakhar Srivastava and Rishab Shaju in Bengaluru; Editing ​by Diti Pujara)

coreStoryFacts.text: Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ:HOOD) shares declined 8.7% in pre-market trading on Wednesday after the online brokerage reported third-quarter 2026 revenue below analyst expectations, despite exceeding adjusted earnings forecasts.
A substantial decline in cryptocurrency trading revenue, higher operating expenses and management's comments about fourth-quarter trading spreads contributed to the market reaction.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Following the pre-market decline, Robinhood shares were indicated at approximately $86.31.
Robinhood reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.60, exceeding the consensus estimate of $0.55.
Robinhood reported cryptocurrency transaction revenue of $120 million, representing a decline of 55% compared with the same period last year.
Comments from Robinhood's management during the earnings conference call added to concerns about the company's near-term revenue outlook.
Cryptocurrency trading volume decreased 38% year over year, reducing the revenue generated from digital asset transactions.
The results indicated continued annual revenue growth, although the company faced weaker performance in certain trading activities and higher operating costs.
Robinhood also reported an increase in operating expenses that exceeded its rate of revenue growth.
The figures demonstrate the continued influence of cryptocurrency trading activity on Robinhood's financial results.

Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ:HOOD) shares declined 8.7% in pre-market trading on Wednesday after the online brokerage reported third-quarter 2026 revenue below analyst expectations, despite exceeding adjusted earnings forecasts. A substantial decline in cryptocurrency trading revenue, higher operating expenses and management's comments about fourth-quarter trading spreads contributed to the market reaction. The stock fell towards $86.31 from its previous closing price of $94.56, following the release of quarterly results the previous evening. Robinhood reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.60, exceeding the consensus estimate of $0.55. However, revenue of approximately $1.42 billion fell short of market expectations, while reported earnings under generally accepted accounting principles declined year over year. Robinhood's third-quarter results showed a difference between adjusted profitability and its reported financial performance. GAAP diluted earnings per share declined 16% from the corresponding quarter of 2025 to $0.51, also falling short of expectations. The results indicated continued annual revenue growth, although the company faced weaker performance in certain trading activities and higher operating costs. Investors focused on these pressures despite the adjusted earnings beat, contributing to the decline in the company's share price before the market opened. The cryptocurrency business was a significant source of weakness during the third quarter. Robinhood reported cryptocurrency transaction revenue of $120 million, representing a decline of 55% compared with the same period last year. Cryptocurrency trading volume decreased 38% year over year, reducing the revenue generated from digital asset transactions. The decline affected the company's overall financial performance, even as other trading categories recorded growth. Revenue from equities, options and event contracts increased during the period, providing some offset to the weaker cryptocurrency business. The figures demonstrate the continued influence of cryptocurrency trading activity on Robinhood's financial results. Comments from Robinhood's management during the earnings conference call added to concerns about the company's near-term revenue outlook. Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma indicated that trading spreads had narrowed at the beginning of the fourth quarter. The observation raised questions about the revenue Robinhood may generate from transaction activity during the final months of 2026. Narrower spreads can affect the amount of revenue earned from certain trading transactions, potentially reducing the company's effective take rate. The comments therefore added uncertainty to the outlook for transaction-based revenue following the third-quarter decline in cryptocurrency activity. Investors will monitor whether the tighter spreads persist and how they affect the company's financial performance during the fourth quarter. Robinhood also reported an increase in operating expenses that exceeded its rate of revenue growth. Operating costs rose 16% year over year, compared with a 12% increase in total revenue. Futures linked to the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average were little changed overnight, while Nasdaq futures recorded a modest increase. The difference between Robinhood's share price movement and the broader market suggested that the decline was primarily associated with the company's quarterly results and management commentary. The combination of weaker cryptocurrency revenue, higher expenses and uncertainty about trading spreads outweighed the positive adjusted earnings surprise. The Federal Reserve announcement will provide additional information about the interest rate environment heading into the final months of 2026. Following the pre-market decline, Robinhood shares were indicated at approximately $86.31. That level remained above the company's reported 52-week low of $63.52 but substantially below its 52-week high of $150.47. The latest movement followed a quarter in which the company reported higher overall revenue but weaker cryptocurrency trading activity and a decline in GAAP earnings per share. The share price reaction also reflected management's comments about tighter trading spreads at the start of the fourth quarter. The company's subsequent performance will depend partly on trading activity, transaction revenue and its ability to manage operating costs. Robinhood reported third-quarter adjusted earnings per share of $0.60, exceeding the $0.55 consensus estimate, while revenue of approximately $1.42 billion fell below market forecasts. Cryptocurrency transaction revenue declined 55% to $120 million, accompanied by a 38% reduction in trading volume. Operating expenses increased 16%, outpacing the company's 12% revenue growth, while GAAP diluted earnings per share fell 16% to $0.51. Management's indication of narrower trading spreads at the beginning of the fourth quarter added uncertainty to the near-term revenue outlook. The shares declined 8.7% in pre-market trading as investors assessed these developments alongside the upcoming Federal Reserve decision.

Crypto markets have been under pressure this year due to shifting expectations for US interest rates, outflows from bitcoin exchange-traded funds and bouts of risk aversion that have unsettled investors and sparked waves of selling. • Robinhood's cryptocurrencies revenue fell 55% in the third quarter to $120 million • Rising oil prices and geopolitical tensions have added to market jitters, while heightened volatility has prompted retail traders to pull back from speculative bets • Robinhood's per-share quarterly profit declined 16% to 51 cents and missed Street expectations of 55 cents, according to estimates compiled by LSEG • Bitcoin, the world's largest digital asset by market cap, has fallen nearly 28% over the past 3 months • Despite the quarter's volatility, Wall Street analysts remain optimistic about Robinhood's long-term growth prospects • "We see Robinhood's legacy brokerage business continuing to perform well in what we see as a near-perfect environment for retail traders," J.P. Morgan's Kenneth Worthington wrote in a note • The company, once heavily reliant on market-sensitive transaction revenue and retail trader sentiment, has rapidly expanded its product offerings in recent years, broadening its business into a full-service financial services firm • Its total net revenue increased 12% in the third quarter to $1.42 billion (Reporting by Manya Saini in Bengaluru; Editing by Shinjini Ganguli)
passages: Oct 28 (Reuters) - Robinhood's shares fell 8% in premarket trading on Wednesday after a prolonged chill in crypto markets dragged the trading platform's third-quarter profit below Wall Street expectations.

Crypto markets have been under pressure this year due to shifting expectations for US interest rates, outflows from bitcoin exchange-traded funds and bouts of risk aversion that have unsettled investors and sparked waves of selling.
• Robinhood's cryptocurrencies revenue fell 55% in the third quarter to $120 million
• Rising oil prices and geopolitical tensions have added to market jitters, while heightened volatility has prompted retail traders to pull back from speculative bets
• Robinhood's per-share quarterly profit declined 16% to 51 cents and missed Street expectations of 55 cents, according to estimates compiled by LSEG
• Bitcoin, the world's largest digital asset by market cap, has fallen nearly 28% over the past 3 months
• Despite the quarter's volatility, Wall Street analysts remain optimistic about Robinhood's long-term growth prospects
• "We see Robinhood's legacy brokerage business continuing to perform well in what we see as a near-perfect environment for retail traders," J.P. Morgan's Kenneth Worthington wrote in a note

• The company, once heavily reliant on market-sensitive transaction revenue and retail trader sentiment, has rapidly expanded its product offerings in recent years, broadening its business into a full-service financial services firm
• Its total net revenue increased 12% in the third quarter to $1.42 billion
(Reporting by Manya Saini in Bengaluru; Editing by Shinjini Ganguli)

Oct 27 (Reuters) – Robinhood Markets missed Wall Street estimates for third-quarter profit on Tuesday, as slower cryptocurrency trading and higher expenses offset strong activity in options ​and prediction markets. Shares of the company fell 4.2% in ‌after-hours trading. The trading platform’s transaction-based revenue from cryptocurrencies fell 55% to $120 million from a year earlier. Crypto markets have come under pressure this year amid heightened volatility and persistent outflows, as inflationary pressures and higher interest ‌rates ​make bonds and other traditional investments ⁠more attractive than speculative ⁠assets. Bitcoin, the world’s largest cryptocurrency, has fallen as much as 8% year to date as geopolitical tensions and rising oil prices add to market uncertainty. Meanwhile, Middle East tensions rattled ​markets globally, prompting investors to buy, sell or rebalance positions more frequently. Robinhood’s overall transaction-based revenue rose about 19% to $867 ⁠million, driven by a more ⁠than sixfold increase in event-contracts revenue and a ​31% jump in options revenue. The company’s operating expenses rose 16% to $739 ​million, driven by higher credit-loss provisions, spending on ‌new businesses such as Trump Accounts and Rothera, and increased marketing. Robinhood CFO Shiv Verma said that prediction markets emerged as an important growth driver for the company. “Prediction markets is almost a $500-million-a-year ⁠business already, and so growing incredibly nicely, and it’s less than two years old because it came out at the start ⁠of the 2024 ‌election,” Verma told journalists over a call. He said ⁠both sports and non-sports event contracts were ​growing ‌strongly, with non-sports contracts accounting for a larger ​share of ⁠overall trading volume. The Menlo Park, California-based company reported a profit of 51 cents per share, below analysts’ expectations of a profit of 55 cents per share, according to estimates compiled by LSEG. (Reporting by Prakhar Srivastava and Rishab Shaju in Bengaluru; Editing ​by Diti Pujara)

facts.text: Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ:HOOD) shares declined 8.7% in pre-market trading on Wednesday after the online brokerage reported third-quarter 2026 revenue below analyst expectations, despite exceeding adjusted earnings forecasts.
A substantial decline in cryptocurrency trading revenue, higher operating expenses and management's comments about fourth-quarter trading spreads contributed to the market reaction.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Following the pre-market decline, Robinhood shares were indicated at approximately $86.31.
Robinhood reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.60, exceeding the consensus estimate of $0.55.
Robinhood reported cryptocurrency transaction revenue of $120 million, representing a decline of 55% compared with the same period last year.
Comments from Robinhood's management during the earnings conference call added to concerns about the company's near-term revenue outlook.
Cryptocurrency trading volume decreased 38% year over year, reducing the revenue generated from digital asset transactions.
The results indicated continued annual revenue growth, although the company faced weaker performance in certain trading activities and higher operating costs.
Robinhood also reported an increase in operating expenses that exceeded its rate of revenue growth.
The figures demonstrate the continued influence of cryptocurrency trading activity on Robinhood's financial results.

extraction.body: Every week, the company has been introducing new devices and products. So here's a nifty roundup. Rather than hold a standard fall hardware event, Amazon has been announcing new products piecemeal over the last several weeks. It's a savvy move on the company's part to help keep its devices in consumers' minds instead of revealing a ton of stuff all at once that people may quickly forget about. Remember that microwave it once made? It seems the company's chief of Alexa and devices Panos Panay might agree. He recently told Engadget that "last year was a fine moment, but it turns out only two products really got any attention and everything else was just there." He also felt that the teams behind the overlooked products didn't get to take the pride that they, he felt, deserved. Well, we're here to help you keep up with all the things the company has announced in recent weeks. For a start, Amazon unveiled a new lineup of tablets that actually won't force you to resort to a workaround to access the Google Play Store . The latest batch of Kindles is here too, along with fresh Ring smart home gear and an updated Fire TV Stick 4K. Bee, a maker of AI note-taking devices, showed off its first new products since joining Amazon last year. Amazon has also teased that there are more Alexa-branded devices on the way . Here's a breakdown of the new devices Amazon announced so far in October. Amazon is transitioning away from Fire tablets to a new, more premium lineup of devices. Alexa tablets are now available in the US, Mexico, Canada, UK, Germany, France, Italy and Spain. They come in three sizes, the two smallest of which are primarily for entertainment purposes. The Alexa Tablet 8 (which starts at $230) has a 8.7-inch display, an 8-core CPU, 2-core GPU, 4GB of RAM and 64GB or 128GB of storage. It's 0.3 inches thick and weighs 16.4 ounces, so it's the most portable of the bunch. Amazon says it offers up to 14 hours of video playback and 19 hours of Kindle reading (more on that shortly) on a charge. Next up, we have the Alexa Tablet 11, which boasts a 2.5K, 11-inch display with a 90Hz refresh rate and a 16:10 cinematic aspect ratio. Along with an 8-core CPU and 2-core CPU, it has a fifth-gen MDLA NPU to support on-device AI processing. The tablet also has 8GB of RAM, the same storage options as its smaller sibling and dual Dolby Atmos speakers. The battery will deliver up to 15 hours of video playback, Amazon claims. This tablet starts at $330. Then there's the flagship model, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, which costs $500. Amazon says it's the most powerful model yet, with "three times faster processing and nine times faster graphics" than any of its previous tablets. The 12-inch, 280 PPI display has a 120Hz refresh rate and a 3:2 aspect ratio. The tablet has an 8-core CPU, 7-core GPU, 8th-gen MDLA NPU, 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage. Battery life tops out at 16 hours for video playback and 20 hours for Kindle usage, Amazon says. As with the Alexa Tablet 11, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro has a fingerprint sensor. There's an anti-glare option that's said to preserve detail and color accuracy. It's called Nanomatte and if you want that on your tablet, that'll run you $50 extra. The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is designed more for productivity. To that end, there are accessories such as the $90 Alexa Tablet Pro Pen and the $150 Alexa Tablet Pro Keyboard, which connects to the device magnetically. All of the tablets have Alexa+ baked in, of course. You can opt in to a feature that allows you to ask the assistant about whatever is displayed on your screen. Amazon designed the Kindle experience (the Kindle app is installed by default) to be distraction free with reduced blue light. The Nanomatte display is said to give ebooks a paper-like feel, and you can add notes to books using the Pro Pen. There are also Kids versions of the Alexa Tablet 8 and Alexa Tablet 11. Like the other Alexa tablets, these have an aluminum design but come with a "kid-proof case" to help protect them. These versions also come with one year of Amazon Kids+ access. As expected, Amazon has bid adieu to Fire OS . Alexa tablets run on Android 16 with a custom layer on top. As such, they offer direct access to the Google Play Store. As someone who had to jump through hoops to access apps outside of the limited selection that Amazon itself offered on Fire tablets, that's a very welcome change. Unfortunately, though, it appears that Alexa tablets do not have a microSD card slot you can use to expand the storage. Amazon has new dedicated reading devices as well . The latest standard Kindle starts at $150 and it costs an extra $20 to remove the lockscreen ads. The six-inch model is a millimeter thinner than the previous model at 6.8mm and it weighs five ounces. The screen is flush with the casing, which is available in a fetching purple called Ube as well as Graphite. Amazon says the new entry-level Kindle is 30 percent faster at opening books than the previous model and that it can run for six weeks on a charge. A variant with an aluminum casing and double the storage (32GB) will run you $190. This comes in Alpine Sky and Seaglass Green color options. The latest Kindle Paperwhite has a seven-inch display, 16GB of storage, an adjustable warm light and what Amazon says is the highest contrast ratio on any Paperwhite to date. It's thinner and lighter than the previous model too. It costs $200, or $220 if you don't want lockscreen ads. Then there's the latest Paperwhite Signature Edition, which costs $250 and has no lockscreen ads, an aluminum back, 32GB of storage, auto-adjusting light and the option to double tap to turn pages. While the standard Paperwhite is only available in Graphite (also an option here), you can snag a Signature Edition in Seaglass Green. As for the updated Kindle Colorsoft, that has improved clarity and edge-to-edge color on the seven-inch display, Amazon says. Again, it's thinner and lighter than the previous model and there are no ads. The standard model with 16GB of storage is $290. The Colorsoft Signature Edition has an aluminum design, a Fig color option, 32GB of storage, an auto-adjusting front light and a double-tap-to-turn-pages feature. That'll run you $320. Both Colorsoft variants run for up to eight weeks on a charge, according to Amazon. Kids versions of the ereaders are available too. They have kid-friendly covers and a year of access to Kids+. In addition, Ring has updated several of its cameras. The Outdoor Cam 4K Plus, Spotlight Cam 4K Plus, Floodlight Cam 4K Plus and Indoor Cam 4K support Retinal 4K video capture . A new Pan-Tilt Indoor Cam 2K can rotate 360 degrees and tilt 175 degrees to automatically follow anything it detects to be moving. OK, Amazon announced this one in September , but isn't September 30 basically October? The company claims the new Fire TV Stick 4K is zippier than previous models. It says the device "turns on faster, apps launch over 35 percent faster, and content starts playing nearly 20 percent faster" than its predecessor and suggests it's faster than an unnamed rival dongle as well as some 4K smart TVs at playing content. This $60 Fire TV Stick 4K (Amazon wisely ditched the Select and Plus variants for this gen) is slimmer than earlier models and it can run on power from your TV's USB port. It has a 4-core processor, 8GB of storage, Alexa+ support and Wi-Fi 6. The company also redesigned the Fire TV remote. Bee announced its first two AI note-taking devices since Amazon bought the startup last year. The $75 Bee Frontier (which replaced the company's Pioneer model) is a Fitbit-esque wearable that has an estimated seven-day battery life and a IP67 rating for dust and water resistance. You can press a button to record audio of a conversation, and you can receive transcripts and summaries. If you hold the button, you can ask the AI assistant a question or create a voice note for yourself. Amazon says that, on Bee devices, "audio is never stored, cannot be accessed or shared, and users are prompted to gain permission from call participants each time a recording is started." As for the Bee Eclipse, that's a rectangular device that attaches to your phone magnetically. It has three microphones and a battery that's said to run for up to 21 days on a charge. Otherwise, it has much the same functionality as the Frontier. The Eclipse will run you $100 but, unlike the Frontier (which you can buy now), you'll have to wait for it. That device is "coming soon."

Along with an 8-core CPU and 2-core CPU, it has a fifth-gen MDLA NPU to support on-device AI processing. The tablet also has 8GB of RAM, the same storage options as its smaller sibling and dual Dolby Atmos speakers. The battery will deliver up to 15 hours of video playback, Amazon claims. This tablet starts at $330. Then there's the flagship model, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, which costs $500. Amazon says it's the most powerful model yet, with "three times faster processing and nine times faster graphics" than any of its previous tablets. The 12-inch, 280 PPI display has a 120Hz refresh rate and a 3:2 aspect ratio. The tablet has an 8-core CPU, 7-core GPU, 8th-gen MDLA NPU, 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage. Battery life tops out at 16 hours for video playback and 20 hours for Kindle usage, Amazon says. As with the Alexa Tablet 11, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro has a fingerprint sensor. There's an anti-glare option that's said to preserve detail and color accuracy. It's called Nanomatte and if you want that on your tablet, that'll run you $50 extra. The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is designed more for productivity. To that end, there are accessories such as the $90 Alexa Tablet Pro Pen and the $150 Alexa Tablet Pro Keyboard, which connects to the device magnetically. All of the tablets have Alexa+ baked in, of course. You can opt in to a feature that allows you to ask the assistant about whatever is displayed on your screen. The latest standard Kindle starts at $150 and it costs an extra $20 to remove the lockscreen ads. The six-inch model is a millimeter thinner than the previous model at 6.8mm and it weighs five ounces. The screen is flush with the casing, which is available in a fetching purple called Ube as well as Graphite. Amazon says the new entry-level Kindle is 30 percent faster at opening books than the previous model and that it can run for six weeks on a charge. A variant with an aluminum casing and double the storage (32GB) will run you $190. This comes in Alpine Sky and Seaglass Green color options. The latest Kindle Paperwhite has a seven-inch display, 16GB of storage, an adjustable warm light and what Amazon says is the highest contrast ratio on any Paperwhite to date. It's thinner and lighter than the previous model too. It costs $200, or $220 if you don't want lockscreen ads. Then there's the latest Paperwhite Signature Edition, which costs $250 and has no lockscreen ads, an aluminum back, 32GB of storage, auto-adjusting light and the option to double tap to turn pages. While the standard Paperwhite is only available in Graphite (also an option here), you can snag a Signature Edition in Seaglass Green. As for the updated Kindle Colorsoft, that has improved clarity and edge-to-edge color on the seven-inch display, Amazon says. Again, it's thinner and lighter than the previous model and there are no ads. The standard model with 16GB of storage is $290. The Colorsoft Signature Edition has an aluminum design, a Fig color option, 32GB of storage, an auto-adjusting front light and a double-tap-to-turn-pages feature. That'll run you $320. Both Colorsoft variants run for up to eight weeks on a charge, according to Amazon. Kids versions of the ereaders are available too. They have kid-friendly covers and a year of access to Kids+. In addition, Ring has updated several of its cameras. The Outdoor Cam 4K Plus, Spotlight Cam 4K Plus, Floodlight Cam 4K Plus and Indoor Cam 4K support Retinal 4K video capture . A new Pan-Tilt Indoor Cam 2K can rotate 360 degrees and tilt 175 degrees to automatically follow anything it detects to be moving. OK, Amazon announced this one in September , but isn't September 30 basically October? The company claims the new Fire TV Stick 4K is zippier than previous models. It says the device "turns on faster, apps launch over 35 percent faster, and content starts playing nearly 20 percent faster" than its predecessor and suggests it's faster than an unnamed rival dongle as well as some 4K smart TVs at playing content. This $60 Fire TV Stick 4K (Amazon wisely ditched the Select and Plus variants for this gen) is slimmer than earlier models and it can run on power from your TV's USB port. It has a 4-core processor, 8GB of storage, Alexa+ support and Wi-Fi 6. The company also redesigned the Fire TV remote. Bee announced its first two AI note-taking devices since Amazon bought the startup last year. The $75 Bee Frontier (which replaced the company's Pioneer model) is a Fitbit-esque wearable that has an estimated seven-day battery life and a IP67 rating for dust and water resistance. You can press a button to record audio of a conversation, and you can receive transcripts and summaries. If you hold the button, you can ask the AI assistant a question or create a voice note for yourself. Amazon says that, on Bee devices, "audio is never stored, cannot be accessed or shared, and users are prompted to gain permission from call participants each time a recording is started." As for the Bee Eclipse, that's a rectangular device that attaches to your phone magnetically. It has three microphones and a battery that's said to run for up to 21 days on a charge. Otherwise, it has much the same functionality as the Frontier. The Eclipse will run you $100 but, unlike the Frontier (which you can buy now), you'll have to wait for it. That device is "coming soon."

sources.title: Amazon’s October Hardware Wave: New Alexa Tablets, Kindles, Ring Devices, Fire TV Stick and AI Wearables - Innovation Village
passages: With Alexa Tablets, revamped Kindles, upgraded Ring devices, refreshed Fire TV hardware and new AI-powered wearables already announced, Amazon’s fall product rollout is far from quiet.

The approach appears to align with the thinking of Panos Panay, Amazon’s head of Alexa and Devices, who recently suggested that large launch events often result in only a few products receiving meaningful attention while many others fade into the background.
Amazon also upgraded its streaming hardware lineup with a new Fire TV Stick 4K .
Amazon has also introduced children’s editions of the Alexa Tablet 8 and Alexa Tablet 11.

The broader theme running through every product launch is clear: Amazon is betting heavily on artificial intelligence, premium hardware experiences and deeper integration across its growing ecosystem of Alexa-powered devices.

extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro. DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.” Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security . He can be reached via encrypted message at zackwhittaker.1337 on Signal. You can also contact him by email, or to verify outreach, at [email protected] .

extraction.body: The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics, seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. The DHS and DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify, a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people.
