“They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out.

This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors.

The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections.

The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest.

TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff .
It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft.

A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.”
When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said.

While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE.

The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work.

Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software.

The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit.
A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023.

Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media.
A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment.

One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status .

The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon.

Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act.

“Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People.
“Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro.

DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.”
Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security .

extraction.body: A leak website was published Wednesday, showcasing internal data on more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors after it was obtained by hackers who claimed to have breached an identity service used by the agency. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and the hacker maia arson crimew got the data from a hacktivist outfit known as the Department of Peace. ”The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in [its] simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government’s hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation — along with key personnel in DHS’s ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs,” said Emma Best, founder of DDoSecrets. CyberScoop was able to verify numerous current Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency employees are listed in the data, along with some former leadership members who left the agency years ago. The data goes back years, with various group names listed in the database making reference to COVID-19 planning and internal summits in 2023. The hacktivists said the breach was a response to the promise of stepped-up operations from Immigrations and Customs Enforcement by DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. ”On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was ’turning up the heat.’ This is what happens to ICE when you do that,” said a spokesperson for the Department of Peace. The spokesperson said they obtained the database from an Okta single sign-on service used at DHS. Okta said it was aware of the report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” an Okta spokesperson said. DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment. ”This dataset is massive in terms of both size and impact,” said crimew, a Swiss hacker and journalist who has been indicted in the United States over past leaks and who created a search tool for the DHS data. “It provides an unprecedented look into the Department of Homeland Security’s organizational structure, highlighting which people do what work across multiple DHS agencies, including ICE.” One researcher said the leak could prove valuable for Freedom of Information Act requests. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People, said. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent.” DHS has suffered notable breaches before, dating back to a 2014 breach that may have exposed the data of 390,000 then-current and former Homeland Security Department employees, job applicants and contractors. In 2018, DHS notified nearly 250,000 people of a breach at the department. Earlier this year, Security firm GitGuardian said it discovered a public GitHub repository that exposed credentials for privileged AWS GovCloud accounts and internal CISA systems dating back to November 2025.

extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro. DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.” Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security . He can be reached via encrypted message at zackwhittaker.1337 on Signal. You can also contact him by email, or to verify outreach, at [email protected] .

extraction.body: A previously undisclosed intrusion at the Department of Homeland Security has exposed the names, job titles, work email addresses, cell phone numbers and office locations of more than 41,000 employees, with the stolen records now circulating publicly online. The dataset covers roughly one-fifth of the department's approximately 220,000-strong workforce, spanning border and immigration agents, cybersecurity personnel and senior officials. A hacker using the handle "Department of Peace" claimed to have pulled the material from an Okta single sign-on system that DHS uses to let employees and contractors across its component agencies reach its central network. According to TechCrunch, which reviewed the data, more than half of the records -- about 21,000 -- belong to employees of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the agency that staffs airports and other ports of entry. Another 10,000 or so are tied to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, while just under 1,000 relate to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). Remaining records cover headquarters staff and other offices, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. Timestamps on the individual records suggest the directory was extracted around mid-August. The material was reportedly passed to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who shared a copy with DDoSecrets, a nonprofit collective that publishes leaked datasets in the public interest. The group is hosting the release under the name "Icepick." "They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs," the hacker wrote in a note accompanying the data. The department did not respond to requests for comment, and it remains unclear whether the vulnerability that permitted the access has been closed or whether officials were aware of the theft before it surfaced. Okta said it had reviewed the matter and found no sign of compromise on its side. "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised," a spokesperson said. Beyond personal details, the files shed light on how DHS organizes access to its internal systems. The records list membership in Active Directory user groups that govern which tools employees may use, including Microsoft 365, Adobe Acrobat and Citrix, along with third-party services. Some of those groups point to surveillance and monitoring products. About 4,500 accounts, including ICE agents and deportation officers, sit in a group labeled "Headspace_users," a reference to the online therapy provider that held an $82,500 federal contract with ICE ending in 2023. A Headspace spokesperson said the company has not served DHS or ICE since then. Dozens of other groups reference Penlink, a web surveillance firm whose technology is marketed as able to track location data from hundreds of millions of mobile devices and to capture real-time intelligence from calls, texts, web activity and social media. The groups range from a handful of users in local field offices to more than 2,000 across HSI nationally. Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One group links more than 200 CBP users to Mobile Fortify, a facial recognition application used by both CBP and ICE to identify individuals and verify immigration status. Others are associated with ChatGPT access, including for senior officials, and with investigative work on the China-linked intrusion sets known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. The incident is the second involving DHS this year, following the same hacker's earlier claim to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and private-sector vendors, including defense contractors and surveillance suppliers. It also adds to a run of federal breaches, among them the theft of personnel records for thousands of FBI agents and the personal data of millions of serving and former military personnel held by the Pentagon's human resources unit. Transparency advocates argue the exposed directory could open new avenues for oversight, particularly through public records requests that depend on pinpointing individual government email addresses. "Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results," said Ryan Shapiro, executive director of the nonprofit Property of the People. DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best described the release as a "catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests." The disclosure lands at a politically charged moment. DHS has moved to shield the identities of CBP and ICE personnel conducting immigration enforcement operations across the country, and the publication of agent contact details could complicate those efforts. The department's enforcement record has become a central issue for voters ahead of the midterm elections. For the cybersecurity industry, the episode puts fresh scrutiny on identity providers that serve as the front door to sprawling government networks. Okta's denial of any compromise shifts attention to how DHS configured and governed its own tenant, and to whether access controls around third-party applications were adequately segmented. Vendors named in the leaked user groups -- among them Penlink and Headspace -- now face questions about how their government customers manage account provisioning, even where the underlying contracts have lapsed. Note: Figures are approximate and based on an analysis of the published dataset; totals exceed the sum of the listed categories because additional DHS offices are included. extraction.body: A leak website was published Wednesday, showcasing internal data on more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors after it was obtained by hackers who claimed to have breached an identity service used by the agency. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and the hacker maia arson crimew got the data from a hacktivist outfit known as the Department of Peace. ”The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in [its] simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government’s hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation — along with key personnel in DHS’s ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs,” said Emma Best, founder of DDoSecrets. CyberScoop was able to verify numerous current Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency employees are listed in the data, along with some former leadership members who left the agency years ago. The data goes back years, with various group names listed in the database making reference to COVID-19 planning and internal summits in 2023. The hacktivists said the breach was a response to the promise of stepped-up operations from Immigrations and Customs Enforcement by DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. ”On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was ’turning up the heat.’ This is what happens to ICE when you do that,” said a spokesperson for the Department of Peace. The spokesperson said they obtained the database from an Okta single sign-on service used at DHS. Okta said it was aware of the report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” an Okta spokesperson said. DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment. ”This dataset is massive in terms of both size and impact,” said crimew, a Swiss hacker and journalist who has been indicted in the United States over past leaks and who created a search tool for the DHS data. “It provides an unprecedented look into the Department of Homeland Security’s organizational structure, highlighting which people do what work across multiple DHS agencies, including ICE.” One researcher said the leak could prove valuable for Freedom of Information Act requests. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People, said. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent.” DHS has suffered notable breaches before, dating back to a 2014 breach that may have exposed the data of 390,000 then-current and former Homeland Security Department employees, job applicants and contractors. In 2018, DHS notified nearly 250,000 people of a breach at the department. Earlier this year, Security firm GitGuardian said it discovered a public GitHub repository that exposed credentials for privileged AWS GovCloud accounts and internal CISA systems dating back to November 2025.

Related Stories Logistics Canal Disruptions Fuel Record Cargo Influx at California Ports Logistics Long Beach Port Eyes Double-Digit September Growth as Peak Season Stretches On A watchmen strike could halt vessel, yard and gate operations at the affected terminals at both ports. “None of the employers’ proposals have been resolved, and significant differences remain,” according to a statement from the PMA, which is represented by 72 shipping lines, stevedore companies and marine terminal operators at ports in California, Oregon and Washington. “A timely agreement matters not only to the parties at the table, but to the entire Southern California supply chain and to the local, state and national economies that depend on it.” Local 26 represents maritime security personnel who handle gate security and cargo watch duties, work that puts a small group at the entry and exit points for containers moving through some of the largest terminals in the country. Eight terminals would be impacted—six container terminals and two non-container terminals—by the labor action. The container terminals are APM Terminals (Pier 400), Long Beach Container Terminal, Total Terminals International, SSA Marine’s Berth C60 and Berth A90 and Pacific Container Terminal. The non-container terminals are SSA Marine-operated: LB 206 and Outer Harbor Berth 55. The watchmen work under a separate agreement from the coastwide six-year longshore contract that was brokered between the ILWU and the PMA in summer 2023. The local union’s contract expired in July 2025, after which the members have worked under an extension while the two sides have met regularly for more than a year with help from federal mediators, the association says. In an Oct. 23 letter to other maritime unions, Local 26 president Luisa Gratz said negotiations had stalled since last year despite the federal mediation request, noting that “nothing of value has resulted from the union’s commitment to bargaining in good faith with our employers and PMA.” The association said every tentative agreement so far has been based on a union proposal, and it described a “strong” economic offer including “meaningful” wage increases and pension improvements. It said full-time watchmen earn an average of more than $170,000 a year, plus fully employer-paid health care and pension benefits, without providing a breakdown. The strike threat arrives while the complex is struggling to move rail-bound cargo inland, a pressure that predates any walkout and would compound if terminal gates and yards stop. According to a compilation of both ports’ daily rail reports from The Dwell, 34,592 import containers were awaiting on-dock rail service on Tuesday. The L.A. port accounted for 18,709 containers, 46.9 percent of which had waited nine days or longer. The Port of Long Beach accounted for 15,883 containers, with 21.7 percent having waited nine or more days. During a media briefing earlier this month, Port of Los Angeles executive director Gene Seroka said the rail dwell times are “something that we’re watching really closely.” The congestion has been brewing since the spring, with rail dwell time escalating every month since March, according to Pacific Merchant Shipping Association data. Average rail container dwell across the complex rose to 7.19 days in September from 6.75 days in August, while average dwell for containers leaving by local truck rose to 3.18 days from 2.95 days. In its October market update, C.H. Robinson identified Southern California intermodal railcar shortages as a constraint that was extending import dwell and slowing inland movement. Both ports handled record monthly volumes in September, with Los Angeles processing about 1.04 million 20-foot equivalent units (TEUs) and Long Beach handling 997,177 TEUs. The combined total of roughly 2.04 million TEUs has left the complex handling holiday cargo at a pace with little slack for a terminal stoppage at facilities handling more than half of its cargo. The terminal backlog has not been matched by a comparable offshore queue, since The Dwell’s congestion tracker reported one ship awaiting a berth during the week of Oct. 26, based on data from the U.S. Maritime Administration and the Marine Exchange of Southern California, a reminder the constraint is inland movement rather than vessels waiting to unload. extraction.body: Long Beach's most read source for local news, investigative reports, arts & culture, food, business, sports, and real-estate. The busiest year on record so far for the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach could run aground if bargaining between a small security workers union and shipping companies isn’t resolved. International Longshore and Warehouse Union’s Local 26, which represents about 250 watchmen who provide security at individual shipping terminals, has authorized a strike that could start at 5 p.m. Sunday. The union represents about 2% of ILWU’s workforce, but their work is spread across six terminals — split between Long Beach and Los Angeles — that handle more than half of the complex’s cargo, including 85% at the Long Beach seaport. If the strike is carried out, officials say thousands of other unionized dockworkers — the longshoremen, marine clerks and foremen — could honor the picket lines and not go to work. That would halt much of the work at the ports — which handle more than 31% of the nation’s containerized cargo — just as the heavy shipping season for holiday merchandise begins to gather steam. Negotiations have carried on since July 2025, after the contract expired between the union and Pacific Maritime Association, which represents the operators of all 12 terminals at the port complex. PMA said in a statement it has “put a strong economic package on the table,” that includes wage increases and pension improvements. But no deal has been struck and “significant differences remain.” “A timely agreement matters not only to the parties at the table, but to the entire Southern California supply chain and to the local, state and national economies that depend on it,” the statement read. “We urge Local 26 to work with us to reach an agreement that avoids a disruption at the nation’s two busiest ports.” A spokesperson for the union did not immediately respond to requests for comment or say when members voted to authorize the strike. In the meantime, the ports’ administrators said Wednesday they are closely watching negotiations and remain hopeful some resolution will come about ahead of the weekend. “Although the Port of Long Beach is not a party to the negotiations, we want to assure our customers that we remain committed to moving cargo through our port safely and reliably,” said Long Beach Port CEO Noel Hacegaba. Agreements for other unionized dockworkers expire in 2028. The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach are by far the nation’s largest container port complex, moving more than 20 million containers in 2025. That trade carried a value of more than $1.6 trillion last year. In Long Beach last month, the seaport saw a record 997,177 containers — 25% more than last September — in a jump that included 509,390, more than 31% higher than the same month last year. Hacegaba said that, “While the affected watchmen provide security within individual terminals, port-wide security provided by the Harbor Patrol and the Long Beach Police Department continues uninterrupted during negotiations.”

Eight terminals would be impacted—six container terminals and two non-container terminals—by the labor action. The container terminals are APM Terminals (Pier 400), Long Beach Container Terminal, Total Terminals International, SSA Marine’s Berth C60 and Berth A90 and Pacific Container Terminal. The non-container terminals are SSA Marine-operated: LB 206 and Outer Harbor Berth 55. The watchmen work under a separate agreement from the coastwide six-year longshore contract that was brokered between the ILWU and the PMA in summer 2023. The local union’s contract expired in July 2025, after which the members have worked under an extension while the two sides have met regularly for more than a year with help from federal mediators, the association says. In an Oct. 23 letter to other maritime unions, Local 26 president Luisa Gratz said negotiations had stalled since last year despite the federal mediation request, noting that “nothing of value has resulted from the union’s commitment to bargaining in good faith with our employers and PMA.” The association said every tentative agreement so far has been based on a union proposal, and it described a “strong” economic offer including “meaningful” wage increases and pension improvements. It said full-time watchmen earn an average of more than $170,000 a year, plus fully employer-paid health care and pension benefits, without providing a breakdown. The strike threat arrives while the complex is struggling to move rail-bound cargo inland, a pressure that predates any walkout and would compound if terminal gates and yards stop. According to a compilation of both ports’ daily rail reports from The Dwell, 34,592 import containers were awaiting on-dock rail service on Tuesday. The L.A. port accounted for 18,709 containers, 46.9 percent of which had waited nine days or longer. The Port of Long Beach accounted for 15,883 containers, with 21.7 percent having waited nine or more days. During a media briefing earlier this month, Port of Los Angeles executive director Gene Seroka said the rail dwell times are “something that we’re watching really closely.” The congestion has been brewing since the spring, with rail dwell time escalating every month since March, according to Pacific Merchant Shipping Association data. Average rail container dwell across the complex rose to 7.19 days in September from 6.75 days in August, while average dwell for containers leaving by local truck rose to 3.18 days from 2.95 days. In its October market update, C.H. Robinson identified Southern California intermodal railcar shortages as a constraint that was extending import dwell and slowing inland movement. Both ports handled record monthly volumes in September, with Los Angeles processing about 1.04 million 20-foot equivalent units (TEUs) and Long Beach handling 997,177 TEUs. The combined total of roughly 2.04 million TEUs has left the complex handling holiday cargo at a pace with little slack for a terminal stoppage at facilities handling more than half of its cargo. The terminal backlog has not been matched by a comparable offshore queue, since The Dwell’s congestion tracker reported one ship awaiting a berth during the week of Oct. 26, based on data from the U.S. Maritime Administration and the Marine Exchange of Southern California, a reminder the constraint is inland movement rather than vessels waiting to unload. sources.title: Google tells platforms to noindex link-shared pages by default - PPC Land
passages: Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist.
The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp.
Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes.
Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link.
Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached.

Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records.
Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths.
It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document.
That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content.

A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content.
The new section does not discuss the interaction.
Google's own products fall within the categories as well.
Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.
Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable.

What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results.
Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website.
Google names no products, companies or technologies.
The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page.
A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage.
It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index.
The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule.
Google does not say which services prompted the change.
PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language.
The change also concerns publishers, SEO teams and marketers who build on those platforms or compete with pages hosted on them.

Research by security firm RedAccess, reported in May 2026, found more than 5,000 apps built with vibe coding tools such as Lovable, Replit, Base44 and Netlify that had essentially no authentication, along with phishing sites impersonating Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe's and McDonald's on Lovable's domain .
RedAccess located the apps by searching Google and Bing for the platforms' default domains.
The UGC Fresh Data Program offers a contrast with today's change.

Within one month, then, Google has documented a faster route into its systems for moderated public discussion, and a default route out of its index for user-created pages that were never meant to be searched.
For platform operators, the monitoring additions carry a cost.

Verifying subdomains, watching Page Indexing reports for unexplained growth, and building internal alerts for concentrated URL creation by a handful of accounts all require engineering and moderation time.
The guide acknowledges this kind of trade-off elsewhere, noting that moderation "adds overhead" to daily workflows.
It does not quantify what Google expects of smaller services.
The "Monitor your service for abuse" list gained two items, both placed at the top.
The first asks operators to verify their site or subdomain in Search Console so that Google can email them if it issues a manual action against the site or detects security issues.

It also names two Search Console reports, Page Indexing and Search performance, to be checked regularly for "unexpected spikes in indexed pages, impressions, or queries" that do not match what the platform is for.
According to Search Engine Roundtable, consultant Marie Haynes asked on X whether the update means new manual actions are coming for AI tools and app-building platforms.

Another clue from Google about new types of spam they are dealing with (likely at a big enough scale to warrant changing their documentation) and ... another clue about what they'll be targeting in the future?"
The question of manual actions has been live for weeks.
The evidence was anecdotal, and Google did not comment.
That update was the fourth spam update of the year, following rollouts on March 24, June 24 and August 18 .

It still suggests applying a noindex robots meta tag to posts from new users who have no reputation on a platform, lifting it once they earn one, and adding a "nofollow or ugc rel attribute" to links in untrusted content.
Pages published on trusted platform domains can compete in results with original sites, and since May those same spam policies have applied to the AI answers that sit above the links.
Platforms that tighten indexing defaults reduce one source of that competition.
Those signals remain, now from third place down.
Will those platforms switch their indexing defaults?
The monitoring section still cites the site: search operator, Google Alerts, web server logs, the Google Safe Browsing API and language detection tools, including the Google Translate API v2.

extraction.body: Web app builders and generated-content tools now sit in the spam guide, next to new Search Console alerts. Will those platforms switch their indexing defaults? Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist. The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp. Google has a help page for websites that let the public post things, and today it said that tools where people make pages, apps or automatically generated content to share by link can be abused by spammers too. Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website. Google now says pages like that should be hidden from search by default, and that the companies running these tools should watch Search Console and their own numbers for sudden jumps in new public pages. The page is titled "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform." It sits in the "Preventing and monitoring abuse" part of Search Central's monitoring and debugging documentation, alongside guides on malware, phishing and deceptive sites, and the Google Safe Browsing Repeat Offenders Policy. Three passages are new or rewritten. Every other paragraph, from the reputation system for new accounts to an example about overnight traffic from Italian IP addresses on a site aimed at Japan, is unchanged word for word. The introduction previously warned that spammers exploit open comment forms, and that "hosting platforms may be similarly open to abuse," with spammers creating large numbers of sites that break Google's spam policies. The revised sentence reads: "Hosting platforms and tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps may be similarly open to abuse; spammers may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies and add little or no value to the web." Two edits sit inside that sentence. The first adds a category of service defined by what its users can publish - shared pages, generated content and web apps - rather than by whether it sells hosting. passages: The timing matters because the traffic data is already moving.

Over the past month I've watched websites with heavy concentrations of AI-generated content, the kind Ahrefs now flags as "Very high" on its AI Content Level metric, begin sliding in Google organic search.
This also lines up with the rollout of Google’s latest June 2026 spam update that recently finished rolling out.
But when declines cluster around a specific site profile right as Google publishes both an algorithm update and research on detecting that exact profile, it deserves attention.
Google's 2023 guidance rewards content for quality regardless of production method; enforcement targets scaled content abuse, meaning high-volume, low-value pages built mainly to manipulate rankings.
A content classifier scans for repetitive, templated narratives and for high-frequency publishing behavior that no human schedule produces.
An infrastructure component ties accounts back to a common source.
When enough accounts in a cluster show the same AI-generated templates, Google removes the whole cluster at once rather than penalizing individual pages.
Automation has been part of publishing for decades, from sports scores to weather forecasts.
The risk calculus for AI-heavy SEO & AEO has changed shape.
The question used to be whether a single page looked low quality.
The question now includes whether your templates, publishing cadence, infrastructure and content similarities make your operation resemble a coordinated spam network.
Gabe's read: Google will not let companies spam their way into AI search , and marketers should expect stronger automated systems plus manual actions.
Traditional quality filters evaluate one piece of content at a time.
Google's researchers acknowledge that generative AI broke that model.
Spammers can now produce endless variations of what the paper calls functionally identical content: every page technically unique, every page effectively the same.
At volume, that flood is built to swamp content-level filters.
SBERT has existed since 2019, and Montti points out the SEO industry has rarely discussed it as a spam-detection mechanism.
Its appearance in a Google paper about catching synthetic spam suggests it may have been put to that use only recently.
One more detail worth knowing: speed of adaptation.
The paper describes using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) to retune classifiers when spammers move to new generative models.
That means days of adjustment instead of months of retraining.
When the next model ships and spam operations migrate, Google can follow almost immediately.
The paper, covered by Roger Montti at Search Engine Journal and shared widely by Glenn Gabe on X , describes the Scalable Cluster Termination System.

Google has recently created an additional “Only index content meant for Search” section within the spam guide it updated on Oct. 26. The new section advises websites with pages made for direct sharing, collaboration or utility to set a noindex tag or use a robots.txt directive to block crawlers by default for those pages. According to Google’s changelog this is an addition relating to “blocking indexing of link-shared content.” The new section includes a link to the introductory page about robots.txt , and according to that introductory page the robots.txt file “is not a mechanism for keeping a web page out of Google.” Google’s new “Only index content meant for Search” section follows the guide’s advice on spotting spammy accounts and reads: “If your service lets users create shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools, consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or only accessed directly by people with a link.” “When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default.” The guide’s opening paragraph said hosting platforms “may be similarly open to abuse.” The updated sentence adds “tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps,” and says spammers may create a large number of “pages or sites” where it used to say sites. The previous version, last updated Dec. 10, 2025, already suggested noindex on posts from new users until they build a reputation on the platform. That advice is unchanged. Google’s robots.txt introduction says a page “that’s disallowed in robots.txt can still be indexed if linked to from other sites.” Google won’t crawl the blocked content in that case, but the URL and possibly the anchor text of links pointing to it can appear in results, without a description. Google’s page on noindex says the rule only works when robots.txt isn’t blocking the page, because otherwise “the crawler will never see the noindex rule.” Google’s “Control what you share” page , updated Oct. 21, lists robots.txt as applicable to “images and video” and noindex as applicable to “all content types.” On July 27, I confirmed that Claude’s share path was blocked by a “Disallow” directive in robots.txt. In addition, the share pages also returned a “none” value for the X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header. Google treats “none” as equal to both noindex and nofollow according to its documentation of robots meta tags . I have been unable to determine what Google saw when it initially found those links. The new spam guide from Google states you should be verifying your website or subdomain through Search Console for your platform to receive emails when it gets a manual action or has a security issue. It further suggests you check the Page Indexing report and Search performance report on an ongoing basis for “unexpected spikes” of indexed pages, impressions or queries which do not align with your platform’s intent. A new bullet under the guide’s monitoring advice suggests tracking creation and indexing at the platform level, with alerts for spikes in newly published public pages or “a small number of users generating a large share of indexable URLs.” Google’s changelog says its Oct. 26 update to the spam guide aims to help platforms “keep user-created pages that aren’t meant for Search out of the index and detect spam earlier.” For share links, generated outputs, and app pages, check that any noindex can reach Googlebot. A robots.txt rule that blocks Googlebot from those pages means Google never reads it. The Page Indexing report that Google’s new monitoring advice points to has a status called “Indexed, though blocked by robots.txt.” Google’s help for that status says to remove the block and use noindex. Share URLs that Google indexes despite a robots.txt block can appear under that status in Search Console. Follow on YouTube. Matt G. coreStoryFacts.text: Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist.
The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp.
Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes.
Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link.
Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached.

Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records.
Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths.
It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document.
That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content.

A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content.
The new section does not discuss the interaction.
Google's own products fall within the categories as well.
Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.
Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable.

What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results.
Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website.
Google names no products, companies or technologies.
The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page.
A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage.
It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index.
The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule.
Google does not say which services prompted the change.
PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language.

extraction.body: Web app builders and generated-content tools now sit in the spam guide, next to new Search Console alerts. Will those platforms switch their indexing defaults? Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist. The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp. Google has a help page for websites that let the public post things, and today it said that tools where people make pages, apps or automatically generated content to share by link can be abused by spammers too. Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website. Google now says pages like that should be hidden from search by default, and that the companies running these tools should watch Search Console and their own numbers for sudden jumps in new public pages. The page is titled "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform." It sits in the "Preventing and monitoring abuse" part of Search Central's monitoring and debugging documentation, alongside guides on malware, phishing and deceptive sites, and the Google Safe Browsing Repeat Offenders Policy. Three passages are new or rewritten. Every other paragraph, from the reputation system for new accounts to an example about overnight traffic from Italian IP addresses on a site aimed at Japan, is unchanged word for word. The introduction previously warned that spammers exploit open comment forms, and that "hosting platforms may be similarly open to abuse," with spammers creating large numbers of sites that break Google's spam policies. The revised sentence reads: "Hosting platforms and tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps may be similarly open to abuse; spammers may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies and add little or no value to the web." Two edits sit inside that sentence. The first adds a category of service defined by what its users can publish - shared pages, generated content and web apps - rather than by whether it sells hosting. The second changes the unit of abuse from "sites" to "pages or sites," which brings individual URLs, not just whole sites, within the scope of the warning. Google names no products, companies or technologies. The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page. The new section, "Only index content meant for Search," is placed after the advice on identifying spammy accounts and before the passage on manual approval. It runs to two short paragraphs. The first asks services whose users create "shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools" to consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or "only accessed directly by people with a link." "When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default." Everything turns on the final two words. The guide does not tell platforms to keep shared content out of Search permanently, nor does it describe what should happen when a user wants a shared page to be found. Exclusion is the starting position. How, or whether, a page later moves into the index is left unaddressed. The "Monitor your service for abuse" list gained two items, both placed at the top. The first asks operators to verify their site or subdomain in Search Console so that Google can email them if it issues a manual action against the site or detects security issues. It also names two Search Console reports, Page Indexing and Search performance, to be checked regularly for "unexpected spikes in indexed pages, impressions, or queries" that do not match what the platform is for. The reference to subdomains is specific. Many hosting and app-building services give each user project its own subdomain, and a subdomain can be verified as a separate Search Console property. Neither item comes with a threshold. Google does not say what size of spike warrants attention, or what share of indexable URLs counts as "large." In the previous version, the monitoring list opened with spam signals such as redirects, large numbers of ad sections, spammy keywords and large blocks of encoded JavaScript, and Search Console was not mentioned anywhere on the page. Those signals remain, now from third place down. The changelog entry is brief. Under "What," Google wrote that it "Updated the user-generated spam prevention guide with guidance on blocking indexing of link-shared content and monitoring abuse in Search Console." The "Why" line says the change was made "To help platforms keep user-created pages that aren't meant for Search out of the index and detect spam earlier." The phrase "link-shared content" appears in the changelog but not on the guide itself, which speaks of "shareable pages" and "direct sharing." The entry offers no figures on the scale of the abuse, no examples and no date for any related enforcement. It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document. The page remains a set of recommendations addressed to site and platform operators. The new section gives platforms two mechanisms, and they are not interchangeable. A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage. It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index. Google's John Mueller explained in September 2024 that pages blocked by robots.txt can still be indexed when other pages link to them, and that a crawler shut out by robots.txt never sees a noindex tag on the blocked page. The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule. That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content. A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content. The new section does not discuss the interaction. It also differs in emphasis from another Search Central page revised five days earlier: on October 21, Google's "Control what you share with Google Search" page listed robots.txt as a blocking method only for images and videos , not as a way to keep web pages out of results. The remainder of the guide predates today's revision. It still suggests applying a noindex robots meta tag to posts from new users who have no reputation on a platform, lifting it once they earn one, and adding a "nofollow or ugc rel attribute" to links in untrusted content. The concern is the use of a platform's domain to publish spam rather than ranking damage to the host: in January, Mueller said that spam links in blog comments have no effect on a host site's rankings . Other recommendations are untouched: a published abuse policy communicated at sign-up; records of signup patterns such as form completion time, request volumes from one IP address range, user agents and chosen user names; manual approval of suspicious interactions; IP blocklists and firewall deny lists, with Akismet named as an option for WordPress; and reCAPTCHA or similar verification at sign-up to keep automated scripts from generating large numbers of sites. The monitoring section still cites the site: search operator, Google Alerts, web server logs, the Google Safe Browsing API and language detection tools, including the Google Translate API v2. Google does not say which services prompted the change. PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language. Chat transcripts are one. When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached. Duck.ai's share pages instruct search engines not to index them in both the page markup and the server response, the two noindex methods that Google's new section lists, and they expire after 48 hours by default. Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records. Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths. App builders are another. Research by security firm RedAccess, reported in May 2026, found more than 5,000 apps built with vibe coding tools such as Lovable, Replit, Base44 and Netlify that had essentially no authentication, along with phishing sites impersonating Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe's and McDonald's on Lovable's domain . RedAccess located the apps by searching Google and Bing for the platforms' default domains. Google's own products fall within the categories as well. Opal, its no-code app builder, expanded from 15 to more than 160 countries in November 2025 , drawing criticism from independent publisher advocate Nate Hake, who argued that promoting mass-generated blog and marketing content conflicted with Google's own Search guidance. Playground, the game builder Google opened to US adults on October 7, 2026, lets creators share games by link or publish them to a public gallery . Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines. Search Engine Roundtable , which reported the change today, described the new section as a significant addition that tells platforms to distinguish between content intended for public discovery and content intended only for direct access. According to Search Engine Roundtable, consultant Marie Haynes asked on X whether the update means new manual actions are coming for AI tools and app-building platforms. SEO consultant Lily Ray wrote on X : "My first thought was Claude artifacts, ChatGPT pages/sites, FB posts, and other social/AI tools that make it easy to churn out indexable UGC at scale. Another clue from Google about new types of spam they are dealing with (likely at a big enough scale to warrant changing their documentation) and ... another clue about what they'll be targeting in the future?" Both readings remain speculation. Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable. What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results. The question of manual actions has been live for weeks. On October 7, Haynes reported a sharp rise in requests for help with manual actions, from essentially none to several a week, as Google's September 2026 spam update ran for 13 days and 16 hours before finishing on October 8. The evidence was anecdotal, and Google did not comment. That update was the fourth spam update of the year, following rollouts on March 24, June 24 and August 18 . The UGC Fresh Data Program offers a contrast with today's change. It gives approved forum and social platforms a dedicated pipeline to send new public posts and engagement signals to Google, on condition that they run active moderation and a user reporting mechanism, and that every post is tied to a creator with a public profile. Within one month, then, Google has documented a faster route into its systems for moderated public discussion, and a default route out of its index for user-created pages that were never meant to be searched. Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes. Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link. If platforms adopt noindex as the default for such pages, content created there will not enter Google's index unless the platform provides, and the user selects, a way to make it public. Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like. For publishers and SEO teams, the change concerns the supply side of search spam. Pages published on trusted platform domains can compete in results with original sites, and since May those same spam policies have applied to the AI answers that sit above the links. Platforms that tighten indexing defaults reduce one source of that competition. The guide's warning applies to every such service, whatever its current defaults. For platform operators, the monitoring additions carry a cost. Verifying subdomains, watching Page Indexing reports for unexplained growth, and building internal alerts for concentrated URL creation by a handful of accounts all require engineering and moderation time. The guide acknowledges this kind of trade-off elsewhere, noting that moderation "adds overhead" to daily workflows. It does not quantify what Google expects of smaller services. And it leaves a commercial tension unexamined: many platforms have grown in part through user pages that rank in Google, and the line between a page "meant for Search" and one made "for direct sharing" is drawn by the platform, not by Google.
